full_text:
Mansoor Delane of the Kansas City Chiefs breaks up a pass intended for Jahan Dotson. "We knew the challenge we had in front of us," Dotson said. "It's about execution." Kevin C. Cox / Getty Images
ATLANTA — The Kansas City Chiefs defense didn’t offer the Atlanta Falcons offense any surprises Sunday, Falcons wide receiver Jahan Dotson said Monday.
“We got some looks we were hunting, that we knew they were going to come out in early in the game,” Dotson said. “We got those looks, and we got the right plays called for it.”
That, somehow, makes Atlanta’s performance in a 35-13 loss worse. The Falcons started the game with four consecutive three-and-outs and didn’t score their first touchdown until midway through the fourth quarter.
“Credit to (Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo) and all he does, (but) we worked those things all week,” Dotson said. “We knew what we were going into. We knew the challenge we had in front of us. It’s about execution. We had a lot of plays we left out there on Sunday. They were there, but it’s for us to make. We were prepared. It’s just about going in and executing.”
Heading into their bye week, the Falcons (3-7) are averaging minus-.49 expected points added per drive, which ranks 26th in the NFL and is Atlanta’s third-worst mark of this century.
“You watch the tape, and it’s frustrating and disappointing,” coach Kevin Stefanski said. “Bottom line is yesterday we were not at our best, and we’re looking at all the areas we need to improve to put ourselves in position to win a game.”
It’s a lot of areas. Atlanta is 1-5 since Week 5, and in that stretch, it is 24th in the league in rushing offense (minus-.12 EPA per carry), 30th in third-down conversions (32.9 percent) and 27th in red zone efficiency (scoring touchdowns on 42.9 percent of their trips inside the 20-yard line).
Quarterback Michael Penix Jr., who led the Falcons to wins in weeks 3 and 4, is 27th in the league in EPA per dropback (minus-.13) and 28th in completion percentage (57.9) with eight passing touchdowns and six interceptions since Week 5.
“Confident in Mike, he’ll be better, like all of us will be,” Stefanski said immediately after the game.
The Falcons’ evaluation of Penix as their potential starter of the future is complicated by the team’s overall issues on offense.
“Anytime you are evaluating any player, you are taking everything into consideration, but bottom line is, all of us just have to be better,” Stefanski said Monday.
Stefanski does not plan to take play-calling duties away from offensive coordinator Tommy Rees, but he did indicate Atlanta will spend its bye week re-evaluating its approach.
“It’s very important that you pull everything apart in the bye week and look at it and get under the hood and find out areas that need our attention,” he said. “You do that every week, but with the amount of time you have, you can really put a fresh set of eyes on it. The truth is we have to do better in multiple areas, and the first part of that is identifying those areas.”
The first quarter is certainly one of them. Atlanta is averaging 2.2 points in the first quarter since Week 5 and has managed only 12 first downs or touchdowns, which ranks 29th in the league.
A change of mindset is one of the first things needed, Dotson said.
“It’s definitely a mentality, and it’s habits,” he said. “It’s what you do every day in practice. It doesn’t just happen on game day. It’s what you do every single day. If you are going to say you want to be (a good offense), then you have to be about it every day, and you have to create those habits.”
The Falcons still have a 14 percent chance to win the NFC South, according to The Athletic ’s playoff simulator . The Carolina Panthers (4-5) lead the division with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) and the New Orleans Saints (3-6) in second place. Atlanta has a win this season over New Orleans but has lost to Carolina and Tampa Bay. It will play each team in the division once more before the end of the regular season.
“I have never been in a situation where you are one game out of the division with that record, but we are,” Dotson said. “We have a perfect opportunity to come out of this bye week and make our mind up as to what we want to do as a football team. I think we have the guys in this locker room to make this thing right and finish this season strong and find ourselves in the postseason, but it’s all up to what we want to do.”
Penix said he is not worried the team will collapse further down the stretch.
“We have a lot of guys that care,” he said. “We have a lot of guys that love this game, a lot of guys that love winning. Obviously, we have not been on that path, so the guys want to fix that.”
Atlanta’s 69 penalties are the 13th most in the league. “We can’t beat ourselves,” Penix said. “No team is going to win putting ourselves in that situation. That’s what it is right now.” … Avieon Terrell’s place on the inactive list as a healthy scratch Sunday was “a numbers thing with special teams in mind,” Stefanski said. Terrell was Atlanta’s second-round pick. He has played 227 snaps this year, fourth among the team’s cornerbacks. … Penix was impressed by the debut of Atlanta’s new place kicker, Jake Moody, who made a 38-yard field goal and a 28-yard field goal Sunday. “He is kind of a quiet guy, but you can tell he means business. You can tell he’s got a different type of focus, very excited to have him,” Penix said.

full_text:
Zay Flowers' fumble with a little over two minutes left was another low in a season increasingly full of them for Baltimore. AP Photo / Stephanie Scarbrough
BALTIMORE — You can forget the idea of veteran quarterback Jacoby Brissett resurrecting the Baltimore Ravens’ season in time for Lamar Jackson to push the team over the finish line. That’s clearly a fantasy.
It’s time to dismiss the notion that the Ravens will be playing meaningful football in December. And beyond, too. It will be several weeks before the Ravens are officially eliminated from postseason contention, but the countdown has officially begun. The 2027 NFL Draft preparation might as well start, too.
If you are yearning for Jackson’s return to the field, that almost certainly will become an offseason pursuit. What good reason is there for Jackson to come back quickly from thumb surgery for a team that now appears destined to spend the last month-plus of the regular season playing out the string and jockeying for draft positioning?
Monday was supposed to represent a season reset and a resuscitation of the Ravens’ playoff hopes. All of the pieces were in place, too, the Ravens were at home and in primetime and the players and coaches said they were refreshed with 10 days between games. They had a competent and experienced quarterback leading the offense and the opposition was the winless Los Angeles Chargers.
Instead, everybody got a reminder of what should be painfully obvious by now. The Ravens are a bad football team with no business fancying themselves as playoff contenders. That should be put to rest for good after they were beaten at home, 23-20, by the Chargers in one of the more embarrassing losses in franchise history, featuring breakdowns in all three phases and total dominance by the visitors at the line of scrimmage.
For the third straight game, the Ravens never even had a lead. This time against a Chargers team that bumbled its way through the first half of the season, finding ways to lose at every turn. The Chargers weren’t great Monday, but the Ravens were worse.
“We have a two-game stretch before our bye to stay alive,” Ravens coach Jesse Minter said. “That’s really where it’s at, from a numbers standpoint, from a postseason standpoint.”
Minter, a first-year head coach who is being tested in a big way, has no choice but to maintain some level of optimism, but he can do the math and so can everybody else in a Ravens’ locker room that hit a new level of frustration.
Baltimore is now 4-6 and losers of five straight games. They are 2 ½ games out of the AFC’s final wild-card spot, currently held by the Cleveland Browns, with seven games to play. To make the playoffs, the Ravens may have to go 6-1, certainly no worse than 5-2, and even the latter may not be good enough.
It’s getting harder and harder to envision the Ravens winning another game, never mind five or six. It certainly doesn’t help that Baltimore lost two of its better players, right guard Vega Ioane (shoulder) and defensive lineman Nnamdi Madubuike (hamstring) heading into a short week before facing the Carolina Panthers on the road Sunday. The Ravens are having trouble matching up in the trenches as it is.
“The standard has been what it is around here since ‘96. Right now, we’re disgracing the standard as leaders, as players, as the team,” said safety Kyle Hamilton. “Whatever flak we get is warranted. I don’t necessarily care about it. I care about the locker room and what we need to do to win games, but we just got to do a better job of winning games. It’s simple.”
In the latest loss, the Ravens did what bad teams do. They had 15 more penalty yards than the Chargers and they lost the turnover battle, 2-0. Wide receiver Zay Flowers fumbled the ball away in Chargers’ territory with just over two minutes to go with the Ravens only one or two first downs away from having an opportunity to kick the game-tying field goal at the very least.
It was Flowers’ fifth career lost fumble; four have come in the fourth quarter. He left the locker room as reporters were allowed in, leaving others to answer for his latest fumble.
“It’s obviously a critical play,” Minter said. “Zay’s a playmaker. He’s been that way for us all year. He’s made some huge plays. You want the ball in his hands, but you also want to understand the situation, understand what they’re going to be trying to do. Know when the journey’s over and know when you’re fighting for extra yards.”
Flowers wasn’t the only one to err. Brissett played relatively well in his first start, especially when you consider that the Ravens couldn’t run the ball all night and the 33-year-old quarterback was under pressure throughout. However, his second-quarter interception came at a time where Baltimore was building momentum and led to a Chargers touchdown.
Rookie wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane, Brissett’s target on the final Hail Mary heave, also had a critical drop in the third quarter. What should have been a first-and-goal from inside the Chargers’ 5 turned instead into a Riley Patterson 36-yard field goal.
“It was obviously a frustrating loss, one that we thought that we should have had and just a tough way for this game to go,” said Brissett, who was 33-for-49 for 340 yards and the one interception. “But, I also saw the look in the guys’ eyes in that room, and obviously the urge to want to get it right, and obviously coach’s message in there to us was we have to get off the mat. That’s the truth.”
However, the biggest reason for the loss — and the biggest reason to doubt the Ravens’ legitimacy as playoff contenders — is they were again dominated at the line of scrimmage. On offense, they managed all of 16 rushing yards on 15 carries. On defense, they allowed 160 rushing yards on 34 carries with Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert gaining 51 of them, including a 22-yard touchdown run where he wasn’t touched.
“If you can’t stop the run in this league and can’t run the ball, it’s going to be hard to win,” Hamilton said. “That’s kind of what you get. And then when you don’t turn the ball over on defense, you’re going to lose. We can’t do that.”
At halftime, the Ravens were being outgained on the ground, 84-0. It was the worst rushing first half in the history of the franchise and things got only marginally better in the second half.
“It wasn’t working,” said a terse Derrick Henry, who did have two touchdowns. “We have to be better.”
Henry was asked later about the team’s sense of urgency. “How many have we lost in a row? OK, so the urgency should tell you right there,” he said. “I don’t mean to be rude, but you all are asking questions I think you all know the answer to.”
Defensively, veteran middle linebacker Roquan Smith pointed fingers at the entire group, including himself.
“Everyone wasn’t doing their job, play-in and play out,” he said. “We can all put a hand in it. We have to get better.”
"Right now we are disgracing the standard." 😳
Kyle Hamilton after the Ravens loss to the Chargers. pic.twitter.com/vglaf5x7do
— NFL Network (@nflnetwork) November 17, 2026
The last part of Smith’s quote has been a common refrain in recent weeks for the Ravens, who haven’t won a game since Oct. 11. Both Minter and Hamilton acknowledged later that they were tired of all the talk about getting better, responding to adversity and turning the season around.
“We keep talking about things,” Minter said. “(Need) more action.”
There won’t be a better opportunity presented to the Ravens to “reset” their season than Monday night. They squandered that, so what is left?
Seven weeks to lament what the Ravens offense could have looked like had Jackson stayed healthy. More than a month’s worth of football games that probably won’t carry notable ramifications for the Ravens. And plenty of time to fantasize about who the Ravens could add in the draft, which is five months away.
By late Monday evening, that’s what the season has officially come to for the 2026 Ravens. It’s impossible to foresee much…

title: NFL Week 11 power rankings: Bills, 49ers still on top, but Kirk Cousins' Vikings on rise Josh Kendall and Chad Graff 20
summary:

Every week during the season, Josh Kendall and Chad Graff rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.
The power rankings are getting ready for the NFL’s stretch run by picking a breakout player for each of the 32 teams.
Kirk Cousins and the Minnesota Vikings
full_text:
Kirk Cousins' return to Minnesota has the Vikings surging, while Drake Maye's injury has Patriots nation worried. Illustration: Will Tullos / The Athletic; Photos: Patrick McDermott / Getty Images and Lennart Preiss / Associated Press
Every week during the season, Josh Kendall and Chad Graff rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.
The power rankings are getting ready for the NFL’s stretch run by picking a breakout player for each of the 32 teams.
Kirk Cousins and the Minnesota Vikings are our big risers of the week as the top of this list continues to solidify around the elite teams.
Breakout player: Greg Rousseau
The sixth-year outside linebacker has been good for a long time. He’s trending toward great this year and has already tied his career high in sacks with eight, which ranks fourth in the league. Third-year wide receiver Keon Coleman is also on track for career highs in yards and catches. Despite just one reception for 11 yards (and one concussion check) on Sunday, Coleman has 24 catches for 315 yards.
Up nex t : vs. Dolphins, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Cowboys 46-40
Breakout player: Renardo Green
The third-year cornerback had a tough day on Sunday against George Pickens and company, but he was dealing with a back injury and had already built up plenty of goodwill this year. Green, a second-round pick in 2024, has four interceptions, three more than he had in his first two seasons combined. Rookie running back Kaelon Black has also been a surprise with 356 rushing yards behind Christian McCaffrey.
Up next: vs. Vikings, Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Jonah Coleman
The fourth-round rookie running back had 36 touches for 192 yards of offense in weeks 8 and 9. That ranked 17th in the league in that stretch. For the season, he’s averaging 9.8 yards per reception, and he could have a big day against a middling Raiders defense this weekend.
Up next: vs. Raiders, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Falcons 35-13
Breakout player: Emmett Johnson
With Kenneth Walker out Sunday, Johnson, a fifth-round rookie running back, had 22 carries for 101 yards against the Falcons, which was almost as much as he had in his first eight games combined. Johnson also has 20 catches this season for 307 yards. In general, it’s tough to pick a breakout player in Kansas City, where it feels like all the contributors have been around forever, but Johnson has been a meaningful addition.
Up next: vs. Cardinals, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Bhayshul Tuten
Jacksonville let Travis Etienne leave in free agency because the Jaguars thought Tuten was ready for a starting role. They were right. The second-year running back already has career highs in rushing yards (609), carries (148) and total touchdowns (eight). He’s 14th in the league in rushing.
Up next: at Giants, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Luther Burden
Ben Johnson was bullish about his second-year wide receiver in the preseason, and we’re seeing why. Burden is 16th in the league with 644 receiving yards, and 385 of those came in his last four games. From weeks 6 through 9, he had more receiving yards than all but five players in the league, and he got 23.5 percent of the Bears’ passing targets. That last number may go up as the season progresses.
Up next: vs. Saints, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Steelers 38-18
Breakout player: Boye Mafe
The Bengals gave the fifth-year pass rusher a three-year, $60 million free-agent deal in the offseason, and it’s proving to be a good move. Mafe had another sack Sunday night and has 6.5 for the season, plus 11 quarterback hits. At this pace, he’ll easily hit his career highs in both categories. He’s had at least one sack in five of his last six games.
Up next: at Commanders, Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Packers 30-10
Breakout player: Levi Drake Rodriguez
We’re going pretty far off the board here, but how often do you get to publicize a guy who played his college football at Southwestern Assemblies of God and East Texas A&M? A seventh-round pick in 2024, the former Prospect X has started every game for the Vikings this year and had two sacks Sunday to give him a career-high three for the season.
Up next: at 49ers, Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Patriots 35-10
Breakout player: Alim McNeill
The sixth-year defensive tackle already has a career high in sacks (6.5) and quarterback hits (11), and the Lions are going to need him more than ever with Aidan Hutchinson out due to injury. Detroit proved again Sunday that its offense is Super Bowl-worthy, but the defense is 28th in the league in defensive EPA (minus-5.2 per 100 snaps).
Up next: vs. Buccaneers, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Raiders 21-13
Breakout player: Drew Lock
The Seahawks’ backup quarterback started his third game Sunday in place of the injured Sam Darnold. Seattle has won all three of those games. Among quarterbacks with more than 50 attempts this season, Lock is third in the league in EPA per dropback (0.32). He has seven passing touchdowns and no interceptions, and that last number has some Seahawks fans wondering if he’s a better option than the turnover-prone Darnold.
Sunday: Beat Cardinals 34-6
Breakout player: Quentin Lake
In his fifth year, the cornerback has already tripled the career interception total he had entering the season, with three. He has also forced two fumbles and has 65 tackles. Lake also has what may be the quote of the year this season, saying on “ The St. Brown Podcast ” that Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert “was throwing deli meat out there.”
Sunday: Lost to Vikings 30-10
Breakout player: Christian Watson
The ambulance clip alone gives Watson the nod here, but the fifth-year wide receiver is having a career year on top of that. Watson is third in the league in receiving yards (916) and tied for third in receiving touchdowns (seven). Watson had not topped 620 receiving yards in any of his previous four seasons.
Sunday: Lost to Bengals 38-18
Breakout player: Jaylen Warren
The fifth-year running back was disappointing Sunday night, but so were all of the other Steelers. For the season, Warren has been great. He has 126 carries for 719 yards and leads all running backs with 5.7 yards per carry. He’s second in the league in yards per carry after contact (4.04).
Up next: at Eagles, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Harold Fannin Jr.
It’s not exactly a breakout year for the Browns’ second-year tight end because he was excellent as a rookie and has been great again in Year 2. He had seven catches for 91 yards on Sunday, and now has 19 for 287 yards in the last three games. Fannin has 44 catches for 544 yards and four touchdowns on the season.
Sunday: Lost to Lions 35-10
Breakout player: Elijah Ponder
The second-year edge rusher had four sacks last year as an undrafted free-agent rookie. This year, he has 7.5, and he had another five tackles against the Lions on Sunday. Wide receiver Mack Hollins, who is on his sixth team in his ninth professional year, is also having a career year with 48.8 receiving yards per game.
Thursday: Lost to Commanders 24-21
Breakout player: Isaiah Likely
Brock Bowers and Trey McBride are the only tight ends in the league with more receiving yards than Likely, who has 575 this year. After following John Harbaugh from Baltimore and getting out of Mark Andrews’ shadow, Likely already has career highs in yards, catches (55) and touchdowns (seven). He had nine catches for a career-high 127 yards against Washington.
Up next: vs. Jaguars, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Zyon McCollum
The fifth-year cornerback has a career-high four interceptions, which is one more than he had in his first four seasons combined. McCollum also has a fumble recovery and 28 solo tackles for a talented defense that makes the Buccaneers the favorites in the NFC South.
Up next: at Lions, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Chuba Hubbard

title: Panthers on pace to set pair of dubious NFL records: Can they cut down their penalties? Carolina set team records with 17 penalties for 152 yards vs. the Saints and has three games with at least 13 penalties this season. Joseph Person 2
summary:

CHARLOTTE, N.C. — David Tepper didn’t love the message posted outside of Dilworth Neighborhood Grille the first night of the NFL draft two years ago. But the sports bar a mile from Bank of America Stadium often accurately captures the day-after mood of Carolina Panthers fans on its aging sign during the season.
A day after flags flew at a record pace for the Panthers at the Caesars
full_text:
Panthers coach Dave Canales saw his team get penalized 17 times Sunday against the Saints. Wes Hale / Getty Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — David Tepper didn’t love the message posted outside of Dilworth Neighborhood Grille the first night of the NFL draft two years ago. But the sports bar a mile from Bank of America Stadium often accurately captures the day-after mood of Carolina Panthers fans on its aging sign during the season.
A day after flags flew at a record pace for the Panthers at the Caesars Superdome, Charlotte commuters on Monday were greeted with this musing from the restaurant’s owner: “20 POINTS, 17 PENALTIES EQUALS FIRST PLACE.”
Carolina survived 17 penalties for 152 yards — both single-game, franchise highs — to beat the New Orleans Saints 20-17 on Sunday and grab sole possession of first in the NFC South. The Panthers became just the 13th team in NFL history to win on the road when called for 17 penalties or more.
Also notable: Carolina won despite a staggering 17-to-3 disparity in accepted penalties.
“I feel like if we’d played a cleaner game as far as penalties, it wouldn’t have even been close,” outside linebacker Princely Umanmielen said.
Mindful of potential fines, Panthers players and coach Dave Canales were careful not to be too critical when discussing the officiating. The NFL juggled its Week 10 crews following Friday’s FAA ground stop, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their residences. Duane Heydt, an umpire since 2022, was the referee for Sunday’s game in New Orleans.
Penalties have been a problem all season for the Panthers, who established a team record for penalty yards (149) in a Week 6 road win against the Philadelphia Eagles, only to break it again four weeks later against the Saints. The Panthers have had three games with at least 13 penalties, are the league’s most-penalized team and are on pace to break the NFL records for penalties (163) and penalty yards (1,358), set by the Oakland Raiders in 2011 over a 16-game schedule.
Carolina would finish with 164 penalties and 1,487 penalty yards at its current pace. Through nine games, the Panthers have already surpassed their penalty yardage total from 2025, when they ranked among the league’s least-penalized teams.
“It feels like there’s a bounty out for the Panthers or something. It’s ridic — I don’t know,” Umanmielen said. “Obviously, we could be more disciplined as a team. It’s frustrating, especially with the pre-snap penalties. It’s just a matter of discipline.”
Canales spent 13 years as an assistant for the Seattle Seahawks, who were annually among the NFL’s penalty leaders and were the most-penalized team during their Super Bowl season of 2013. Former Seattle coach Pete Carroll considered some of the flags as the cost of the Seahawks’ aggressiveness.
That attitude is shared by Canales, who doesn’t have a problem with “competitive, aggressive” penalties.
“If you’re not getting penalized at all, you’re not playing hard enough,” Canales said. “What I’m talking about is pre-snap. I’m talking about post-snap. Those are the things that we have to figure out, that we have to clean up. And there are things that we’re working (on) to do that.”
Sunday’s game started with Ryan Fitzgerald sailing the opening kickoff out of bounds for a penalty. It ended on Fitzgerald’s game-winning 54-yard field goal, which was set up by a pass interference penalty against the Saints, one of the few calls that went the Panthers’ way.
In between, the Panthers were whistled for seven pre-snap penalties, including four encroachment or neutral-zone infractions on defense. The five personal fouls assessed against the Panthers included judgment calls on a horse-collar tackle by Jaelan Phillips on a sack of Tyler Shough and an unnecessary roughness penalty against linebacker Devin Lloyd.
“It’s just unfortunate. There’s a lot of things I could say. There’s a lot of things that people could speculate when it comes to that,” Lloyd said. “But at the end of the day, we’ve gotta look at the ones that are self-inflicted and make sure they don’t happen.”
The usually calm Canales became a little worked up after a second-quarter holding call on Panthers center Luke Fortner negated a Chuba Hubbard touchdown.
“Some of those judgment calls, I got a little frustrated just because I want our guys to be able to play physical and be aggressive, and not have to worry about those types of things,” he said.
Canales wondered whether some of the offside calls were the result in the more attacking style of interim defensive coordinator Todd Wash, who wants the defensive linemen getting upfield rather than reading and reacting.
Canales is considering having the scout team offense use different snap counts this week against the defense. But defensive tackle Derrick Brown, who had one of the neutral-zone penalties, said players should know better.
“We’ve played long enough,” Brown said. “From the time you’re in Little League, you can’t jump offsides. It just is what it is.”
As Umanmielen indicated with his “bounty” comment, it could be that the Panthers’ reputation precedes them. They’ve had 30 penalties assessed against them the past two weeks against New Orleans and Denver, tied for the 10th-highest total in a two-game span since at least 1944. But cornerback Marco Wilson showed it’s possible to improve in the flag department.
Wilson drew three pass interference calls and a taunting penalty against the Broncos, but was not among the many offenders in New Orleans.
“Just like going against your opponent, you kind of know what to expect, now the refs know that we’ve been penalized a good amount. So we’re being very conscious moving forward that obviously that’s what they see on film and we’re gonna have to clean some stuff up, me especially,” Wilson said.
“I had a game where I had a few penalties. So I just worked on the next week, coming in and figuring out what I did wrong and how I could eliminate those things.”

title: The Bears failed to meet their standard vs. Bucs. They don't expect it to happen again At 7-2, and with Jeffery Simmons now on board, the Bears believe they are built for the long haul. Dan Wiederer
summary:

Without question, the Chicago Bears were thrilled with the result of their most recent game, a 27-24 escape against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. But that Week 9 performance left a lot to be desired.
Too many costly penalties. So much offensive sloppiness. A rare flood of Caleb Williams turnovers. Thus, the vibes inside the Soldier Fi
full_text:
Bears rookie Zavion Thomas, turned upside down here, was involved in two plays that hurt Chicago with costly penalties against Tampa Bay. Geoff Stellfox / Getty Images
Without question, the Chicago Bears were thrilled with the result of their most recent game, a 27-24 escape against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. But that Week 9 performance left a lot to be desired.
Too many costly penalties. So much offensive sloppiness. A rare flood of Caleb Williams turnovers. Thus, the vibes inside the Soldier Field locker room felt subdued and somewhat awkward after that performance.
Bears players seemed fully aware that, at some point — and probably soon — their margin for error will become much thinner with their missteps carrying greater consequences. Against Tampa Bay — final score aside — they hadn’t met their established standard.
Said defensive lineman Daniel Hardy: “We’re not proud of the way we played. … It almost feels like a loss. The way that went tonight? That’s not who we are.”
Outcome bias hasn’t been a thing for this group — and doesn’t figure to become one. And with these Bears confident they can make a run at the Super Bowl this season, honest reflection has become a postgame prerequisite.
“Just the resilience and everyone playing until the final whistle means a lot for sure,” tight end Colston Loveland said. “We came through when we really needed it. But we have so much to clean up.”
Was it any wonder that coach Ben Johnson, while pleased with his players’ resolve, openly vowed to stew over the bye week about all the ways his team stumbled against the Buccaneers?
“There’s a certain standard we want to hit week in and week out,” Johnson said. “And I think the good teams, even when they get victories, if they don’t hit those benchmarks, then there’s more to be desired. I felt that from our crew. Which is a good thing. I think that’s the next evolution of this team; it’s not just that we win but the manner in which we play.”
With the Bears back from their bye week, now’s an ideal time for a midseason mood check.
Jeffery. Freakin’. Simmons.
How could the Bears not be thrilled with their late-October addition of one of the game’s most ferocious defenders? And how could the rest of the league not take notice of how instant and significant Simmons’ impact has been?
In two games as a Bear, Simmons has 10 tackles, two sacks and two quarterback hits. Just as notable, the attention he commands is freeing so many other defenders to make splash plays more regularly, starting with Devin Bush,  Montez Sweat and Austin Booker.
Since Simmons’ arrival, the NFL’s best third-down defense has become even better, too. The Bears lead the league with opponents converting only 22.8 percent of their third downs this season. Over the past two games, with Simmons aboard, the Seahawks and Bucs went a combined 3-for-23.
“Quarterbacks don’t have all that time to sit back there and read out different route concepts,” safety Cam Lewis said. “So we’re kind of covering for two, three seconds, which is so much better than five, six seconds.”
So far Simmons has been everything he was advertised to be. Powerful. Athletic. Smart. Effort-driven. He also has natural leadership traits and an infectious competitive edge.
“You feel (his impact) on the sideline,” Johnson said. “That’s always the ultimate compliment you can give a player — when they are elevating the people around them. He does that.”
It’s a credit to the Bears that, amid all the disorder during that Tampa Bay game, they maintained confidence and composure through the finish line. Their closing contribution was an eight-play, 49-yard drive to set up Cairo Santos’ walk-off 38-yard field goal.
That was another indicator of this team’s poise and purpose under pressure. And it came after the defense continually bowed up following Williams’ interceptions. On the Tampa Bay possessions following each of Williams’ picks, the Bears outscored the Buccaneers 7-3. (Credit cornerback Jaylon Johnson for his 67-yard interception return score in the third quarter.)
Over the last two seasons, under Ben Johnson’s guidance, the Bears have been solid in the late stages of close games. Including the playoffs, they are 11-6 in one-score games and 3-1 this season. In that time, they have eight victories in which they have scored their game-winning points in the final two minutes of regulation or overtime.
The Bears’ current four-game winning streak includes three straight victories in primetime, each presenting different tests of focus and fortitude.
Johnson believes this team’s success under pressure has been by design, that the program he has been building creates a feel as if the brightest lights are always shining. The goal, he reiterates, is to reach the Super Bowl but to arrive there feeling as if its just like every other game they’ve played.
The daily preparation habits Johnson’s group has subscribed to provide a combination of toughness and purpose for intense and demanding situations.
The Bears have been flagged for 80 penalties this year, including nine or more in each of their past four games. There’s been sloppiness across all three phases and from just about every position group. The clean-up process will require urgency.
Against Tampa Bay, for example, the Bears drew momentum-turning flags on offense, defense and special teams.
A post-play unnecessary-roughness foul against rookie receiver Zavion Thomas late in the first quarter took the offense from second-and-goal at the Buccaneers’ 6 to second-and-goal at the 21. Williams threw his first interception on the next snap.
A 91-yard kickoff return by Thomas in the third quarter was nullified by D’Marco Jackson’s holding infraction.
Booker’s face-mask penalty on quarterback Baker Mayfield wiped away a third-down sack with the Bears protecting a 24-16 lead late in the game.
Center Garrett Bradbury (six penalties) and Jaylon Johnson (five) have been the most penalized Bears so far.
The Bears’ eight accepted penalties per-game average is tied for the sixth-highest total in the league. According to TruMedia, their penalty yardage differential (minus-109) checks in as the eighth-worst total — and four of the teams worse than the Bears have played one additional game.
Through September, strengthened by a 291-yard outburst in the season opener at Carolina, the Bears led the NFL in rushing yards per game (184.3) and yards per attempt (5.3), feeding optimism that one of last season’s most productive ground attacks had carried its momentum into this year. But the Bears have since faltered with consistency in the run game, averaging less than 4.0 yards per attempt in six of their last seven games. Top back D’Andre Swift has averaged just 3.4 yards per rush during that span.
Johnson vowed to spend a chunk of his bye week studying what his rushing attack has done well and looking to make tweaks to emphasize those things. Last season during the bye, Johnson and his staff, with a Week 5 break, found answers to energize their run game. And the Bears — ranked 24th in rushing through four games — wound up vaulting to No. 3 by season’s end.
“I’m hoping we’re going to be able to find some nuggets like that,” Johnson said last week, “just with areas where we really can make it more consistent.”
The Bears categorize runs of 12 yards or longer as explosive but, according to TruMedia, have only nine such rushes since Week 1. (For context, 15 individual players around the NFL have more.) Has that been the major drag on the Bears’ per-carry average? Or is more movement at the line of scrimmage needed to create more opportunity?
Kyle Monangai has missed the past five games with a toe injury and should add pop to the ground game as soon as this week. Furthermore, after averaging 23.2 quarterback rushing yards per game last season, the Bears’ total has dipped slightly to 19.2 this season.

full_text:
Joe Burrow was 11-for-11 and sacked just once when blitzed by the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday night. Jeff Dean / Getty Images
CINCINNATI — On Sunday night, Pittsburgh Steelers defensive coordinator Patrick Graham decided to play the role of aggressor once again. He had leaned on the blitz over the Steelers’ four-game winning streak, and he wasn’t going to back off even with Joe Burrow standing across the line of scrimmage.
The message from Burrow and the Cincinnati Bengals’ offensive brain trust was simple: Thank you.
“It is a big-play opportunity for us,” offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher said on Monday. “That’s how we have to look at it. There is not an ounce of us that feels like, ‘Oh no, here comes the blitz.’ It’s, ‘Please blitz us.’”
Pitcher might need to enact stronger begging methods moving forward after Burrow’s surgical evisceration of those blitzes on Sunday.
The quarterback was sacked just once, for a 1-yard loss, when blitzed, while also going 11-for-11 for 181 yards and a touchdown. Six of those passes went for at least 14 yards, including explosive completions of 43, 35, 27 and 17 yards. Nine of those 12 blitzes came in the first half as the Bengals built a 24-3 lead, with Burrow’s effectiveness forcing the Steelers to withdraw.
On eight of the 11 passes, Burrow spit the ball out in 2.4 seconds or less, according to TruMedia. Not only did the plays consistently produce efficient gains, but also Burrow was only pressured twice.
That’s a product of another dominant performance from Cincinnati’s protection, from the offensive line to the tight ends and running backs, all deployed aggressively in pass protection.
Pitcher praised the “consistency of our pickups” for unlocking the big plays, but Burrow’s ability to process and distribute before the rush reached him led to the largest gains.
He twice unleashed deep balls over the top to Ja’Marr Chase. On one, he climbed the pocket thanks to a stonewall block by Chase Brown against a charging blitzer. On another, he immediately hit Ja’Marr Chase streaking into the zone vacated by the blitzer, with Chase sprinting 35 yards down the sideline.
Once the corners sat back, worried about Burrow attempting another over-the-top throw against the blitz, he calmly connected on intermediate stops, comebacks and crosses for chunks.
“I thought Joe played really fast,” Bengals coach Zac Taylor said. “There was times where he got the ball out of his hands quickly to maybe a quick outlet instead of waiting on the big chunk, which is fine. That’s a frustrating way for a defense to play.”
Taylor called Burrow’s decision-making, specifically against the blitz, “responsible.” There were multiple plays called where he had the opportunity to attempt longer throws, but instead he quickly checked down to Brown or Drew Sample or Mike Gesicki for positive yardage.
“There were a couple times in the first quarter of last night’s game where he plays first and second down in a way that maximizes efficiency,” Pitcher said. “There might have been a bigger throw or two at a point in that quarter where you look back on the play and say, ‘Oh geez, why didn’t he hold on to it for another second and take this shot or that shot?’ Well, he’s playing responsibly. He’s understanding that there’s a tremendous responsibility on him when we play the way we play to keep us moving and know the right time to take those strikes.”
Burrow’s ability to be consistently correct with those micro-decisions in the face of pressure was the biggest reason Graham had to throw out his strategy.
“Sometimes they want you to hold on a little longer so maybe they can win on a rush and get you if you are waiting for something down the field,” Taylor said. “But he just played so fast that it allowed for guys to get the ball in their hand quickly and get a lot of yards after contact. And then as the game unfolded and maybe they start tightening up, he got some of those bigger plays down the field.”
Over the last four weeks, Burrow is 36-for-42 (86 percent completion) for 474 yards, seven touchdowns, one interception and four sacks when blitzed.
He leads the NFL over that span against the blitz in EPA/dropback, completion percentage, success percentage, passing yards and explosive play percentage.
The Bengals’ next opponent, the Washington Commanders, rank fourth in the NFL in blitz rate.
Perhaps Pitcher was pleading with Washington defensive coordinator (and former Bengals staffer) Daronte Jones to join the list of those trying to blitz Burrow.
“We have just supreme confidence in our guys’ ability to protect it,” Pitcher said. “And then you guys can see what our skill guys and our quarterback can do.”
After winning the coin toss on Sunday, Taylor opted to receive. That was the first time he made such a choice this season, but it sent a deliberate message about his approach to the game. The Bengals — 3-0 when scoring first this season — wanted to jump out early and force Pittsburgh to play from behind. Cincinnati kicked a field goal on the opening drive, and the rest was history.
When did Taylor know he wanted to use that strategy?
“I think I texted Joe (Burrow) Monday morning at 8 a.m.,” Taylor said.
He admitted he felt the same way back in 2021 and 2022 when the Bengals were rolling to back-to-back AFC Championship games. In fact, over those two seasons, they were 18-1, including the playoffs, when scoring first. The 2022 team went 11-0 when scoring first, one of only five teams in the last five years to post a perfect record in that situation with double-digit wins.
That success dissolved in recent seasons, mostly due to the struggling defense. But now, with Burrow back to playing dominant football and an early-season issue of slow starts, Taylor wants to use his star quarterback to set the tone.
“You can look back and see times we felt the way we did,” Taylor said. “You take the ball.”
The Bengals’ offense would be correctly characterized as one-dimensional. They’ve happily leaned into what they do best and stopped attempting to run consistently in the name of balance.
Burrow’s league-leading completion rate allows the passing game to serve as an extension of the running game. And they are seeing signs of progress in the ground attack.
In fact, over the last five weeks, they rank in the top 10 in the NFL in success rate on running plays. They have one of the lowest percentages of rushes for zero or negative yards.
They aren’t about to become the San Francisco 49ers, but they are averaging 4.1 yards per carry and have even sprinkled in nine rushes of double-digit yards in the last five games.
Using the run game to keep the dropbacks in manageable distances is all that matters right now. For that part, the run game is succeeding even without volume production.
“The way we’re playing right now throwing the football, it’s allowing us to be explosive, it is allowing us to possess the ball, it allows us to be efficient, and we’re protecting, and so, with all those things being true, the run game, it’s just gonna depend on how things play out,” Pitcher said. “It’s just about executing every given call, knowing where that fits for us, and then situationally being able to run the football. The fourth-and-one conversion and the low red zone touchdown are great examples of that.”
The Steelers laid back in Cover 2 with the Bengals in a goal-to-go situation, and Cincinnati was able to force a run in for a touchdown by Samaje Perine.
Those are the moments when the run game matters. Despite the lack of attempts, they are succeeding more often than not.

title: Finding where Fernando Mendoza must improve after QB1 debut: Week 10 film review Also, the NFL's best three offenses, kudos for Brett Veach's Chiefs retooling and Sean McVay's key Rams adjustments. Ted Nguyen 1
summary:
Fernando Mendoza had some highs in his starting debut on Sunday, but the Seahawks defense exposed his inexperience as the game progressed. Ethan Miller / Getty Images
Our Week 10 NFL film review starts with Las Vegas Raiders rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza making his starting debut following the trade deadline in the most difficult circumstances. Still, he needs to be better and he knows it.
Some believed the Kansas City Chiefs’ roster had deteriorated too much after their dynasty, but it’s
full_text:
Fernando Mendoza had some highs in his starting debut on Sunday, but the Seahawks defense exposed his inexperience as the game progressed. Ethan Miller / Getty Images
Our Week 10 NFL film review starts with Las Vegas Raiders rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza making his starting debut following the trade deadline in the most difficult circumstances. Still, he needs to be better and he knows it.
Some believed the Kansas City Chiefs’ roster had deteriorated too much after their dynasty, but it’s been rebuilt and has a chance to compete. Should general manager Brett Veach get more credit?
We’ll also take a look at which three offenses have separated themselves and how the Rams have reinvented themselves after key injuries.
Facing the Seattle Seahawks, the league’s top pass defense, was hard enough for his first start, but Mendoza also had to do it with his top weapon, Brock Bowers, hurt on the first drive. Bowers tried to return but wasn’t effective. He left the game for good in the second quarter after he couldn’t push off his ankle properly on a run block.
The Raiders’ receiving corps without Bowers could be the league’s worst. They also have the NFL’s least-efficient run game. That’s a lot of extremes working against each other.
Mendoza didn’t have a disastrous game despite the circumstances, and he did a lot of positive things overall. But he missed opportunities and took too many sacks because he didn’t operate fast enough. He was stuck on his first read too often.
8:35 remaining in the third quarter, third-and-9
On third-and-9, the Seahawks got into an exotic front with seven players on the line of scrimmage and defensive tackle Byron Murphy II in a two-point stance. The tricky part with these fronts is deciphering who will actually rush and who will drop back.
Nickel Devon Witherspoon, who had two sacks on Sunday, was also on the line and was capped, meaning a defensive back was behind him. Being capped should have been a strong indicator that Witherspoon would rush.
The offensive line slid left and was responsible for the four defenders on the slide side. Running back Ashton Jeanty was responsible for defensive back Nick Emmanwori if Emmanwori rushed. If Emmanwori didn’t blitz, Jeanty would look to Witherspoon. Mendoza should have looked to this side first because if both rushed, then he would have to throw hot because the defense had one more rusher than the offense could block to that side.
Both Emmanwori and Witherspoon rushed. Jeanty blocked Emmanwori and no one was left for Witherspoon.
Jalen Nailor was the primary receiver, so Mendoza looked to him first. Nailor was open, but Mendoza needed an extra half-second. If Mendoza had diagnosed the potential issue to his right, he would have found tight end Michael Mayer open on a hot route.
On this play, Mendoza was squarely at fault, but Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald also called some well-timed and well-designed blitzes on which Mendoza didn’t have a chance. Macdonald has flummoxed much more experienced quarterbacks with his pressures, so this isn’t a major red flag for Mendoza.
This is why you play Mendoza now, so he can see firsthand what NFL speed looks like and, in this case, how a Super Bowl defense operates. Now, Mendoza has to look over the film, find ways to speed up his process and get ready for another fast and furious defense in Denver. After that, the Raiders play the Cleveland Browns, who also have an elite pass defense. Then Mendoza will get a bye week to take a step back, and maybe things will slow down for him after that. Welcome to the NFL, rook!
Veach isn’t mentioned in many midseason picks for NFL executive of the year, but his work this offseason has turned the Chiefs back into contenders, especially in a season in which the AFC is wide open. Veach’s boldest move was to trade away All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie and let corner Jaylen Watson walk in free agency.
The Chiefs replaced them with rookie Mansoor Delane, who looks like a future star, and Nohl Williams, whom Veach picked in the third round last year. Defensive end R Mason Thomas, a second-round pick this year, isn’t a starter, but he’s been effective when he’s played and provides much-needed juice off the edge. His 11.2 percent pressure rate is second among Kansas City defensive linemen.
The youth movement has been successful. The defense is an improved unit despite getting cheaper.
Offensively, the Chiefs have rebuilt their identity. Perhaps no other position group in the NFL has improved more than Kansas City’s running back room. Free-agent signing Kenneth Walker is a candidate for offensive player of the year and fifth-round rookie Emmett Johnson looks phenomenal as a runner and pass catcher. Walker missed Week 10 with an injury and you could hardly tell with the way Johnson was breaking tackles. After Sunday, Johnson actually has a higher missed tackle rate (24.2 percent) than Walker (21.6 percent).
Last year’s first-round pick Josh Simmons hasn’t played a snap this season because of a back injury. His replacement at left tackle, Kahlil Benson, has been functional, which is more than a team can hope for from an undrafted rookie playing a premium position.
The Chiefs’ biggest question is at wide receiver, where Veach has swung and missed the most. This might decide whether he deserves this award and whether his team is a true contender. The Chiefs traded for Josh Downs at the deadline, and in his first game, he looked as advertised. In just 11 snaps (eight routes), Downs caught four passes for 53 yards and a touchdown.
:24 remaining in the second quarter, first-and-10
With only 24 seconds remaining before halftime, the Chiefs had Downs lined up inside as part of a bunch. Downs had a stutter rail route.
The Falcons were in quarters. The corner and safety were occupied with Xavier Worthy running deep, which left nickel Billy Bowman Jr. in man-to-man against Downs. The Chiefs newcomer was patient and hit Bowman with a hesitation move to freeze him before wheeling downfield.
Downs did a good job of maintaining his line and going up to catch a beautiful back-shoulder pass from Patrick Mahomes, who remarkably made this throw on the run.
With Downs in the lineup, Worthy can run clear-out routes, which he does at a high level, while Downs can run more nuanced routes. Downs isn’t a No. 1 wide receiver, but if he can reliably beat man coverage on the outside, he’ll make the ceiling for this offense so much higher.
What happens when an unstoppable force meets a highly movable object? The Dallas Cowboys ended up with the most yards they have ever given up at AT&T Stadium (584). They were beaten by trick plays, traditional run plays, Brock Purdy creation plays and screens. Every button 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan pressed worked, and when it didn’t, Purdy got outside the pocket and found open receivers.
The Cowboys offense kept them in the game, but when they needed a stop down by six points with three minutes left in the game, the 49ers caught the Cowboys in a zero-blitz. That ended in Christian McCaffrey beating Von Miller on a route for a 66-yard touchdown.
Receiver Mike Evans hasn’t played in a few weeks and the offense hasn’t missed a beat. Keenan Allen, whom the 49ers traded for last week, caught five passes for 61 yards. What Shanahan and Purdy are doing is incredible. A lot of credit goes to the offensive line, which has looked like a much-improved unit from last season.
The Bengals’ offensive line has evolved into one of the NFL’s best pass-blocking groups. Right tackle Amarius Mims should be in the running for the protector of the year award. Tee Higgins, who was already an All-Pro-caliber player, looks even better. Pairing two No. 1 receivers has always given the Bengals a sky-high ceiling, but now their floor is higher and their ability to protect Joe Burrow lets them hit their ceiling more often.
Burrow’s feel for when to be aggressive and check the ball down also helps the line and keeps the offense efficient.…

We’ll also take a look at which three offenses have separated themselves and how the Rams have reinvented themselves after key injuries.

Bowers tried to return but wasn’t effective. He left the game for good in the second quarter after he couldn’t push off his ankle properly on a run block.
The Raiders’ receiving corps without Bowers could be the league’s worst. They also have the NFL’s least-efficient run game. That’s a lot of extremes working against each other.
Mendoza didn’t have a disastrous game despite the circumstances, and he did a lot of positive things overall. But he missed opportunities and took too many sacks because he didn’t operate fast enough. He was stuck on his first read too often.
8:35 remaining in the third quarter, third-and-9
On third-and-9, the Seahawks got into an exotic front with seven players on the line of scrimmage and defensive tackle Byron Murphy II in a two-point stance. The tricky part with these fronts is deciphering who will actually rush and who will drop back.
Nickel Devon Witherspoon, who had two sacks on Sunday, was also on the line and was capped, meaning a defensive back was behind him. Being capped should have been a strong indicator that Witherspoon would rush.
The offensive line slid left and was responsible for the four defenders on the slide side. Running back Ashton Jeanty was responsible for defensive back Nick Emmanwori if Emmanwori rushed. If Emmanwori didn’t blitz, Jeanty would look to Witherspoon. Mendoza should have looked to this side first because if both rushed, then he would have to throw hot because the defense had one more rusher than the offense could block to that side.
Both Emmanwori and Witherspoon rushed. Jeanty blocked Emmanwori and no one was left for Witherspoon.
Jalen Nailor was the primary receiver, so Mendoza looked to him first. Nailor was open, but Mendoza needed an extra half-second. If Mendoza had diagnosed the potential issue to his right, he would have found tight end Michael Mayer open on a hot route.
On this play, Mendoza was squarely at fault, but Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald also called some well-timed and well-designed blitzes on which Mendoza didn’t have a chance. Macdonald has flummoxed much more experienced quarterbacks with his pressures, so this isn’t a major red flag for Mendoza.
This is why you play Mendoza now, so he can see firsthand what NFL speed looks like and, in this case, how a Super Bowl defense operates. Now, Mendoza has to look over the film, find ways to speed up his process and get ready for another fast and furious defense in Denver. After that, the Raiders play the Cleveland Browns, who also have an elite pass defense. Then Mendoza will get a bye week to take a step back, and maybe things will slow down for him after that. Welcome to the NFL, rook!
Veach isn’t mentioned in many midseason picks for NFL executive of the year, but his work this offseason has turned the Chiefs back into contenders, especially in a season in which the AFC is wide open. Veach’s boldest move was to trade away All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie and let corner Jaylen Watson walk in free agency.
The Chiefs replaced them with rookie Mansoor Delane, who looks like a future star, and Nohl Williams, whom Veach picked in the third round last year. Defensive end R Mason Thomas, a second-round pick this year, isn’t a starter, but he’s been effective when he’s played and provides much-needed juice off the edge. His 11.2 percent pressure rate is second among Kansas City defensive linemen.
The youth movement has been successful. The defense is an improved unit despite getting cheaper.
Offensively, the Chiefs have rebuilt their identity. Perhaps no other position group in the NFL has improved more than Kansas City’s running back room. Free-agent signing Kenneth Walker is a candidate for offensive player of the year and fifth-round rookie Emmett Johnson looks phenomenal as a runner and pass catcher. Walker missed Week 10 with an injury and you could hardly tell with the way Johnson was breaking tackles. After Sunday, Johnson actually has a higher missed tackle rate (24.2 percent) than Walker (21.6 percent).
Last year’s first-round pick Josh Simmons hasn’t played a snap this season because of a back injury. His replacement at left tackle, Kahlil Benson, has been functional, which is more than a team can hope for from an undrafted rookie playing a premium position.
The Chiefs’ biggest question is at wide receiver, where Veach has swung and missed the most. This might decide whether he deserves this award and whether his team is a true contender. The Chiefs traded for Josh Downs at the deadline, and in his first game, he looked as advertised. In just 11 snaps (eight routes), Downs caught four passes for 53 yards and a touchdown.
:24 remaining in the second quarter, first-and-10
With only 24 seconds remaining before halftime, the Chiefs had Downs lined up inside as part of a bunch. Downs had a stutter rail route.
The Falcons were in quarters. The corner and safety were occupied with Xavier Worthy running deep, which left nickel Billy Bowman Jr. in man-to-man against Downs. The Chiefs newcomer was patient and hit Bowman with a hesitation move to freeze him before wheeling downfield.
Downs did a good job of maintaining his line and going up to catch a beautiful back-shoulder pass from Patrick Mahomes, who remarkably made this throw on the run.
With Downs in the lineup, Worthy can run clear-out routes, which he does at a high level, while Downs can run more nuanced routes. Downs isn’t a No. 1 wide receiver, but if he can reliably beat man coverage on the outside, he’ll make the ceiling for this offense so much higher.
What happens when an unstoppable force meets a highly movable object? The Dallas Cowboys ended up with the most yards they have ever given up at AT&T Stadium (584). They were beaten by trick plays, traditional run plays, Brock Purdy creation plays and screens. Every button 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan pressed worked, and when it didn’t, Purdy got outside the pocket and found open receivers.
The Cowboys offense kept them in the game, but when they needed a stop down by six points with three minutes left in the game, the 49ers caught the Cowboys in a zero-blitz. That ended in Christian McCaffrey beating Von Miller on a route for a 66-yard touchdown.
Receiver Mike Evans hasn’t played in a few weeks and the offense hasn’t missed a beat. Keenan Allen, whom the 49ers traded for last week, caught five passes for 61 yards. What Shanahan and Purdy are doing is incredible. A lot of credit goes to the offensive line, which has looked like a much-improved unit from last season.
The Bengals’ offensive line has evolved into one of the NFL’s best pass-blocking groups. Right tackle Amarius Mims should be in the running for the protector of the year award. Tee Higgins, who was already an All-Pro-caliber player, looks even better. Pairing two No. 1 receivers has always given the Bengals a sky-high ceiling, but now their floor is higher and their ability to protect Joe Burrow lets them hit their ceiling more often.
Burrow’s feel for when to be aggressive and check the ball down also helps the line and keeps the offense efficient.…

full_text:
Defensive lineman Elijah Williams had one of the Vikings' eight sacks of Packers quarterback Jordan Love on Sunday. Mike Roemer / Associated Press
EAGAN, Minn. — Seemingly every season, around this time, Minnesota Vikings defense coordinator Brian Flores finds himself standing behind a lectern, smiling in response to a question about his blitzes.
He hears the unfathomability in the tone of the query. He understands the astonishment. He usually offers a verbal shrug.
As in, Yeah, I don’t know, we just do what we do. As in, What can I say? This is who we are.
Flores reacts as if all this is normal, a strategy that’s only outlandish in the eyes of outsiders.
This happened again a few weeks ago. More than ever, the Vikings had been sending extra men at the opposing quarterback. Could this continue? Where would it end? Flores acknowledged the latest round of external disbelief, then broached what he believes gets lost in the nuance of the blitz discussion.
“What people call blitzes or pressures or max blitzes or max coverage is a little bit different per individual, group or team,” Flores said. “We like to pressure a good amount. It helps us in the run game. It helps us in the pass game. It’s something we believe in.”
He describes the approach the way an aggressive poker player would. Risk exists, yes. But in his worldview, the worst way to go about it would be refusing to take any shot at all.
This style begets attitude. It’s confidence, bordering on arrogance. That’s the method to the madness.
That’s the ethos of a terrifying unit that is unquestionably one of the stories of the 2026 NFL season.
Opponents are scoring a league-low 14 points per game against these Vikings. On Sunday, the Green Bay Packers found themselves caught in the vise grip of the Vikings’ defense. Walls caved in on quarterback Jordan Love from all sides. Minnesota sacked him eight times and pressured him on almost 60 percent of the snaps, the second-highest pressure rate in an NFL game all season.
Yet the Vikings blitzed on only 70.3 percent of their defensive snaps. The presence of the word only there tells you everything you need to know.
“They do a good job with what they do,” Packers coach Matt LaFleur said. “You know they’re going to fire (blitzers) from all angles. Certainly, we didn’t have our guys coached up well enough.”
Through nine games, the Vikings have the highest blitz rate since Next Gen Stats began tracking the metric in 2015. Only two teams previously eclipsed 50 percent for the season. One of them was the 2023 Vikings under Flores.
Because Flores believes in sending enough men at the quarterback to make him uncomfortable, and because the Vikings have had success dating back to his arrival in the Twin Cities, it’s easier for the players to commit to the plan.
In recent weeks, veteran Minnesota safety Harrison Smith joined Richard Sherman’s podcast. When asked about the absurdity of what his defense was doing defensively, Smith mirrored Flores’ disposition. He confessed that what the Vikings are doing “is wild.” But he also challenged the conventional wisdom in the process.
“We talk about it sometimes, but it’s, like, ‘Who decided that four defenders is the baseline amount that you’re supposed to send?'” Smith said. “Like, was that decided when Walter Camp came up with football? What does that mean?”
In a way, Smith hinted at one of the misnomers, something this story often misses even now: Not all blitzes are created equal. Sending five men is classified as a blitz, but it is the equivalent of mild sauce. Yes, it ratchets up the taste a bit. But not at the expense of one’s taste buds.
To that end, it’s worth highlighting that the majority of the Vikings’ blitzes reside in this category. Sometimes, off-ball linebacker Eric Wilson plunges inside to add to the pass rush. In other instances, Smith joins the party from the edge. These become bets on timing. A quarterback can only hold the football for so long when an extra defender is sprinting at him. This prevents defenders on the back end from having to stay with shifty receivers for longer periods of time.
Depending on the situation, the Vikings will crank up the spice level. Yet even when they rush six or more defenders, their coverage players know the likely voids, and they have both the athleticism and acumen to retreat to them before the quarterback can get the ball out. As a cherry on top, the Vikings play with two deep safeties on 64.1 percent of snaps. In other words, they’re typically covering for their courage.
This is the intentionality behind the chaos. It’s aggressive, sure, but well-reasoned aggressiveness. This is the fastball that has flustered just about every offense the Vikings have faced.
And the personnel amplifies the possibilities. Edge rusher Dallas Turner can long-arm a tackle into oblivion, but he can also drop from the line of scrimmage and deflect a pass. Edge rusher Andrew Van Ginkel can match a receiver’s pattern, but he can also spin past a tackle for a sack.
“We knew we had advantages in certain places,” safety Josh Metellus said after Sunday’s win. “But to see it come together, to see the stunts and games, to see all the guys showing up, different guys here and there, the rush plan came together. And when that happens, we’re just feasting on the back end.”
The beauty of the system is its ability to morph and change. That wouldn’t be possible without a group of players capable of comprehending and applying Flores’ plan. They know what they’re trying to do and why.
Flores does, too. You can think of him as the guy on a heater at the roulette table, continuing to get away with risk after risk. That would be fair given the abnormality of this approach in the NFL — and it would also be wrong.

title: QB stock report, Week 11: Vikings' Kirk Cousins returns to the top 10. You like that?! Mike Jones 1

Based on how effective Kirk Cousins was in Sunday’s 30-10 win over the Green Bay Packers — after just two full-speed practices with the Minnesota Vikings and the potential his new-old team now boasts — it appears the third-round pick Las Vegas received as compensation for the 38-year-old quarterback
full_text:
Minnesota Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins helped orchestrate a 30-10 win Sunday over the Green Bay Packers. Jeff Hanisch / Imagn Images
In the end, the Las Vegas Raiders may not have gotten enough.
Based on how effective Kirk Cousins was in Sunday’s 30-10 win over the Green Bay Packers — after just two full-speed practices with the Minnesota Vikings and the potential his new-old team now boasts — it appears the third-round pick Las Vegas received as compensation for the 38-year-old quarterback may have been a rip-off.
After weeks of eking out victories on the strength of Brian Flores’ dominant defense and despite an anemic offense, the Vikings lit up the scoreboard Sunday against the Packers. After Minnesota averaged just 18.3 points through eight games, the Cousins-led Vikings scored 30 points for only the second time all year. After mustering just 266.8 total yards (second-fewest in the NFL), the Vikings racked up 312 yards in Green Bay. After converting just 33.3 percent of third downs this season (30th in the NFL), Minnesota went 8-for-16 on those money downs Sunday. For only the fourth time all season, the Vikings actually managed to turn turnovers into points (nine).
Just like that, all of the ills that plagued Minnesota offensively before Sunday vanished. And just like that, the 7-2 Vikings look like bona fide Super Bowl contenders.
Cousins, who ranks fifth in the NFL in passing yards this season, delivered something of a pedestrian performance against Green Bay (210 yards while completing 21 of 31 pass attempts). He did, however, record two more touchdown passes, upping his season total to 22 — No. 2 behind Joe Burrow’s 27.
Given the limited preparation, Cousins performed admirably. Praised by coach Kevin O’Connell and Vikings teammates for his poise, leadership and execution, Cousins made his contributions in all of the areas and moments where they mattered the most. He completed 9-of-12 third-down passes for 110 yards, a touchdown and an interception. He got rid of the ball in just 2.2 seconds. His two touchdown passes came on throws over the middle of the field — tying Minnesota’s season total for touchdown throws in that area of the field. When the Packers scored 10 unanswered points to pull within two scores entering the fourth quarter, Cousins directed back-to-back fourth-quarter scoring drives to slam the door shut.
Prior knowledge of O’Connell’s offense — he played for the coach in Minnesota in 2022 and 2023 and in Washington in 2017, when O’Connell was the QBs coach — served Cousins well. So too did pre-existing relationships with Vikings teammates, including wide receiver Justin Jefferson, who on Sunday recorded a season-high nine catches for only his third 70-plus-yard game of the year. But above all, Cousins delivered thanks largely to the preparedness and study habits he has prided himself on during his 15-year NFL career.
O’Connell runs an offense that relies heavily on timing. The unit sputtered greatly with Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz shackled by indecision. But Cousins routinely recognizes coverages before they unfold, understands how to manipulate defenses and throws with anticipation. Cousins’ proficiency enabled the Vikings to move up and down the field at an efficient pace while remaining in manageable down-and-distance situations. The Vikings on Sunday ran 69 offensive plays, far more than their season average (60.6) and well above the 48 plays from last week’s Wentz-led debacle. As a result, Minnesota won the time of possession battle handily (35:16 to 24:44).
Cousins’ return to the Vikings restored confidence and optimism within the organization. There’s an understandable belief that, given a full week’s worth of preparation, as well as the healthy returns of No. 2 wide receiver Jordan Addison and tight end T.J. Hockenson, Cousins will advance the offense even further up the ranks.
Now fielding an offense that can both complement Flores’ dominant defense and better capitalize on opportunities provided by that unit, the Vikings belong among this year’s Super Bowl favorites. Following the win over Green Bay, the Vikings jumped up to fourth in the odds, according to The Athletic 's NFL Playoff Simulator . If Cousins and the Minnesota offense progress as anticipated, those odds will only strengthen and make Vikings brass look very wise for the in-season trade.
There’s not a team in the league that wouldn’t give up a third-round pick for a Lombardi Trophy.
Deshaun Watson’s once-improbable quest to resurrect his career and lead the Browns back to respectability took yet another step in a positive direction following Sunday’s 27-24 victory over the Houston Texans. With the win, the Browns improved to 6-4 on the season and 4-0 at home.
In overcoming a traditionally sluggish start to rally his team from a 17-0 deficit and direct five scoring drives, Watson recorded his fourth fourth-quarter comeback of the season. He has now directed game-winning drives in each of Cleveland's victories. According to NFL research, Watson on Sunday became only the third quarterback since 1970 to lead a game-winning drive in each of his team’s first six wins of a season, joining Matthew Stafford (2016) and Troy Aikman (1990).
And so continues yet another redemption quest for the quarterback whom Cleveland fans booed lustily during the preseason, in part because of his frequent injury-shortened campaigns and lack of success in three previous seasons, and also because of the sexual assault allegations leveled against him during his time in Houston. Watson, who lamented during the preseason that he felt more comfortable playing on the road than in Cleveland, now owns a perfect record at Huntington Bank Field and has given the long-suffering Browns fans reason to cheer.
Despite a change in fortunes for Watson and the Browns, the quarterback remains a mind-bending case study. For the season, Watson, who last enjoyed a healthy season in 2020 and appeared in just 19 games for Cleveland from 2022-2024 — he spent all of 2025 rehabbing from surgery to repair a torn Achilles tendon — has completed 65.1 percent of his passes (his best showing since 2020, when he completed 70.2 percent).
Unsurprisingly, where Watson has thrived is in the second half of games (65.8 percent). With his team tied with two minutes to go, Watson has completed 83.3 percent of his passes while posting a passer rating of 114.2. When trailing with two minutes remaining, he has completed 75 percent of his passes with a 151.4 passer rating.
Sunday was representative of this season's typical rollercoaster for Cleveland. While trailing 17-0, Watson and the Browns saw their win probability fall as low as 5.3 percent. When they went on a 20-0 run, the Browns saw their win probability reach 75.2 percent with 14 minutes left in the game. But when Watson threw an interception with 5:19 left, Cleveland’s win probability dipped to 16.1 percent. However, by the time Watson completed a 30-yard pass to tight end Harold Fannin Jr. to place the ball at the Houston 5-yard line with 1:11 left, the win probability jumped to 54.9 percent.
Coach Todd Monken and members of the Browns organization find themselves perturbed that Watson’s effectiveness differs so drastically from start to finish. A switch seems to flip with the game on the line, and Watson finds a way to shrug off the early-game struggles and execute with greater precision.
“I wish, collectively, him and I together would play better early and coach better early so that we didn't have to get to this," Monken said Sunday.
However, the Browns and Watson certainly will embrace and celebrate the late-game heroics while taking additional steps towards a once-unlikely goal of reaching the postseason.
The Browns entered the season with a 10.7 percent chance of making the playoffs, according to our playoff simulator. Those odds have increased to 58 percent just past the midway point of the season.

summary:
