Every week during the season, Josh Kendall and Chad Graff rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.
The power rankings are getting ready for the NFL’s stretch run by picking a breakout player for each of the 32 teams.
Kirk Cousins and the Minnesota Vikings
full_text:
Kirk Cousins' return to Minnesota has the Vikings surging, while Drake Maye's injury has Patriots nation worried. Illustration: Will Tullos / The Athletic; Photos: Patrick McDermott / Getty Images and Lennart Preiss / Associated Press
Every week during the season, Josh Kendall and Chad Graff rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.
The power rankings are getting ready for the NFL’s stretch run by picking a breakout player for each of the 32 teams.
Kirk Cousins and the Minnesota Vikings are our big risers of the week as the top of this list continues to solidify around the elite teams.
Breakout player: Greg Rousseau
The sixth-year outside linebacker has been good for a long time. He’s trending toward great this year and has already tied his career high in sacks with eight, which ranks fourth in the league. Third-year wide receiver Keon Coleman is also on track for career highs in yards and catches. Despite just one reception for 11 yards (and one concussion check) on Sunday, Coleman has 24 catches for 315 yards.
Up nex t : vs. Dolphins, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Cowboys 46-40
Breakout player: Renardo Green
The third-year cornerback had a tough day on Sunday against George Pickens and company, but he was dealing with a back injury and had already built up plenty of goodwill this year. Green, a second-round pick in 2024, has four interceptions, three more than he had in his first two seasons combined. Rookie running back Kaelon Black has also been a surprise with 356 rushing yards behind Christian McCaffrey.
Up next: vs. Vikings, Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Jonah Coleman
The fourth-round rookie running back had 36 touches for 192 yards of offense in weeks 8 and 9. That ranked 17th in the league in that stretch. For the season, he’s averaging 9.8 yards per reception, and he could have a big day against a middling Raiders defense this weekend.
Up next: vs. Raiders, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Falcons 35-13
Breakout player: Emmett Johnson
With Kenneth Walker out Sunday, Johnson, a fifth-round rookie running back, had 22 carries for 101 yards against the Falcons, which was almost as much as he had in his first eight games combined. Johnson also has 20 catches this season for 307 yards. In general, it’s tough to pick a breakout player in Kansas City, where it feels like all the contributors have been around forever, but Johnson has been a meaningful addition.
Up next: vs. Cardinals, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Bhayshul Tuten
Jacksonville let Travis Etienne leave in free agency because the Jaguars thought Tuten was ready for a starting role. They were right. The second-year running back already has career highs in rushing yards (609), carries (148) and total touchdowns (eight). He’s 14th in the league in rushing.
Up next: at Giants, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Luther Burden
Ben Johnson was bullish about his second-year wide receiver in the preseason, and we’re seeing why. Burden is 16th in the league with 644 receiving yards, and 385 of those came in his last four games. From weeks 6 through 9, he had more receiving yards than all but five players in the league, and he got 23.5 percent of the Bears’ passing targets. That last number may go up as the season progresses.
Up next: vs. Saints, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Steelers 38-18
Breakout player: Boye Mafe
The Bengals gave the fifth-year pass rusher a three-year, $60 million free-agent deal in the offseason, and it’s proving to be a good move. Mafe had another sack Sunday night and has 6.5 for the season, plus 11 quarterback hits. At this pace, he’ll easily hit his career highs in both categories. He’s had at least one sack in five of his last six games.
Up next: at Commanders, Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Packers 30-10
Breakout player: Levi Drake Rodriguez
We’re going pretty far off the board here, but how often do you get to publicize a guy who played his college football at Southwestern Assemblies of God and East Texas A&M? A seventh-round pick in 2024, the former Prospect X has started every game for the Vikings this year and had two sacks Sunday to give him a career-high three for the season.
Up next: at 49ers, Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Patriots 35-10
Breakout player: Alim McNeill
The sixth-year defensive tackle already has a career high in sacks (6.5) and quarterback hits (11), and the Lions are going to need him more than ever with Aidan Hutchinson out due to injury. Detroit proved again Sunday that its offense is Super Bowl-worthy, but the defense is 28th in the league in defensive EPA (minus-5.2 per 100 snaps).
Up next: vs. Buccaneers, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Raiders 21-13
Breakout player: Drew Lock
The Seahawks’ backup quarterback started his third game Sunday in place of the injured Sam Darnold. Seattle has won all three of those games. Among quarterbacks with more than 50 attempts this season, Lock is third in the league in EPA per dropback (0.32). He has seven passing touchdowns and no interceptions, and that last number has some Seahawks fans wondering if he’s a better option than the turnover-prone Darnold.
Sunday: Beat Cardinals 34-6
Breakout player: Quentin Lake
In his fifth year, the cornerback has already tripled the career interception total he had entering the season, with three. He has also forced two fumbles and has 65 tackles. Lake also has what may be the quote of the year this season, saying on “ The St. Brown Podcast ” that Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert “was throwing deli meat out there.”
Sunday: Lost to Vikings 30-10
Breakout player: Christian Watson
The ambulance clip alone gives Watson the nod here, but the fifth-year wide receiver is having a career year on top of that. Watson is third in the league in receiving yards (916) and tied for third in receiving touchdowns (seven). Watson had not topped 620 receiving yards in any of his previous four seasons.
Sunday: Lost to Bengals 38-18
Breakout player: Jaylen Warren
The fifth-year running back was disappointing Sunday night, but so were all of the other Steelers. For the season, Warren has been great. He has 126 carries for 719 yards and leads all running backs with 5.7 yards per carry. He’s second in the league in yards per carry after contact (4.04).
Up next: at Eagles, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Harold Fannin Jr.
It’s not exactly a breakout year for the Browns’ second-year tight end because he was excellent as a rookie and has been great again in Year 2. He had seven catches for 91 yards on Sunday, and now has 19 for 287 yards in the last three games. Fannin has 44 catches for 544 yards and four touchdowns on the season.
Sunday: Lost to Lions 35-10
Breakout player: Elijah Ponder
The second-year edge rusher had four sacks last year as an undrafted free-agent rookie. This year, he has 7.5, and he had another five tackles against the Lions on Sunday. Wide receiver Mack Hollins, who is on his sixth team in his ninth professional year, is also having a career year with 48.8 receiving yards per game.
Thursday: Lost to Commanders 24-21
Breakout player: Isaiah Likely
Brock Bowers and Trey McBride are the only tight ends in the league with more receiving yards than Likely, who has 575 this year. After following John Harbaugh from Baltimore and getting out of Mark Andrews’ shadow, Likely already has career highs in yards, catches (55) and touchdowns (seven). He had nine catches for a career-high 127 yards against Washington.
Up next: vs. Jaguars, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Zyon McCollum
The fifth-year cornerback has a career-high four interceptions, which is one more than he had in his first four seasons combined. McCollum also has a fumble recovery and 28 solo tackles for a talented defense that makes the Buccaneers the favorites in the NFC South.
Up next: at Lions, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET

title: A way-too-early look at potential Giants draft targets: How determined is NY to upgrade at RB? The Giants didn't address needs at running back and defensive tackle ahead of the trade deadline. Will they target those spots in the draft? Charlotte Carroll and Dane Brugler 4

full_text:
Should the New York Giants be interested in drafting Utah running back Wayshawn Parker in April? David Becker / Getty Images
The New York Giants lead the NFC East, and I’m writing about the 2027 NFL Draft?!?
Maybe I’ve lost my mind, or maybe it’s just a reflex after years of covering the Giants. Once the calendar hits November, it’s time to start talking about players who can help the Giants in the future.
Fortunately for Giants fans, despite all the down-to-the-wire, late-game moments this year, that’s not the case. They enter Week 11 at 5-3-1 and in control of their playoff fate.
So, why write about the draft now? Well, for one thing, it’s always fun to talk about the draft, especially when The Athletic ’s draft expert, Dane Brugler, agrees to take part. For another, we spent a lot of time recently thinking about the Giants’ positional needs before the trade deadline. And though not for lack of trying, the Giants didn’t make any major moves ahead of the deadline — unless you want to count the late-September addition of quarterback J.J. McCarthy — so those positional needs remain.
Though some fans were disappointed by the lack of activity before the deadline, the upside of not trading away any draft picks is … they still have draft picks! The Giants are currently in possession of their own first-, second-, third- and sixth-round picks. They also have an extra sixth-rounder from the Daniel Faalele trade.
So, which players might fill the positions the team was looking to upgrade at the deadline, and who should Giants fans start keeping an eye on?  For answers, we turn to Brugler, who provided some Day 2 and Day 3 targets to dream on.
Brugler: A bouncy athlete, Parker is averaging 6.2 yards per carry this season and has scouts excited about his NFL potential. He has outstanding reaction quickness with the awareness to find his blocks, allowing him to stack his cuts as he weaves through traffic. Aside from his running ability, the Giants will love his impact on passing downs, both as a receiver and blocker.
Since coach John Harbaugh’s arrival, the Giants have demonstrated clear interest in upgrading at running back. They were interested in free agent Kenneth Walker III and were widely considered a suitor for Notre Dame prospect Jeremiyah Love ahead of the 2026 draft, but he was selected by the Arizona Cardinals at No. 3. (No complaints for Giants fans, as the player they took at No. 5, linebacker Arvell Reese, is an NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year candidate.)
And then there was the buildup to the trade deadline, where there was a near-constant buzz about the Giants’ interest in Indianapolis Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor. Though the Giants didn’t acquire him, it’s not hard to see running back remaining a focus once the clock shifts to the offseason. Perhaps a player like Parker would fit the mold the Giants are looking for to play alongside incumbent Cam Skattebo.
Brugler: Parker would be more of the quick, elusive option at running back, while Fletcher is the big, physical bruiser. The Giants already have that bruising style with Skattebo, but Harbaugh might be drawn to a back like Fletcher, who will remind him stylistically of the superstar he had in Baltimore: Derrick Henry. The Miami back is also stout in pass pro and serviceable in the screen game.
After an early running-back-by-committee approach, Skattebo has emerged as the featured back ahead of Tyrone Tracy Jr. (who is on injured reserve) and Devin Singletary. Skattebo’s 496 rushing yards lead the Giants, with Singletary the only other back with more than 100 rushing yards (114). Singletary will be a free agent, so it could be just Skattebo and Tracy in the RB room this offseason. Will the Giants want to invest a significant pick to add to their stable at the position? We’ll find out in a few months.
Brugler: At 6 feet 2 and 300 pounds with under 32-inch arms, Holmes doesn’t have elite measurables, but the tape shows a disruptive force. The Houston transfer leads all FBS interior linemen in pressures (45) and sacks (8.0) due to his ability to create knockback at the snap and maneuver through gaps. Holmes would immediately upgrade the Giants’ interior depth.
Though running back targets garnered the most chatter at the deadline, defensive tackle was also a spot the Giants could have addressed. The position was thin even before the Giants dealt away Dexter Lawrence this past offseason. And though offseason acquisitions D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris have been solid in the middle, Reader is 32, Harris is 35, and Harris is slated to be a free agent after this season. Though rookie Bobby Jamison-Travis has played well the past few games, the Giants must add some young talent here.
Brugler: Aside from Xavier Gilliam in the top half of Round 1, I don’t love this defensive tackle class, similar to last year. However, Washington has the talent to become an impactful NFL starter. At 6-3 and 319 pounds with almost 34-inch arms, he has outstanding tools but is still figuring out how to translate his ability into more consistent disruption. Right now, NFL scouts consider him a borderline top-50 prospect.
Brugler’s insight into the lack of depth in the tackle class, along with the Giants’ lack of 2027 draft picks, has us wondering whether the Giants might be better off targeting defensive tackle in free agency or via trade this offseason. We’re still a long way off from that kind of thing, but for those forward-looking Giants fans, it’s something to consider.
Brugler: Depending on which underclassmen declare, safety could be a sneaky stacked position in this draft class. I don’t think Jelani McDonald (Texas) or Ty Benefield (LSU) will make it to the Giants’ second-round pick, but Bowen could be an option.
Similar, in ways, to 2026 first-round pick Caleb Downs, Bowen doesn’t have exceptional size (5-11, 200 pounds) or 4.3 speed, but he plays fast and physical, and he competes with equal parts toughness and brains. After leading the Sooners in interceptions last season, he is doing so again in 2026 with three interceptions. The Giants will love his intangibles.
If the Giants want to continue adding to their secondary after selecting cornerback Colton Hood with a second-round pick in this past draft, safety might be the way to go based on Brugler’s insight into the class. Jevon Holland picked up his fourth interception of the season Thursday, but the Giants have played musical chairs at that second safety spot, with Jason Pinnock, Ar’Darius Washington and Tyler Nubin all playing significant snaps at different times this season.
Brugler: Potentially the top senior receiver drafted this year, Barkate can work inside or outside and win downfield or create after the catch in the screen game. He is a loose athlete at the top of routes and plays with the finishing toughness at the catch point. Barkate also checks the intangibles box with no need to worry about the smarts, considering he earned his economics degree from Harvard in only three years. He would give the Giants flexibility on offense.
The Giants have a No. 1 receiver in Malik Nabers, and third-round pick Malachi Fields has progressed nicely over the last few weeks, finding a solid connection with McCarthy. Beyond those two, however, the Giants’ young depth is thin. Adding a young playmaker to the room, even with tight end Isaiah Likely serving as the No. 2 target, would help make this offense even more difficult to defend.

full_text:
Mason McCormick was carted off the field on Sunday night. Katie Stratman / Imagn Images
The medical staff rushed onto the field Sunday in Cincinnati as Mason McCormick writhed in pain on the turf. The severity of the injury and the way the Pittsburgh Steelers’ feel about their starting left guard were clear from the player’s reaction. As the doctors and trainers fastened an air cast to McCormick’s right ankle and prepared to cart him off the field, teammates gathered around on a knee. Emotions flowed.
“It made a lot of us sick to our stomach,” tackle Troy Fautanu said. “I’ve never seen anything like that before.”
During the 38-18 blowout, the Bengals exposed the weaknesses on the Steelers’ roster , particularly Pittsburgh’s defensive backs and injury-marred receiving corps. As the Steelers look to move past the letdown, they will now be challenged to maintain their strength in the trenches without a key cog.
Pittsburgh built an identity and rode a four-game winning streak heading into Sunday night thanks in large part to their young and developing offensive line. From Weeks 5 through 8, only one team accumulated more rushing yards than Pittsburgh’s 564, and only two had a better yard per carry average than the Steelers’ 5.3. At a position group in which continuity and chemistry are critical, the Steelers’ offensive line will be tested to maintain that high level of play without one of the players most responsible for its success.
“It’s definitely a time to rally around it, because that was definitely a dynamic of this football team that we all want, especially me,” Steelers coach Mike McCarthy said. “I believe it starts in the trenches. I think the tradition, the history of the Steelers reflects that.
“We’ll continue to go down that road, but it’s time for others to step up. This is how every season goes. Unfortunately, you have injuries, and it’s opportunity for others. But it’s also an opportunity for us to make sure we’re utilizing all of our resources.”
The Steelers’ most significant investments up front may have come at tackle, with a pair of first-round picks in Fautanu and Max Iheanachor, and at center with second-round selection Zach Frazier. But the personality of the offensive line and the heartbeat flowed through the two trash-talking guards. Thrust into a starting role in the middle of his rookie season, McCormick has consistently improved to become a mauling run blocker, reliable pass protector and excellent communicator.
“I’ll just tell you from my perspective, Mason is clearly one of the leaders on the team,” McCarthy said, adding that McCormick is on the team’s leadership council.
Fautanu has often said there’s no one else he’d rather play alongside. Now, he has no choice in the matter. On Monday, McCarthy acknowledged that McCormick sustained a significant injury but did not have a definitive timeline. If the Steelers are going to maintain their playoff position and make some noise in December and January, they’ll need to weather this injury.
Versatile lineman Spencer Anderson appears to be the next man up. Drafted in the seventh round in 2023, Anderson has exceeded his draft position and proven to be a malleable piece of the offensive line. Over the years, he’s contributed at tackle, guard and as the sixth offensive lineman in jumbo packages.
“Spencer’s just a 360 football player in my view,” McCarthy said. “Just coming in here to see to see him play in different positions… He’s a gifted football player. This will be his opportunity.”
Where the starting left guard position goes from here will hinge upon a number of factors, including McCormick’s recovery timeline, Anderson’s performance and the readiness of rookie third-round pick Gennings Dunker, who is one of the x-factors.
At the University of Iowa, Dunker was arguably the most consistent lineman from a group that won the Joe Moore Award as the top offensive line in college football. The Hawkeyes’ run-heavy style of play was reflected in Dunker’s performance early in camp. His tape told two stories. As a run blocker, Dunker is already an old-school mauler, using his tree-trunk legs to punish defenders. However, he still needed considerable refinement as a pass protector, especially as he makes the transition from college tackle to NFL guard. McCarthy said that Dunker is “definitely part of the conversation” as the Steelers consider different possibilities.
Whether it’s Anderson, Dunker or some combination of the two, the Steelers will need to continue to lean on the men up front, even with one of the most important pieces missing. How well they handle the injury will play a major role in determing where the season goes from here.

CINCINNATI — After one of the worst games of his career, Aaron Rodgers made his way to the middle of the field. Yet because Rodgers has already achieved what Burrow currently hunts — a Super Bowl
full_text:
Aaron Rodgers tosses the ball to Jaylen Warren during the first half of the Steelers' lopsided, 38-18 loss to the Bengals on Sunday night. Joshua A. Bickel / Associated Press
CINCINNATI — After one of the worst games of his career, Aaron Rodgers made his way to the middle of the field. He embraced Joe Burrow, the young, cocky and artful quarterback with a rifle for a right arm, the quarterback Rodgers used to be. Yet because Rodgers has already achieved what Burrow currently hunts — a Super Bowl, MVPs, legend status — opponents sought him out. Sometimes just to touch his jersey. Photographers circled him as well. One got too close with his cell phone, so Rodgers reached for the photographer’s arm and moved it away.
It was his instinct to deflect, but we can’t stop looking at the conclusion of Aaron Rodgers’ NFL journey.
Rodgers, the league’s oldest player, has competed for so long, at such a high level, that he commands our attention. He has been crafting his hero’s tale that will be forever celebrated inside the Pro Football Hall of Fame, and the time to remember all the bombs thrown and his “I still own you!” bravado will come soon enough. But this season, like the one before it and the one before that , has changed the conversation. A performance like Sunday’s , when Rodgers started the game 0-for-8 and amassed all of 27 passing yards through three quarters before fluffing up the numbers in trash time, offers another visual of the story he has been writing for far too long.
It was a portrait of Aaron in autumn. And though he doesn’t care much for an observer’s “dramatic” view of him, the requiem of Aaron Rodgers’ career, this twilight, deserves the truth — that he should’ve retired three years ago.
As sports fans, we romanticize an era, a segment of a star’s prime, but hardly ever consider the totality of a career. Rodgers will likely get that pass too. Those who loved him in Green Bay, or even tolerated him in New York and Pittsburgh, might look past his QBR, which has plummeted over the past three seasons: 44.7, 44.4 and presently 46.8. Those who believe we must speak reverently of the elderly will ignore that in his final season, Rodgers is producing the third-lowest touchdown percentage in 19 years of full-time quarterbacking.
For the rest of us, this ending shouldn’t be glossed over. We shouldn’t be so blinded by the gold of his soon-coming jacket from Canton that we all but blot out what is happening now. As though we don’t notice a quarterback orchestrating a shockingly below-average offense akin to a check-down party; once upon a time, he threw the ball downfield in the range of 10 air yards per attempt, but now he averages 6.5 AY/A, ranking 20th in the NFL.
As if we can’t read the lips of a teammate — Rodgers is a captain, mind you — who earlier this season dropped a barrage of expletives on one of his wide receivers after he dropped a pass. Though he saved his poutiest profanity for his head coach when Mike McCarthy didn’t call a play quickly enough during a Thursday night game.
As though we are not witnessing a 42-year-old man in complete and utter misery.
When the game isn’t going his way, Rodgers’ annoyance at everything and everyone is palpable. During national broadcasts, he features in montages that show various states of his frustration. On Sunday night, NBC cameras caught Rodgers shaking his head and whispering to himself after rookie Germie Bernard dropped one of his targets. Another time, his eyes’ laser beams were intended to annihilate someone on the Steelers’ sideline; the slo-mo replay showed Rodgers mouthing a word that started with the letter “F.”
You know it’s not going well for the Steelers when NBC gives you the exasperated Aaron Rodgers montage to commercial break. pic.twitter.com/IuS2Ffptbo
— Andrew Fillipponi (@ThePoniExpress) November 16, 2026
Rodgers kept it clean and in a monotone when addressing reporters after the 38-18 loss. But he wouldn’t let an opportunity pass to give attitude to a reporter. When ESPN’s Brooke Pryor asked how the Steelers can keep a loss like this from changing the trajectory of the season, Rodgers, again with the instincts, flashed a sly grin and replied: “Aww, that’s very dramatic there, Brooke. But uh, I’ve been a part of this league for a long time. There’s big wins, there’s tough losses. So we’ll deal with this appropriately.”
The sum of his 22nd season, all of this, makes it awkward to watch. Like being forced to endure weekly tantrums from the world’s oldest toddler. Yet even more unpleasant than his abysmal body language is Rodgers’ performance as a QB1. Whatever he has left constrains Pittsburgh’s offense, which ranks 19th in the league. The Steelers aren’t in the playoff hunt because of a gunslinger of a quarterback who decided to unholster his talents for one more year. They are surviving because of an elite defense that has nothing to do with the curmudgeon who’s tossing short passes and cursing out teammates.
This is not an assault on age. Stephen Curry, forever boyish even at 38 years old, still makes basketball look like one of life’s simple pleasures. When Curry is healthy — and it’s basketball’s loss that he’s not at the moment — he’s still unquestionably his team’s best player, able to sink 3s from any distance and shame Luka Dončić with his artistry of dribbles . Joy will color the epitaph of his career.
For Rodgers, however, drab is starting to define his.
Behind the scenes, Rodgers is painted with a much more forgiving palette. Though the production team showed one thing, NBC’s Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth shared stories of Rodgers inviting guys over on Mondays and of those team dinners Saturday night on the road. And yes, even receivers speak glowingly of the exacting legend who quizzes them in team meetings and offers notes whenever possible.
“Challenging me on the football field. You know, knowing the coverages, knowing the playbook, knowing what to do,” Bernard said Sunday inside an emptying locker room, recalling Rodgers’ impact in his rookie season. “He’s always asking me what I think in this coverage, and then, you know, whatever my answer is, he’ll coach me up on that because he’s been playing the game for a long time, so he has a lot of knowledge and everything like that. So I just try to take in everything that he’s thrown my way. It’s been very beneficial for me.”
And this from receiver Brandon Smith: “One thing I’ve learned through my (career), never let someone else’s expectations of you exceed your own. No matter how hard he is on us, our expectations (are higher) than what his is for us. If I mess up anything — which I did a couple times (Sunday) with a bunch of checks — I take that to heart. Anything, no matter what he does or what he says, (and) he’s not too bad, he’s just correcting. But nothing he does or says is worse than what I’m already telling myself.”
It would be an insult to reality to behold the respect that teammates and rivals have for Rodgers, and not weigh that against his own production during these final years. Especially this one. Rodgers can and should be praised for his glory years in green and gold. However, since he chose to come back as a Jet, and now a Steeler, this phase must be evaluated and remembered as truthfully as the greatness that came before it.

full_text:
Kirk Cousins' return to Minnesota has the Vikings surging, while Drake Maye's injury has Patriots nation worried. Illustration: Will Tullos / The Athletic; Photos: Patrick McDermott / Getty Images and Lennart Preiss / Associated Press
Every week during the season, Josh Kendall and Chad Graff rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.
The power rankings are getting ready for the NFL’s stretch run by picking a breakout player for each of the 32 teams.
Kirk Cousins and the Minnesota Vikings are our big risers of the week as the top of this list continues to solidify around the elite teams.
Breakout player: Greg Rousseau
The sixth-year outside linebacker has been good for a long time. He’s trending toward great this year and has already tied his career high in sacks with eight, which ranks fourth in the league. Third-year wide receiver Keon Coleman is also on track for career highs in yards and catches. Despite just one reception for 11 yards (and one concussion check) on Sunday, Coleman has 24 catches for 315 yards.
Up nex t : vs. Dolphins, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Cowboys 46-40
Breakout player: Renardo Green
The third-year cornerback had a tough day on Sunday against George Pickens and company, but he was dealing with a back injury and had already built up plenty of goodwill this year. Green, a second-round pick in 2024, has four interceptions, three more than he had in his first two seasons combined. Rookie running back Kaelon Black has also been a surprise with 356 rushing yards behind Christian McCaffrey.
Up next: vs. Vikings, Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Jonah Coleman
The fourth-round rookie running back had 36 touches for 192 yards of offense in weeks 8 and 9. That ranked 17th in the league in that stretch. For the season, he’s averaging 9.8 yards per reception, and he could have a big day against a middling Raiders defense this weekend.
Up next: vs. Raiders, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Falcons 35-13
Breakout player: Emmett Johnson
With Kenneth Walker out Sunday, Johnson, a fifth-round rookie running back, had 22 carries for 101 yards against the Falcons, which was almost as much as he had in his first eight games combined. Johnson also has 20 catches this season for 307 yards. In general, it’s tough to pick a breakout player in Kansas City, where it feels like all the contributors have been around forever, but Johnson has been a meaningful addition.
Up next: vs. Cardinals, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Bhayshul Tuten
Jacksonville let Travis Etienne leave in free agency because the Jaguars thought Tuten was ready for a starting role. They were right. The second-year running back already has career highs in rushing yards (609), carries (148) and total touchdowns (eight). He’s 14th in the league in rushing.
Up next: at Giants, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Luther Burden
Ben Johnson was bullish about his second-year wide receiver in the preseason, and we’re seeing why. Burden is 16th in the league with 644 receiving yards, and 385 of those came in his last four games. From weeks 6 through 9, he had more receiving yards than all but five players in the league, and he got 23.5 percent of the Bears’ passing targets. That last number may go up as the season progresses.
Up next: vs. Saints, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Steelers 38-18
Breakout player: Boye Mafe
The Bengals gave the fifth-year pass rusher a three-year, $60 million free-agent deal in the offseason, and it’s proving to be a good move. Mafe had another sack Sunday night and has 6.5 for the season, plus 11 quarterback hits. At this pace, he’ll easily hit his career highs in both categories. He’s had at least one sack in five of his last six games.
Up next: at Commanders, Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Packers 30-10
Breakout player: Levi Drake Rodriguez
We’re going pretty far off the board here, but how often do you get to publicize a guy who played his college football at Southwestern Assemblies of God and East Texas A&M? A seventh-round pick in 2024, the former Prospect X has started every game for the Vikings this year and had two sacks Sunday to give him a career-high three for the season.
Up next: at 49ers, Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Patriots 35-10
Breakout player: Alim McNeill
The sixth-year defensive tackle already has a career high in sacks (6.5) and quarterback hits (11), and the Lions are going to need him more than ever with Aidan Hutchinson out due to injury. Detroit proved again Sunday that its offense is Super Bowl-worthy, but the defense is 28th in the league in defensive EPA (minus-5.2 per 100 snaps).
Up next: vs. Buccaneers, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Raiders 21-13
Breakout player: Drew Lock
The Seahawks’ backup quarterback started his third game Sunday in place of the injured Sam Darnold. Seattle has won all three of those games. Among quarterbacks with more than 50 attempts this season, Lock is third in the league in EPA per dropback (0.32). He has seven passing touchdowns and no interceptions, and that last number has some Seahawks fans wondering if he’s a better option than the turnover-prone Darnold.
Sunday: Beat Cardinals 34-6
Breakout player: Quentin Lake
In his fifth year, the cornerback has already tripled the career interception total he had entering the season, with three. He has also forced two fumbles and has 65 tackles. Lake also has what may be the quote of the year this season, saying on “ The St. Brown Podcast ” that Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert “was throwing deli meat out there.”
Sunday: Lost to Vikings 30-10
Breakout player: Christian Watson
The ambulance clip alone gives Watson the nod here, but the fifth-year wide receiver is having a career year on top of that. Watson is third in the league in receiving yards (916) and tied for third in receiving touchdowns (seven). Watson had not topped 620 receiving yards in any of his previous four seasons.
Sunday: Lost to Bengals 38-18
Breakout player: Jaylen Warren
The fifth-year running back was disappointing Sunday night, but so were all of the other Steelers. For the season, Warren has been great. He has 126 carries for 719 yards and leads all running backs with 5.7 yards per carry. He’s second in the league in yards per carry after contact (4.04).
Up next: at Eagles, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Harold Fannin Jr.
It’s not exactly a breakout year for the Browns’ second-year tight end because he was excellent as a rookie and has been great again in Year 2. He had seven catches for 91 yards on Sunday, and now has 19 for 287 yards in the last three games. Fannin has 44 catches for 544 yards and four touchdowns on the season.
Sunday: Lost to Lions 35-10
Breakout player: Elijah Ponder
The second-year edge rusher had four sacks last year as an undrafted free-agent rookie. This year, he has 7.5, and he had another five tackles against the Lions on Sunday. Wide receiver Mack Hollins, who is on his sixth team in his ninth professional year, is also having a career year with 48.8 receiving yards per game.
Thursday: Lost to Commanders 24-21
Breakout player: Isaiah Likely
Brock Bowers and Trey McBride are the only tight ends in the league with more receiving yards than Likely, who has 575 this year. After following John Harbaugh from Baltimore and getting out of Mark Andrews’ shadow, Likely already has career highs in yards, catches (55) and touchdowns (seven). He had nine catches for a career-high 127 yards against Washington.
Up next: vs. Jaguars, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Breakout player: Zyon McCollum
The fifth-year cornerback has a career-high four interceptions, which is one more than he had in his first four seasons combined. McCollum also has a fumble recovery and 28 solo tackles for a talented defense that makes the Buccaneers the favorites in the NFC South.
Up next: at Lions, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET

full_text:
Linebacker Sonny Styles, right, has helped lead a rising Commanders defense. Sarah Stier / Getty Images
Sonny Styles had seen this before and, this time, he refused to watch the Giants skate past him with the game on the line.
So, before New York could get fully set in an empty formation Thursday night, the Commanders rookie warned his teammates, yelling and furiously pointing to the left side. Sure enough, a receiver motioned inside from the left, J.J. McCarthy took the snap, and just as the Giants set up two crack blocks, Styles sprinted through the gap to take down the quarterback for a loss of two.
“I was just really thinking about the last time we played them,” Styles said. “… When they went empty, kind of just looking at the tight end, looked like he was cracking, because I think someone else, I think Charles (Omenihu), somebody said something too. Kind of had the idea it was a QB run, so I just reacted.”
The Giants ran a similar play in overtime against the Commanders in Week 5, again against the Houston Texans two weeks later and again in the third quarter of Washington’s win on Thursday, each time using running back Cam Skattebo on the toss.
But Styles’ stop late in the fourth quarter, after his quarterback had thrown interceptions on consecutive possessions, set in motion a Washington defensive rally that all but saved this season .
The Commanders (3-5-1) have grown accustomed to close finishes; six of their nine games have been decided by one score, and most have ended with them on the losing side. Critical mistakes and late-game blunders cost them repeatedly, but since their Week 7 bye, when the team made some necessary adjustments to its schemes, the defense has found a groove.
The communication breakdowns that Washington players and coaches have cited as an issue for years were clearly lessened. The fourth-quarter defensive lapses that plagued the team early in the season have been replaced by defensive stops and havoc-wreaking plays. And the critical situations the defense once struggled with have, in recent weeks, become the Commanders’ forte.
Washington’s defense still has plenty of work to become a top-tier unit, but its progress in only a short time under first-year coordinator Daronte Jones has been unmistakable — and sorely needed.
Last season, the Commanders finished at or near the bottom of the league in most major defensive statistical categories, including yards allowed (32nd), scoring (27th), takeaways (31st), defensive EPA per play (31st), opponent explosive play rate (30th), first downs (31st) and red zone efficiency (31st), according to TruMedia.
They were slightly improved in most categories over the first six games this season, but not by much.
Over the past three games, however, the Commanders have turned a corner — allowing only 17.0 points per game (seventh-fewest in the NFL in that span) after giving up an average of 28.7 points (28th) in the first six games — while coming up with multiple late-game stops. They totaled five sacks and forced two turnovers in a dominant win over the Eagles in Week 8, had two more takeaways and held the Rams to only three of 14 third-down conversions in a Week 9 loss, then shut down the Giants late to preserve a win that also preserved their season (and possibly the job of coach Dan Quinn).
Over the last three games, the Commanders have allowed 4.9 yards per play to rank 14th in the NFL in that span, up from 22nd in the first six games (5.6 yards). They’ve also jumped eight spots to rank 16th in defensive EPA/play (0.04), are seventh in both opponent explosive pass rate (9.4 percent) and turnovers per drive (17.1 percent) and have the eighth-best third-down defense (29.3 percent conversion rate) after tying for 25th (44.4 percent) in the first six games. They are tied for ninth in red-zone efficiency (50 percent), a massive leap from 32nd (81.8 percent) before their bye.
But the biggest sign of their improvement didn’t show up on the stat sheet. After Stefon Diggs’ go-ahead touchdown catch with about a minute remaining on Thursday, Jones’ defense didn’t ease up to simply attempt to prevent a subsequent Giants score. Rather, it dialed up the pressure with Cover 0 blitzes during New York’s final drive.
Twice, safety Jeremy Reaves got a hand on McCarthy’s arm as he dropped back to the throw. Cornerback Rasul Douglas deflected the ball on one of those deep pass attempts, then intercepted the second one, intended for Malik Nabers.
It was the second time in three games that Douglas came up with a game-sealing interception.
“I mean, that’s the situation we want to be in, being up and being able to close it out,” Douglas said. “We take pride in that. That’s what we practice, that’s what went over, that’s what we harped on. So it’s just good to finally execute it.”
But Washington’s work is just beginning.
“We’re still giving up too many yards and some explosive plays in the secondary — well, not in the secondary, on the defense, but specifically in the passing game,” Quinn said Monday. “And that’s the spot that’s the last hurdle … because I like how hard they’re playing. I like the disguises. I like that Daronte’s in and out of packages. But that would be the last step, and I feel like we’re much closer to that.”
Next Monday will be the Commanders’ toughest challenge yet, against a Cincinnati Bengals offense that just pasted 38 points and 484 yards of offense on the Pittsburgh Steelers .
Although it has many of the same stars, this Cincinnati team isn’t the same one the Commanders stunned on a Monday night in 2024. Quarterback Joe Burrow now has a sound offensive line and a menacing defense to boot.
The changes have helped the Bengals flourish into one of the most prolific offenses, with the best passing attack (298.9 yards per game) through Week 10.
For Washington to have a chance, it’ll need every bit of its defensive improvement — and then some — to show up.
“Yeah. It’s a challenge. It’s a challenge for every defense,” Quinn acknowledged. “… In this game, it’s gonna take extreme precision to make sure of right leverage, right location, because these receivers and quarterback are capable of attacking a certain leverage. … That’s usually what it comes down to — right leverage, right location, making plays on the ball. And it’ll take us playing a really clean game in that sense against an excellent offense.”

title: Cardinals Hit Rock Bottom With Stunning Chiefs Betting Spread
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are currently 16.5-point underdogs to the Kansas City Chiefs ahead of Week 11.
That ties the Miami Dolphins (against the Buffalo Bills this week) for the largest betting spread of the 2026 season.
"Kansas City has jumped out as a 16.5-point favorite after this line first opened at -14 when they host the Cardinals," CBS Sports' Tyler Sullivan wrote .
"The Chiefs are coming off a dominant win over the Falcons, in which Patrick Mahomes threw five touchdowns. They head back to Arrowhead Stadium where they are 3-1 ATS and have an average margin of victory of 15.8 (second-best in the NFL). Arizona is 4-2 ATS on the road."
Kansas City is one of the hottest teams in the league at the moment, having out-scored opponents 70-25 within the last two weeks. Patrick Mahomes looks healthy after avoiding a major elbow injury while Andy Reid and co. typically handle business at Arrowhead.
The last time the Chiefs saw the Cardinals, Kansas City easily handled Arizona in 44-21 fashion to begin the 2022 season.
This will be Carson Beck's first road start of his career. The third-round rookie made his NFL debut last week and managed to play somewhat well despite several injuries impacting the offensive side of the ball.
Sledding won't get any easier against the Chiefs, who are allowing a third-best 17.3 points per game.
Reality has hit the 3-7 Cardinals hard over the last few weeks, which has prompted head coach Mike LaFleur to begin the evaluation process for the future over the remaining seven games on Arizona's schedule.
“I believe in the guys in that room. I love this locker room," LaFleur told reporters on Monday after their blowout loss to the Los Angeles Rams in Week 10.
"They want to do right, trust me. They want to do right and they play hard. That fourth quarter got a little out of whack. It wasn't an effort thing — guys were trying to do a little too much and that's when those things can happen. It ends up being leaky yards in 15 straight carries or whatever it was. These guys will step up, they will. We need to step up and not just continue to fight, but we have to go execute and we have to make some plays.”
The spread could certainly shift over the coming days, though the Cardinals will undoubtedly be eye-opening underdogs when action begins in Kansas City.

title: Cardinals' Injury Crisis Deepens With 2 More Players Sidelined
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals have struggled with health since the first day of training camp.
As we enter Week 11 of the regular season, the hits keep coming.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur told reporters that outside linebacker Jordan Burch would be out for the rest of the season with an MCL injury while starting safety Andrew Wingard suffered a wrist injury and will miss extended time. Wingard won't be placed on injured reserve at this point in time.
"Not shocked at anything. Again, I'll just always go back to really it sucks for the player," LaFleur added in his Monday press conference.
"Yeah, it sucks for our club and and all those kind of things but injuries happen. It sucks for the player, and the list just continues to grow. But that's who I'm feeling for more. He [Wingard] hated missing a few games, whatever it was, three games, four games, and he wanted to be out there with his boys. He got back out there, and here we are.
"So we'll see how long it's going to be, but it's most likely not going to be the year or anything like that. But he'll be out for some time."
Prior to this week, the Cardinals had 15 players on some sort of injury designation list, spanning from PUP to IR. Health has simply not been on Arizona's side this season, as the Cardinals are now thin on both sides of the ball.
LaFleur, fresh off the Week 10 loss to the Los Angeles Rams where the Cardinals practically had a practice squad offense on the field, wasn't looking for excuses.
"We got what we've got right now," LaFleur told reporters after Sunday.
"It is what it is, and I told the guys there's no magic wand. There's no magic savior. We have seven more weeks of a massive evaluation to see how this roster's going to look. I put it on front street for the guys. It's shared accountability. It's collective. There's absolutely no doubt, but we can play better than that. We can make plays better than that. We can block better than that. We can stop the run better than that with what we have. There's no doubt in my mind and credit to them. They're a dang good football team. We know that. These next seven weeks are going to be awesome, starting with this week."
Arizona faces the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 11.

title: 3 Big Things Carson Beck Said After Cardinals Debut, And Why They Matter
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Beckoning is officially taking over the desert.
Arizona Cardinals quarterback Carson Beck now has his first NFL start under his belt. Despite the team's 34-6 loss to the Rams, Beck managed to play well despite a poor statistical outing and an even more disappointing cast of players around him .
After the game, Beck met with reporters.
The three biggest things he said — and why they matter:
Beck: “It was a super cool opportunity to go out there and have the chance to be a quarterback for this football team. (It was) obviously not the result that we wanted, but we just probably needed to make a couple more plays. Myself and — we weren't able to do that. But again, for (my) first time being out there, I felt comfortable. I felt like the game came to me well early. Again, I’m just really, really excited about the opportunity that I was given. And again, obviously we didn't get the result we wanted, but we have more games ahead and we'll watch the film, look to get better and then move from there.”
Why it matters : It's all about settling in your own as a rookie quarterback, and that's one of the positives Beck showed on the field. The moment didn't look too big for him. Beck wasn't out of sorts and didn't look lost at any point — which is a huge building block.
Beck: “I just (wanted) to go around to everyone and just tell them that I appreciate them; I appreciate their effort. This is a team game and I am unable to do what I do without all the other ten around me. I’m just appreciating (them) and saying thank you for their effort, thank you for their attention to detail and their sacrifice throughout the week. These weeks aren't easy; you prepare, you prepare, you prepare, and you look for the result you want. We weren't able to get that today, but that doesn't mean that the preparation was put to waste. You love on those guys, you thank them, you tell them you appreciate them, and that's that. We're teammates at the end of the day. We've got to stick together and we have to figure out how to turn this thing around."
Why it matters : Beck was walking around the locker room and personally thanking teammates for their efforts in the blowout loss. Even as a rookie who just played his first game, Beck understands his role as a leader in this moment.
Beck: “I thought for me personally (from a) preparation standpoint, (it) was good. I thought my week of prep and how much (Cardinals QB) Coach (Matt) Schaub, (Cardinals Offensive Coordinator Nathaniel) Coach (Hackett) and Coach LaFleur poured into me and making sure that I was ready for the game, knew the plan and knew what they were doing on defense.
"They did an amazing job (in) helping me be prepared and out there, I felt comfortable. I knew our plan and I felt like I was seeing it well. With all that being said, I think when we have the plays, I’ve got to make them. Especially when you’re playing against a good defense, you can’t afford to not make the big plays and (not) make the big explosives because those are game shifters.
"When you’re not able to do that, the game gets away from you. I think for me it’s just in those moments — it’s the NFL, everybody’s good, so when you are playing these elite defenses, you have to make the plays when they show themselves and we weren’t able to do that in some cases. There were just a couple of third downs in there where we get a conversion, we keep drives going, and get our defense off the field for a little bit. Maybe you get an explosive after.
"Obviously, I just got off the field so I couldn’t kind of pinpoint some of them but really (it’s) just converting better, playing better on third down and then being able to hit some of those deep shots and the explosive plays when we need them because again, those change games.”
Why it matters : Beck is a process-oriented player, which focuses more on the prep rather than the final outcome. That might not mean much in the moment, but when looking at the big picture, the mindset to keep going instead of simply throwing everything away after a loss will prove to be pivotal in the long run.

title: 4 Brutal Truths Cardinals Must Face After Another Blowout Loss
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals drop to a 3-7 record after their Week 10 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, pouring in a very forgettable day even with hope and optimism high around the team with rookie quarterback Carson Beck playing his first action in the NFL.
The 34-6 loss completely dimmed that light.
Four brutal truths the organizaton has to face moving forward
The Cardinals' current roster is nowhere close to what the team looks like totally healthy. Arizona, once again, has been battered by injuries — an unfortunate reality for everybody involved.
Yet we're closing in on the fourth year of Monti Ossenfort's tenure in the desert. While injuries have piled, so too have losses — and after head coach Jonathan Gannon was sent packing last offseason, all signs point towards Ossenfort suffering the same fate.
Ossenfort isn't responsible for health, though the bottom line suggests that he is the mastermind of the product Cardinals fans have seen within the last four seasons with little success on the field, in free agency or during the draft.
It truly feels like a matter of when — not if — Ossenfort is relieved of his duties.
Oh, how quickly Nick Rallis' defense has crashed down to earth.
It wasn't long ago where we were celebrating a revamped Arizona defense. What was once one of the worst units in the league suddenly pulled themselves up by the bootstraps and turned things around, playing with a level of motor and confidence not seen all season.
The Rams' humbling 30-burger — capped by L.A. getting the ball with over 12 minutes left in the fourth and keeping it until the clock hit zero — suggests we may have struck fool's gold in previous weeks.
The Cardinals' defense (pending Monday Night Football) is tied for a league-worst 28.9 points per game allowed.
The Cardinals decided to retain two of the biggest trade deadline names in Josh Sweat and Budda Baker. Exactly why remains to be seen, though interest was significant enough in both veteran defenders that it was a bit surprising to see Arizona not pull off a deal and continue stacking 2027 draft picks.
Neither player was impactful on Sunday — but in fairness, that's valid for practically everybody who suited up yesterday. But the Cardinals now find themselves at 3-7, a massively depleted roster, and truly no reason for either Baker or Sweat to be on this roster to finish out the season.
While Baker reportedly fetched a second-round pick in trade discussions, Sweat's price tag wasn't quite known — though it's believed Arizona wanted a Day 2 pick. Baker has one year left on his deal after this season while Sweat will either demand a new contract or a trade this offseason.
If this is the result we're expecting for the majority of games the rest of the way, Arizona would have much better off looking ahead to the future and preparing for a big 2027 offseason than keeping Sweat and Baker around.
Hindsight will forever be 20/20, and in fairness, the Cardinals weren't going to play a rookie third-round pick over veterans in Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew in the beginning of the season. If we're stretching this even further, the only reason Beck played as early in the season as he did was due to injuries.
Beck finished with a forgettable box score in his NFL debut, though that was mostly due to a very poor offensive line that allowed five sacks and a receiving corps that couldn't hold up its end of the deal. As far as the eye test, Beck passed .
Yet it's tough not to wonder how Beck and the Cardinals' offense would have looked with a fully healthy attack. Building blocks such as Paris Johnson, Chase Bisontis, Michael Wilson and Jeremiyah Love are just some of the key names missing around Beck that could have really made a difference.
Not just in terms of winning a football game, but also forming opinions on Beck and his evaluation ahead of 2027.

title: Cardinals Winners & Losers: Carson Beck Shines Despite Ugly Rams Loss
full_text:
ARIZONA — Carson Beck's debut was a mixed bag of results for the Arizona Cardinals.
The box score was ugly in the team's 34-6 thumping by the Los Angeles Rams in Week 10. However, Beck played mostly well given the poor circumstances.
The rest of the team can't really say much.
The Cardinals continue to see injuries impact their squad, and when evaluating winners and losers from Sunday, there's much left to be desired.
Beck finished with 11 completions on 18 passing attempts for 108 yards and two interceptions. These numbers may be the worst ever for a "biggest winner" category, but circumstances and individual play on the field tell a much different story.
Beck, quite frankly, was let down by his teammates. Numerous drives were killed by drops. Beck's first interception was massively unlucky after the pass slipped through the receiver's hands while his second pick was a wrong route run by the running back.
Beck, as much as he could, showed promise moving into the future. He did numerous things well and his debut was only a failure on a macro level because his teammates couldn't hold their end of the bargain.
The Cardinals' defense has been impacted by injuries all season, though they were the much healthier side entering Week 10. They didn't play like it.

title: Carson Beck Debut Reveals Cardinals' Big-Picture Problem
full_text:
GLENDALE — It's hours after action at State Farm Stadium concluded, and the Arizona Cardinals' roof is no longer open. The once sun-filled top of the stadium now sits capped with stadium lights illuminating the field where the Los Angeles Rams handed Carson Beck a 34-6 loss in his debut.
It's a perfect representation for how the Cardinals' season has quickly turned. A win last week in Seattle would have pushed Arizona to 4-5 on the year, keeping them alive in the playoff hunt and injecting a massive boost of hope in a year that wasn't expected to yield anything close.
Yet including today, the Cardinals' last two losses now sink them to 3-7 on the season. Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur knows what's at stake to finish these last seven games — and what isn't.
"We got what we've got right now," LaFleur told reporters post-game, as injuries have plagued Arizona's roster.
"It is what it is, and I told the guys there's no magic wand. There's no magic savior. We have seven more weeks of a massive evaluation to see how this roster's going to look. I put it on front street for the guys. It's shared accountability. It's collective."
Beck was the lone bright spot for Arizona on a day where practically nothing went their way, and that speaks volumes on Arizona's biggest issues.
"All in all, for the amount of plays and what we asked him to do, I was impressed with what we asked," LaFleur said of Beck. The third-round pick completed 11-of-18 passes for 108 yards and two interceptions.
" ... It's just a collection of errors on offense. All you ask these guys to do is do their job and I thought he did his job."
The box score doesn't show, but Beck looked competent and in control — something Cardinals fans have been clamoring for. Beck pushed the ball to all three levels of the defense and was massively held back by his teammates.
Beck's arrival to the field was met with a harsh reality — that even if he was their best player on the field tonight, the Cardinals have so many other holes to fill across the roster.
Beck was sacked five times by Los Angeles' defense. The Cardinals rushed for just 34 yards tonight on 11 carries. While Trey McBride paced Arizona in receiving, Beck's crew of scout-team pass-catchers had drops in key moments through the first two quarters before things got out of hand.
Defensively, the Cardinals again didn't stop a team from reaching 30 points. Week 10 marked the seventh time in the last nine weeks where Arizona allowed a team to reach that coveted benchmark. Their performance today was capped by allowing the Rams to get possession with 12:15 left in the fourth quarter... and couldn't muster a single stop before the clock hit zero.
Collectively , the Cardinals can't get anything going on both sides of the ball. That's been a familiar tune for much of the regular season.
The issue isn't Beck playing well. It's that the Cardinals are trying to solve the most important position in sports, and their rookie quarterback played considerably well with absolutely no help around him, and nothing to show for it.
"We have seven more weeks and like I said, we're going to take it one week at a time, but it's going to be a great evaluation over these next seven weeks to see what we've got and see how we're going to build this thing," a clearly frustrated LaFleur added post-game.
Whether Beck is a building block for LaFleur and the Cardinals in the future still remains to be seen. That's a question that will be answered in due time.
However, Beck's performance offered a clear reality check: While injuries have thrown this season sideways, the Cardinals' overall philosophy on team-building and lack of depth again has been exposed.
And that's not something that can be fixed in free agency — or a single draft class. Getting key players back healthy will be needed, though this was a similar drum beat we heard prior to the start of last season.
The Cardinals can't afford to equate health for progress. Their third-round rookie quarterback made that clear tonight in his debut.

title: Carson Beck's Cardinals Debut: The Good, Bad And Ugly
full_text:
GLENDALE — Carson Beck's debut for the Arizona Cardinals drew plenty of hype, attention and chatter ahead of Week 10's matchup against the Los Angeles Rams.
Eyes in the desert were glued to action at State Farm Stadium to see what the rookie quarterback could muster in spite of a truly underwhelming cast around him and a Rams defense that holds two of the league's best pass rushers.
Those eyes either turned their televisions off or hit the exits by the middle of the third quarter.
The Cardinals' 34-6 defeat to Los Angeles was eye-opening for a few reasons — Arizona ran just 34 offensive plays. Beck turned the ball over twice. Glimmers of hope were eradicated by halftime.
Yet it's not all bad in the desert, as Beck's box score doesn't tell the entire story of what happened.
That sounds incredibly odd given the score and Beck's 108 passing yards with no touchdowns and two turnovers, but the reality is Beck operated at a high level given the horrid circumstances handed to him — which we'll touch on later.
Beck spread the ball around effectively through short, intermediate and deep passes while proving himself as a mobile presence in the pocket. Drops by numerous wideouts truly killed any chances of sustaining momentum after the second drive.
Tape doesn't lie. While Beck clearly has room for improvement, he was the furthest reason as to why the Cardinals pack their bags as losers from State Farm Stadium. Pound for pound, he delivered on his end.
Beck wasn't completely off the mark for a majority of passes, though the ones that were missed weren't pretty.
After his first interception wasn't close to falling on his shoulders, Beck's second pick of the day was an unfortunate mix of a poor throw and great play by Rams linebacker Wesley Bailey — who peeled off his own receiver to undercut the ball.
WESLEY BAILEY RIPPED IT AWAY FOR HIS FIRST NFL INTERCEPTION 😤 📺 @NFLonCBS | #RamsHouse pic.twitter.com/upvqsq5djk
Beck's eyes were central the whole time, tipping Bailey to the middle and unfortunately for Arizona, that gamble paid off.
The other throw was a big missed opportunity deep downfield, where Zay Jones was streaking open. Beck floated the ball a bit too much, forcing Jones to adjust inside (rather than placing the ball ahead or outside) and ultimately the pass fell incomplete.
This was Beck's first taste of legitimate NFL action, and there does need to be some patience with the rookie quarterback in terms of growth and acclimation to the speed and timing of the game. Still, those are the two top passes he'd love to have back.
The Cardinals trotted out a patchwork offensive line, practice squad receivers and a depleted running back room against one of the league's fiercest defensive fronts. It was a recipe for disaster that no chef could stop.
Beck, as an individual, played up to par given expectations. The same can't be said for the rest of the offense, or his defense that has now allowed 30 or more points in seven of the last nine weeks.
Beck was sacked five times on the day. Arizona's 34 offensive plays matches the amount of yards they had on the ground. The Cardinals went 0-6 on third down and had just one drive of five or more plays after the first quarter. Numerous drops from players stalled any potential scoring drives.
Beck had an ugly supporting cast around him, to say the least.

title: 4 Big Instant Reactions After Cardinals' Frustrating Loss vs Rams
full_text:
In some ways, a new era started for the Arizona Cardinals; in some ways it did not.
Rookie quarterback Carson Beck notched his first start in a 34-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams — an unfortunate scoreline that is nothing new for Arizona.
Starting on a positive note, the rookie signal-caller finished his much-anticipated debut going 11-for-18 through the air for 108 yards and two interceptions. On paper, those numbers are pretty porous. However, this is one of those cases where the tape did not reflect the stats.
Starting with the interceptions, Beck's first pick was not his fault. It was a great pass to an open wideout that bounced off the receiver's hands and into the hands of Rams safety Kamren Kinchens. The second interception was a great catch by Rams linebacker Wesley Bailey while Beck was targeting Cardinals running back Tyler Allgeier.
Sure, Beck could have looked to throw elsewhere. But Bailey made an amazing play, so it's hard to fault Beck that much.
Another reason Beck was better than his numbers? Many of his completions weren't simple dink and dunks. There is a time and place to go short in the NFL, but often, rookie quarterbacks avoid big plays and check the ball down. That wasn't the case, as Beck pushed the ball downfield more than Cardinals fans are used to, including a 31-yard strike (23 being air yards before the reception) to wideout Devin Duvernay.
Did Beck look like the next Kurt Warner for Arizona? No, but there were still plenty of positives against a tough Rams defense.
With both teams going into this matchup with their star receivers out, it seemed like a big day for the tight ends. That was the case for the Rams, as Los Angeles tight ends Davis Allen and Tyler Higbee both caught touchdown passes against the Cardinals' defense.
Meanwhile, for Arizona, Trey McBride had only 37 yards and no touchdowns on the day. This was McBride's second-lowest receiving output of the season, with his lowest being 31 yards in Week 4.
Now, to be fair, I am not blaming McBride at all. However, this falls on the coaching staff. Head coach Mike LaFleur knew that the top Cardinals receiver, Michael Wilson , would be out for this game. Having McBride be so limited is a coaching error by LaFleur.
Arizona's defense started this game on a fantastic note. Through the first quarter and most of the second, the Cardinals defense looked like a Super Bowl-caliber unit. They held the Rams to field goals, stuffed the run, and intercepted Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford.
This all changed before the second half. The game looked like it would be a 10-3 lead for Los Angeles going into the half. However, after a Beck interception with 43 seconds left in the half, the Rams scored another touchdown to go up 17-3. The defense then spiraled from there.
In the second half, the Rams added another 17 points to reach 34 total. Stafford looked completely comfortable in the second half, which was the opposite of how he looked in the first half. While I had the Rams winning, it was unfortunate, given how bad their defense looked after such a promising start.
While another loss is to be expected with the number of injuries Arizona has, the lack of incomplete halves is a trend that needs to stop. In most games this season, it seems like the Cardinals are either bad, to the point of nothing working in either the first or second half.
While it is never fun to call for someone's job, the world of football is tough, and I think Arizona's coaches and front office have seen enough to move on from defensive coordinator Nick Rallis , especially after this bad defensive outing. Offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett is also not safe, and he could get let go, as the Cardinals offense put up back-to-back bad offensive games.
Overall, another ugly division loss, which is nothing new for Arizona. After the past two weeks of playing NFC West teams, they play an AFC West team next week as they travel to Kansas City to face the Chiefs.

title: Evaluating Carson Beck's Cardinals Debut: How Rookie QB Actually Played
full_text:
GLENDALE — Arizona Cardinals rookie quarterback Carson Beck took the field for his NFL debut on Sunday.
It was anything but ideal.
After an enticing opening two drives, the Cardinals' offense stalled in major fashion en route to a 34-6 Los Angeles Rams victory at State Farm Stadium.
Beck finished the day with 11/18 passing for 108 yards and two interceptions with zero touchdowns and a 38.4 passer rating.
The box score didn't look pretty, but Beck's overall performance yields more optimism than some want to give after a massively disappointing score:
All in all, Beck had a fairly promising performance on Sunday. The odds felt like they were always going to be stacked against him given the circumstances entering his first NFL start.
As fate would have it, the talented Rams defense would hold Arizona to minimal damage. Beck's offensive line failed him with five sacks on the day and no rushing game to balance things out. His receivers (minus Trey McBride) were incredibly disappointing and ended a few potential scoring drives with drops.
Beck showed a willingness to push the ball downfield and looked composed in his first taste of action against one of the best defensive fronts he'll see in his lifetime thanks to Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett. Mistakes were made, though expected from an inexperienced quarterback such as Beck.
A loss never feels good. A blowout to a divisional rival sprinkles salt in the wound. Two interceptions, on the surface, is anything but ideal.
Still, Beck showed some promising flashes, and the hope is the Cardinals will build from there.

title: Falcons Have Nobody to Blame but Themselves for Disappointing Season
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons are 3-7 at the bye, and their biggest problems are largely self-inflicted. Turnovers, penalties, and slow starts have repeatedly put this team in difficult positions, turning winnable games into double-digit losses.
Despite their record, the Falcons still have a chance to get back into the playoff race. They have to stop beating themselves first .
Unbelievably, the Falcons are still within striking distance in the NFC South. The division-leading Panthers have only a one-game advantage (and the tiebreaker), but recent results have done little to inspire confidence that this team has what it takes to get over the hump and reach the postseason for the first time since 2017.
They have lost three straight games by double digits, with all of them feeling out of reach by the fourth quarter. In each one, the Falcons have hurt themselves.
In the 16-point loss to the Buccaneers, Michael Penix Jr. threw four interceptions. In a 17-point loss to the Bengals, they committed 12 penalties. In a 22-point loss to the Chiefs, they had a historically slow start, entering the fourth quarter with 186 yards of offense, plus two turnovers and nine penalties by the final whistle.
“You watch the tape, and it's frustrating and disappointing, but ultimately, as a football team, we're going to own it, and then we're going to move on from this one,” head coach Kevin Stefanski said Monday about the most recent loss. “Learn some lessons, some hard lessons as they are, but then use this bye week to our advantage.”
Stefanski has taken responsibility for how his team has played. He has made several assurances that the mistakes will be corrected, but so far, the lessons haven't taken hold.
After those 12 infractions in Madrid that Stefanski called “inexcusable,” they hurt themselves with game-altering mistakes. They turned Chiefs field goals into touchdowns and ended their own possessions with false starts and holding penalties. Analyst JJ Watt openly called out right tackle Jawaan Taylor on the CBS broadcast.
A struggling Penix didn’t settle in until the game was out of reach (155 of his 286 passing yards came in the fourth quarter), and he kept struggling under pressure. He missed open receivers and was rushed, even when no one was in his face.
Since winning NFC Offensive Player of the Week in the win over the 49ers, the Falcons’ quarterback has completed only 51 of 98 passes for 573 yards, one touchdown, and six interceptions.
Penix's struggles have been compounded by the Falcons' inability to consistently lean on their most reliable offensive weapon: Bijan Robinson.
The running back carried the ball only seven times in the first half of Sunday’s loss to the Chiefs, and the Falcons already trailed by double digits by the time they started using him more.
The Falcons identified their rushing attack as a defining trait of their offensive identity, but their star back has had more than 20 carries just once during the last five games – and he hit that mark in their only win during that span.
Robinson took his role in stride.
“I do whatever I can for the team, no matter what the situation is,” the star running back said after the game. “I know that they have a plan, and I gotta follow that plan as best as possible. Yeah, I’ll just leave it from there.”
But the Falcons have kept their biggest weapon in the holster, and the results speak for themselves.
The playoffs are in sight, but there is not a lot of confidence that this team can get there – at least until they get out of their own way.
“You can’t win football games in this league without not beating yourself first, and we did that [Sunday against the Chiefs],” wide receiver Jahan Dotson said. “Penalties, pre- and post-snap, and just little things like not lining up correctly and just simple things that don’t take effort. That’s what it comes down to.
“We gotta look ourselves in the mirror and fix the internal things.”
Those mistakes have doomed them, and their upcoming slate of games could, too. Following this week off, the Falcons will face three straight opponents with six or more wins, including the team that fired Stefanski in January.
“We can make this run because the division is still wide open,” cornerback A.J. Terrell said. “We still control our destiny and things like that.”
The odds are certainly stacked against them. According to Statehead, only two teams in history have made the playoffs after starting 3-7, and the Falcons have the added benefit of playing in a winnable division. This team will need to start winning games for any of that to matter.
The next several weeks will be difficult, but the Falcons still see a chance to save the season .
“I think the way our team is wired, and the way we were brought on this year – it's not pretty, but we're gonna keep fighting,” guard Matthew Bergeron said. “You just gotta turn that frustration into motivation. And listen, we have a week to fix the bumps and bruises and get back to work.”
The Falcons still have an opportunity to save their season, but the margin for error has all but disappeared. The bye week gives them time to address their mistakes. Now they have to prove they can actually correct them.
Garrett Chapman is a sports broadcaster, writer, and content creator based in Atlanta. He has several years of experience covering the Atlanta sports scene, college football, Georgia high school football, recruiting for 24/7 Sports, and the NFL. You can also hear him on Sports Radio 92.9 The Game.

title: J.J. Watt Exposes Embarrassing Falcons Problem During Chiefs Loss
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons may have been giving away more information than they realized before the snap, and NFL legend J.J. Watt made sure everyone watching Sunday’s game against the Kansas City Chiefs knew about it.
During CBS’ broadcast of Atlanta’s 35-13 loss to Kansas City, Watt identified a potential pre-snap tell involving Falcons offensive tackle Jawaan Taylor that could allow opposing defenses to anticipate whether the offense is preparing to run or pass.
Watt broke down Taylor’s positioning, using several graphics to show how his foot placement changes when lining up in a three-point stance. He also highlighted differences in Taylor’s hand placement when operating out of a two-point stance.
Look closely... 👀 @JJWatt accurately predicts a pass vs. a run based on Falcons OT Jawaan Taylor's stance. CBS | Paramount+ pic.twitter.com/naMymtucuX
The former NFL defensive star explained that Taylor’s positioning could provide defensive linemen with valuable information before the ball is even snapped.
“As a defensive lineman, you watch every single guy. This isn’t something that anybody in the league doesn’t already know,” Watt explained during the broadcast.
Watt also pointed out that this was exactly the type of information the Chiefs would be studying throughout the week.
“This is the type of stuff the Chiefs are studying this week,” Watt said.
There was another reason why Kansas City could have been particularly familiar with Taylor’s tendencies. The offensive tackle spent the previous three seasons with the Chiefs before joining Atlanta in free agency.
CBS even showed an example of Michael Penix Jr. changing a play at the line of scrimmage, apparently switching from a pass to a run. Taylor immediately adjusted his hand placement, giving Watt another opportunity to demonstrate the potential tell.
Watt also identified a specific foot positioning that indicated a pass was coming.
“You’ll see, when he’s in that deep stagger, that’s when it’s gonna be a pass,” Watt explained.
The concerning part for Atlanta is that this wasn't identified internally, or at least fixed internally.  NFL defensive coordinators and defensive linemen spend countless hours studying film, making it reasonable to question whether opposing teams had already recognized similar patterns before being exposed by Watt.
Following Sunday’s loss, Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski was asked about Watt’s observations and whether Atlanta was aware of Taylor potentially tipping plays.
“Every team has tendencies; we’re aware of ours,” Stefanski said.
That response suggests the coaching staff understands that opposing defenses are constantly searching for small advantages when studying Atlanta’s offense.
However, the Falcons will need to make sure those tendencies are not giving opponents an unnecessary advantage.
Taylor also had a difficult afternoon against his former team, committing two false-start penalties as Atlanta struggled to establish consistency offensively.
The Falcons managed just three points and 186 total yards through the first three quarters before Kansas City eventually pulled away.
Atlanta is now 3-7 after suffering another disappointing defeat , with plenty of questions surrounding the team’s offensive execution.
Taylor’s stance might seem like a relatively minor detail, but at the NFL level, small advantages can make a significant difference. If opposing defenses can consistently identify whether Atlanta is running or passing before the snap, it becomes considerably more difficult for the offense to find success.
The Falcons now have their bye week to evaluate what went wrong and make necessary adjustments before returning to action against the Minnesota Vikings on November 29.
If Watt can identify Atlanta’s tendencies from the broadcast booth, the Falcons need to make sure opposing defenses cannot continue to take advantage of them.
