title: Are Falcons Checking Out? Three-Game Skid Puts Atlanta at a Crossroads
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons’ losing streak has reached three .
And from what’s been on display, there’s not much reason to believe they’re capable of a turnaround.
As the season spirals, running back Bijan Robinson posed a question after Sunday’s 35-13 home loss to the Kansas City Chiefs : “Is this how we want to go about the rest of the season with this product, or are we going to change? Are we going to strain for each other, go out there and play for each other no matter the situation?”
The Falcons (3-7) may verbally answer with what sounds good to the ear of fans, who showered them with boo birds in Mercedes-Benz Stadium on Sunday.
But the on-field play tells another story.
Especially with a cloud hanging over the franchise’s future as tanking talks get louder after the Falcons became trade deadline sellers in exchange for draft picks last week.
“I don’t think you have to worry about the fight of this football team,” head coach Kevin Stefanski told reporters in Sunday’s postgame press conference when asked how to keep his team from checking out.
“Our guys understand what’s in front of us.”
Atlanta moved its star free safety and team captain Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars and starting center Ryan Neuzil to the Baltimore Ravens .
Entering the week, Tankathon has Atlanta slated for the No. 8 overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft.
The pick may hold up or even rise with Minnesota and Detroit as the next two games. More than half of the season is gone, and Atlanta is looking like one of the worst teams in the NFL through Week 10.
“Nobody feels bad or cares about how the Atlanta Falcons feel except for us. And we can make a change to the narrative,” said Falcons cornerback A.J. Terrell Jr. “We still got the season in front of us, and we can either take advantage of that or plummet.”
Through the struggles, Atlanta has a saving grace: NFC South bedlam.
The Falcons are currently in the division’s fourth and final spot, with the Carolina Panthers leading the way with a 4-5 record.
Again, welcome to the NFC South, where you can compete for the division crown and a draft pick simultaneously.
“You’re always going to have a chance as long as there are games left on the schedule in the NFC South,” said Corey Levin, the newly appointed starting center for the Falcons .
American football will get a break from the uninspiring product the Falcons have put on the field in recent weeks. They’re on a bye for Week 11.
Then the gauntlet continues at the Minnesota Vikings and former Falcons quarterback Kirk Cousins on Nov. 29, kicking off Atlanta’s final seven regular season games.
“The biggest thing for us is to stay together,” Robinson said. “I think the teams that start to lose a lot later in the season are the teams that drift apart and go amongst themselves.”
Can the Falcons reverse course in the next month and a half and ultimately land a playoff spot?
But Stefanski’s and the players’ optimism has yet to translate into results, leaving the Falcons with seven games to prove their words carry weight.

title: Falcons Winners and Losers: Atlanta's Offense Disappears in Loss to Chiefs
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons suffered another frustrating loss, falling 35-13 to the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday. The offense struggled to find any consistency; the passing game never developed a rhythm, and the defense gave Patrick Mahomes too many opportunities to make explosive plays.
There were a few individual bright spots, particularly among Atlanta's young defensive players, but this was another performance that gave a clear indication the team was thinking more about the 2027 NFL Draft than they are about winning the NFC South.
Here are the winners and losers from Sunday's loss.
Hellams deserves credit for stepping into a much larger role following the trade of Jessie Bates . Replacing a veteran safety and team leader is not an easy assignment, but Hellams showed he was capable of handling the opportunity.
He finished with 10 total tackles, including six solo tackles and four assists, leading the way in the secondary. He was active around the football and helped make several stops against the Chiefs.
There will naturally be growing pains with Bates no longer in Atlanta, but Hellams provided some encouraging signs in his expanded role.
A bright spot for Atlanta's future
The rookie linebacker duo continued to show why Falcons fans should be excited about their development.
Perkins finished with five tackles, including four solo tackles and one assist. Daniels contributed seven tackles, with two solo tackles and five assists.
Both players were flying around the football and showed good energy throughout the afternoon.
With Divine Deablo missing another week, this was valuable experience for two young linebackers who could have significant roles moving forward. Their development is one of the few positives Atlanta can take away from this game.
Moody provided some stability after recently taking over for Nick Folk .
He finished the afternoon perfect on all three kicking attempts, converting two field goals from 28 and 38 yards and making his lone extra point.
He accounted for seven of Atlanta's 13 points and didn't leave any points on the field.
Moody also executed a picture-perfect onside kick; the first successful onside kick this season.
you won’t see an onside kick prettier than this. pic.twitter.com/1oSTxR1Hq0
While the Falcons have much bigger problems to address, Moody did exactly what was expected of him. After making a midseason change at kicker, getting a reliable performance is encouraging.
There are legitimate questions about Tommy Rees' offensive approach following Sunday's performance.
Atlanta struggled to establish any consistency, and the play sequencing was questionable at times. One of the biggest concerns continues to be the lack of involvement for Bijan Robinson.
Robinson finished with 71 rushing yards on 16 carries and added six receiving yards on four catches. He averaged 4.4 yards per carry, yet Atlanta struggled to consistently build its offense around him.
Another concerning trend is the Falcons' approach on third down.
There seems to be a lack of trust in the traditional dropback passing game, particularly when Atlanta knows opposing defenses are going to bring pressure. The Chiefs were able to create problems with their blitz packages, and the Falcons didn't consistently have answers.
Rees needs to find ways to get the football out quicker, create easier opportunities for Penix and put his playmakers in better positions.
The talent is there. The offensive execution and playcalling need to improve.
This was a particularly rough afternoon for the veteran left tackle.
Matthews was flagged three times, although the official play by play identifies two holding penalties and one false start. Those mistakes repeatedly put Atlanta behind the chains.
The holding penalties were particularly damaging because they erased positive plays and forced the offense into difficult situations.
For a veteran who has been one of Atlanta's most dependable offensive linemen for years, this was a performance he'd like to forget.
Another frustrating afternoon
Penix finished with 23 completions on 43 attempts for 286 yards, with the majority of those yards in garbage time, zero touchdowns, and an interception. He also rushed four times for 29 yards.
Atlanta finished with 370 yards, but most of them came once the game was well out of reach. They converted only five of 16 third downs. Their first four drives were three-and-outs.
Penix never seemed to find a consistent rhythm. There were flashes, including some productive connections with Drake London and Jahan Dotson, but they weren't enough to sustain drives.
He doesn't deserve all the blame. The offensive line, playcalling and overall offensive execution all contributed to the struggles.
However, Atlanta needs more from its quarterback if it wants to compete consistently.
The continued lack of involvement for Pitts is becoming increasingly difficult to understand.
He finished Sunday's game with four catches for 50 yards on four targets, without a touchdown. He had two catches for nine yards in the first half, and his third catch came with the Falcons down 35-13, and he promptly fumbled.
Those numbers are particularly disappointing considering how much the coaching staff has emphasized getting him involved in the offense.
Offensive coordinator Tommy Rees has previously acknowledged that the Falcons are better when Pitts is involved. However, that philosophy hasn't translated into consistent production this season.
Pitts has the athletic ability to create mismatches against linebackers and safeties. Yet Atlanta continues to struggle to make him a meaningful part of the passing attack.
At some point, the coaching staff has to figure out how to get one of its most talented offensive weapons involved.
This deserves its own category because the Falcons' secondary had a difficult afternoon against Patrick Mahomes.
Mahomes finished with 22 completions on 35 attempts for 348 yards, five touchdowns and zero interceptions, posting a 135.5 passer rating.
Kansas City consistently found opportunities downfield, finishing with 453 total yards and five passing touchdowns.
Terrell recorded five tackles, while Henderson finished with two. However, the tackle totals don't tell the entire story.
There were multiple explosive plays that exposed Atlanta's coverage, including a 50-yard completion to Rashee Rice with Henderson involved in the coverage and a 39-yard touchdown to Cyrus Allen.
The Chiefs also connected on a 43-yard touchdown to Ashton Armstrong late in the fourth quarter.
For Terrell, who is the 11th highest-paid cornerback in the NFL, these are the types of performances that raise questions about the return on investment.
For Henderson, the timing is notable. He recently received a significant two-year contract extension after stepping into a starting role and showing improvement. Atlanta needs that version of Henderson consistently, not performances where opposing quarterbacks can repeatedly attack the secondary.
Losing Jessie Bates certainly doesn't make things easier, but the remaining defensive backs have to do a better job limiting explosive plays.
Mahomes was far too comfortable against this defense, and the coverage issues were a major reason why Kansas City was able to pull away.
There weren't many positives from Sunday's loss. Hellams, Perkins, and Daniels showed encouraging signs, and Moody delivered a perfect performance. However, the offensive struggles, questionable playcalling, and secondary issues continue to raise serious concerns about where this Falcons team is headed.
The Falcons have the week off before they face Kirk Cousins and the Minnesota Vikings (7-2) on Sunday, November 29th in Minnesota.

title: 5 Brutal Takeaways From Atlanta Falcons Loss to Kansas City Chiefs
full_text:
ATLANTA – The Atlanta Falcons lost their third straight game, and the fifth of their last six, on Sunday. They fell to the Chiefs 35-13, marking the third double-digit loss.
The Falcons had a start to forget on offense, surrendering four consecutive three-and-outs to begin the game, marking their worst start in 26 years. Michael Penix Jr. faced pressure on several dropbacks and had a few misfires that put the Falcons behind the chains early. The offense faced third-down distances of 10, 10, 17, and 4 yards.
But the biggest issue was that Bijan Robinson only touched the ball three times over those four possessions. Unsurprisingly, the star running back snapped the drought on the fifth drive with a 17-yard rush that set up the Falcons’ first points of the game.
The Falcons seemed to find some rhythm on that possession, but they quickly went back to another three-and-out, their fifth of the first half. Robinson finished the half with only eight touches and fewer than 20 carries for the fifth time in the last six games (all ended in a loss).
The second half didn’t go much differently, and the Falcons’ drives ended in a punt, turnover on downs, punt, and punt before finally finding the end zone down 28-3 with 8:15 left.
Penix never got comfortable, and he and offensive coordinator Tommy Rees are struggling to find success. Since his outstanding performance against the 49ers, the offense has averaged a dreadful 10.0 points per game.
Fans voiced their displeasure with the team, showering the offense with boos.
"They put in their hard-earned work every single week to try to make it to these games, and it's our job to make it count for them," running back Bijan Robinson said of the fans. "So yeah, when they boo us, we deserve it."
Atlanta was 5-of-16 on third down and only scored one touchdown on five red zone trips.
With the Falcons’ offense struggling to find any semblance of rhythm, the defense was forced into some unfortunate possessions. They started slowly, too, allowing an easy touchdown drive to begin the game, but locked the Chiefs up for much of the game.
The defense just didn’t get any help, and eventually Patrick Mahomes broke through again. After that opening drive score, both of his subsequent touchdown throws came after shortcomings from another unit: the first on an offside negated a field goal and the second after a failed fourth-down conversion at midfield.
Mahomes’ fourth touchdown came in the fourth quarter, with the game firmly in hand and the Falcons’ defense reeling. The fifth came on a scramble drill.
The Falcons held the Chiefs' rushing attack (without Kenneth Walker III) to 122 yards, but Mahomes would finish with 348 yards and five touchdowns – the first time he hit that scoring mark since 2022.
The rookie linebacker was making plays all over the field on Sunday. He finished with five tackles and a tackle for loss, but he was effective in both coverage and as a pass rusher. Perkins delivered big hits and was constantly finding himself around the football.
He has taken full advantage of Divine Deablo’s absence and is pushing for the staff to find ways to keep him on the field once the veteran is back healthy.
Michael Penix Jr. continued to struggle when the defense applied pressure. He was sacked three times and kept accelerating his progressions to check down and avoid getting hit. Even without a blitz, the Chiefs sent simulated pressure that still got Penix off his spot and sped him up. He struggled for most of the game, completing 23-of-43 passes for 286 yards (most of which came with the game out of reach) and an interception.
Until he can find his way under pressure, the Falcons’ offense will keep struggling.
A week after 12 penalties crushed the Falcons in Madrid, some ill-timed infractions came back to bite them in Atlanta. They committed nine penalties for 65 yards, but seven came on offense, and both defensive penalties extended drives that ended in touchdowns.
The worst of which was an offsides penalty that turned a field goal try into a touchdown at the end of the first half. Kansas City took a 14-3 lead into the locker room instead of 10-3, and received the ball to start the second half.
Jawaan Taylor and Jake Matthews were both flagged several times for false starts or holds that snuffed out offensive possessions.
"When you're playing good football teams, you have to be at your best," Kevin Stefanski said. "And we were not at our best."
But beyond the penalties, the Falcons turned the ball over twice in the fourth quarter. For the second week in a row, the Falcons could not get out of their own way.
Corey Levin took over for Ryan Neuzil at center and had one bad snap exchange that ended in a fumble (Penix jumped on it), but it snuffed out a potential touchdown opportunity. The offensive line did not have its best day, allowing three sacks and rushing for 100 yards.
New kicker Jake Moody connected on both field-goal attempts from 28 and 38 yards, but he nailed an onside kick in the fourth quarter to give the Falcons new life. He put the football right in the outstretched arms of Chris Blair, who toe-tapped on the sideline to steal a possession. That play capped a strong afternoon for the Falcons’ special teams.
Tommy Rees also made his first appearance on the sideline instead of in the booth this season. He was seen sitting with Penix during defensive possessions, but the offensive issues persisted, and his unit finished with five three-and-outs.
DeMarcco Hellams stepped in for recently traded Jessie Bates III at safety and was a big winner in this game. His first start since 2023 was outstanding, and he finished with a game-high 11 tackles.
The Falcons lost the fifth of their last six games heading into their bye week, and the schedule gets no easier after next Sunday. Atlanta will face the Vikings, Lions, and Browns before it finally eases up a bit, with winnable games against the Commanders and NFC South opponents to end the season.
At 3-7, any hope of their first winning season since 2017 feels bleak, but they are still alive in the woeful NFC South. They trail the first-place Panthers by one win, don’t hold the tiebreaker, but are still unbelievably alive in that race.
Both the players and Stefanski were confident after the game that they won't lose the locker room amid this skid, but the bye week will be a welcome sight for this team.
Garrett Chapman is a sports broadcaster, writer, and content creator based in Atlanta. He has several years of experience covering the Atlanta sports scene, college football, Georgia high school football, recruiting for 24/7 Sports, and the NFL. You can also hear him on Sports Radio 92.9 The Game.

title: FalconsSI Staff Unanimous in Falcons vs. Chiefs Predictions
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are looking to get back on track in Week 10, but they face a difficult challenge with Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs coming to Mercedes-Benz Stadium.
Atlanta has lost four of its last five games and is coming off a disappointing performance against the Cincinnati Bengals in Madrid. Now, the Falcons will have to find a way to slow down another talented quarterback while dealing with significant changes to their own roster.
Kansas City will enter the matchup without running back Kenneth Walker III , which could make things more manageable for Atlanta’s struggling defense. However, Mahomes and Travis Kelce remain major threats, and the Chiefs have plenty of weapons to exploit the Falcons’ defensive weaknesses and deficiencies.
How will the game play out? The FalconsSI staff delivers its weekly predictions.
The Falcons have had some frustrating games this year, suffering through two weeks of Cooper Rush and a monsoon in Tampa, for example. But last week in Madrid was different. The Cincinnati Bengals simply showed the Falcons aren't good enough this year.
Their defense has been patched together with duct tape and one-year contracts, and it simply couldn't hold up against Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins. General manager Ian Cunningham saw the same thing we did, and rather than deluding himself into thinking 3-6 in a weak NFC South was good enough, he sold at the trade deadline.
Now Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce come to Mercedes-Benz Stadium, and the Falcons are without All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III after trading him to the Jaguars. Mahomes and the Chiefs aren't as explosive as the Bengals, but, well, they're still Mahomes and the Chiefs... and they're better on defense.
We'll see if Michael Penix Jr. and the offense can play well enough to take another step towards feeling good about Penix in 2027, but the Falcons are staring 3-7 in the face.
Prediction: Chiefs 31, Falcons 17
The notion of the Falcons playing up to the competition is fading away.
Plus, there’s a belief that Atlanta is now playing for draft positioning instead of ending its playoff drought.
The Chiefs present too many issues for the Falcons. We all know what Patrick Mahomes can do in the passing attack. And we all watched the Atlanta secondary struggle with Bengals playmakers in Madrid. With Kenneth Walker III out, that may soften the blow against the Falcons’ dwindling run defense .
Offensively, Atlanta is looking pretty “eh.” Michael Penix Jr. has gotten off of his heater and must prove himself as the franchise quarterback against one of the top pass defenses in the league. Additionally, Kansas City is top-10 at stopping the run and will likely stack boxes to stonewall Bijan Robinson as the Falcons deal with the key loss of powerback Brian Robinson Jr.
Atlanta is looking at a third consecutive loss on the road to the 2027 NFL Draft.
Prediction: Chiefs 34, Falcons 21
The Falcons have lost four of their last five, and the road to snapping that skid will run through the Kansas City Chiefs. The perennial contenders will be without Kenneth Walker, but Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce are still willing and able to run wild on a reeling Falcons defense that just moved Jessie Bates.
On offense, Corey Levin will be taking over at center , and he'll have a pretty difficult challenge opposite him.
This should be a tight game, but I'm not sure the Falcons can overcome this team opposite them right now.
Prediction: Chiefs 20, Falcons 17
Expects a closer game with Walker sidelined, but Mahomes will ultimately make the difference.
Atlanta’s defense has continued to struggle, and the departure of Bates doesn’t provide much confidence that things will improve against Kansas City’s passing attack.
The Falcons also face questions offensively with a new starting center stepping into the lineup midway through the season. That transition could create additional problems against a talented Chiefs defense.
Atlanta remains competitive, but Kansas City will pull away late to secure the victory.
Prediction: Chiefs 23, Falcons 16
Despite being only a half game back from first place in the division, it really seems like the clock is ticking on the Falcons’ season. The performances in recent weeks and the trades the Falcons made at the deadline make this game feel like a “crap or get off the pot” moment for this team.
There is hope, though. The Chiefs are good, but the Falcons have beaten better teams this year (which sounds crazy given they’ve only won three games). The blueprint for beating the Chiefs is pretty straightforward: stop the run.
The issue is, the Falcons have struggled to do that, especially against inside runs, and the Chiefs are an inside-running team. If they can pull it off, the Falcons’ pass defense matches up well against the Chiefs’ passing offense on paper (even without Jessie Bates).
On the other side of the ball, the Chiefs’ defense has been solid, but I think they have a real weakness in the secondary with the injury to their rookie Mansoor Delane. To exploit it, though, the Falcons will need to get the run game going. Their passing offense has been pretty ineffective when the ground game stalls.
This is a game the Falcons can win... but whether they will is a different story.
Prediction: Chiefs 24, Falcons 16
Despite differences in the projected final scores, all five contributors are picking Kansas City to win in Week 10.

title: Falcons Beleaguered Defense Catches a Break vs. Chiefs
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons received some significant injury news ahead of their Week 10 matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs. Star running back Kenneth Walker III has been ruled out for Sunday’s game with a groin injury, giving Atlanta’s defense a major break heading into one of its toughest matchups of the season.
NFL insider Jordan Schultz first reported the news Saturday, saying Walker would not suit up against the Falcons. Schultz also noted the injury isn't considered a long-term concern, but Kansas City is playing it safe with its star running back.
Walker has been one of the NFL's most productive running backs this season.
Through eight games, he has rushed for 872 yards and seven touchdowns while averaging an impressive 5.5 yards per carry. His 109 rushing yards per game lead the NFL, and he currently ranks second in total rushing yards behind Atlanta’s Bijan Robinson.
Losing that kind of production is a major blow for Kansas City, but it is a good opportunity for a struggling Falcons run defense that will no longer have to prepare for one of the league’s most dangerous ball carriers.
Without their leading running back, Kansas City will likely turn to rookie Emmett Johnson to handle an expanded workload.
The Falcons' run defense began the season as one of its strengths, but it has been pushed around in recent weeks , including 324 yards in a loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
Johnson has shown some promise in limited opportunities, recording 111 rushing yards and a touchdown on 26 carries. He has also contributed in the passing game, totaling 237 receiving yards and another touchdown on 14 receptions.
While Johnson can certainly make plays, replacing a back who has averaged 109 rushing yards per game is a significant challenge.
For Atlanta, this creates an opportunity to put more attention on Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs’ passing attack. The Falcons can potentially be more aggressive defensively without having to account for Walker’s ability to consistently break off explosive runs and control the ground game.
That does not mean Kansas City suddenly becomes an easy matchup. Mahomes remains one of the NFL’s most dangerous quarterbacks, and the Chiefs have plenty of weapons that can create problems for Atlanta’s defense.
However, losing Walker takes away a major component of Kansas City’s offensive identity.
The Falcons have their own injury concerns heading into Sunday, but this is unquestionably encouraging news for Atlanta. Facing a Chiefs offense without the NFL’s second leading rusher is a considerably different challenge than preparing for one with Walker in the backfield.
Atlanta still has to take advantage of the opportunity, but the latest injury news gives the Falcons a major break heading into Sunday’s showdown.

title: Jessie Bates III Recalls ‘Teary-Eyed’ Falcons Goodbye after Trade to Jaguars
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons may not have enjoyed the on-field success that Jessie Bates III may have hoped for.
But the franchise is dear in the star free safety’s heart after spending 3.5 seasons in Flowery Branch.
The All-Pro selections and his momentum-swinging defensive plays, including his ball-hawking interceptions and patented rendition of the “Peanut Punch,” come secondary to the impact he and the franchise had on each other as he heads to the Jacksonville Jaguars via trade .
“You spend somewhere four years; you create relationships, you create bonds that’ll last a lifetime,” Bates told Juston Lewis of the Jacksonville-Times Union .
“There are people over there from the staff, the players, the janitors, the cafeteria people – those are my people. I would see those people every single day, and they did a lot for me. So there’s so much appreciation and love for those guys and girls over there.”
Bates was the first move Atlanta made as sellers in this year’s trade deadline .
On Monday, the Falcons moved the nine-year NFL veteran to Jacksonville for a 2027 NFL Draft second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder.
It marked the end of an era for one of Atlanta’s fan favorites who withstood three different coaches, no playoff appearances, and a world of “what-ifs.”
Bates had become a staple for the Falcons, having been named a team captain and sharing a locker with potential franchise quarterback Michael Penix Jr.
Now he leaves behind the foundation he’s built for a fresh start for a Super Bowl contender.
“It was tough,” Bates said when asked about the moment he departed the Falcons facility. “When I left that building, there were teary eyes from myself and coaches, trainers, equipment guys – a lot of love there. I take pride in not just being a great football player, but just being a great person, being a great light in the building.”
The rationale behind the Bates-to-Jags trade was that the Falcons looked as though they weren’t going to re-sign the safety as he entered unrestricted free agency following the season. At 29, Bates’ age was a factor in the decision, as the Falcons look to start a youth movement and build through the draft .
The Bates move predated the Falcons getting another draft pick for starting center Ryan Neuzil . He was traded on Tuesday to the Baltimore Ravens for guard Andrew Vorhees on an expiring deal and a conditional 2028 sixth-round pick.
On Friday, the Falcons inked younger players to multiyear deals, defensive end Cameron Thomas (three years, $33 million) and cornerback CJ Henderson (two years, $20 million) .
Fans will have to wait to see Bates' debut for the Jaguars. Head coach Liam Coen said Bates will not play against the 1-7 Titans, with no bye week a factor. The Jaguars have already had their bye, but the Falcons haven't. His decision gives Bates the week off that he didn't get with the Falcons.
Meanwhile, the Falcons (3-6) will make their first post-Bates appearance when the Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) come to town for an NFL Week 10 clash. DeMarcco Hellams is expected to step into the free safety role. The Falcons enter their bye week after facing the Chiefs.
Kickoff is also at 1 p.m. and will be aired on CBS.

title: Falcons' Biggest Defensive Problem Is Becoming Impossible to Ignore
full_text:
ATLANTA – The Atlanta Falcons are coming off the fourth loss in five games, and they just traded away their best defender , Jessie Bates III. A once-dominant run defense is reeling, having allowed 98 yards or more in each of those games.
Not to say the Falcons have always struggled against the run, because they haven’t.
In the first four weeks, they allowed 193 combined yards (2.7 yards per carry) and were the NFL’s best run defense by a wide margin. Then, Derrick Henry and the Ravens ran wild in Week 5, piling up 208 yards on the ground. From there, it snowballed, and the Falcons have been the league’s third-worst team since that overtime loss.
And the defensive issues haven’t stopped there.
The Falcons were eighth in defensive EPA, second in defensive success rate, and leading the league in quarterback pressure rates over those first four weeks. But like the run defense, those numbers have plummeted to 22nd, 30th, and 21st in the games since.
Injuries to Za’Darius Smith, Samson Ebukam, and Divine Deablo in the front seven have hurt, as have the absences of C.J. Henderson and A.J. Terrell Jr. on the back end. But Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich was the first to take ownership of the sharp regression, saying the team has been playing well below expectations.
“That's the 100% truth, and I think everybody is taking that upon themselves,” Ulbrich said Wednesday. “I do feel fortunate that we have a group of a bunch of thumb pointers, where [it’s], ‘What can I do more?’ I feel like we have that collectively.”
But these issues start on the ground, the proclaimed identity of this Falcons’ defense.
“We're just not playing it well enough, so that's me, from a scheme perspective, making sure that we're getting guys in the right spaces to be successful,” he said. “At times, we've done that and didn't play well enough. There are times we didn't do that (scheme-wise), and it wasn’t on the players; it was 100% on coaching.
“We all have to do more and do better in regard to defending the run.”
The numbers have been scary, but the defensive coordinator insisted there is no ‘panic’ within the locker room about getting back on track, but there might be if these issues continue on into Sunday. The Kansas City Chiefs are coming to town, and there is no room for error in a game like this.
A unit typically known for its future Hall of Fame quarterback Patrick Mahomes is now feared for what it can do on the ground. Kenneth Walker III (872) ranks second only to Bijan Robinson (880) in rushing yards and threatens to continue the Falcons' run-defense slide.
Ulbrich said stopping a back like this is going to “take all 11.” Walker can get downhill quickly and create havoc at the second level if defenders don’t stick to their run fits or tackle well.
“That's where we have to be at our best. And it's a unique challenge in that way because there's not a whole lot of backs like him,” he explained. “On top of all that, he has gas. He has real finishing speed, and he's a guy that can hit the home run at any time. There's a reason I think he's the first- or second-most efficient runner in the league right now. It’s going to be a great challenge.”
Walker will be the next big challenge for the Falcons, but stopping a back like this is what they want to be known for. Doing it consistently has eluded them in recent weeks.
“I've never been a part of a great defense that didn't defend the run well,” Ulbrich said. “That has to become part of who we are. That has to become part of our identity. And right now it is not.”
The 3-6 Falcons still have time to rediscover the defensive identity that made them one of the NFL's best units early in the season. Those opportunities are running out.
With the bye week coming after Sunday's matchup, the Falcons desperately need to respond against Walker and the Chiefs. If they can't, their season could slip further out of reach, and they have one glaring issue to blame.

title: Falcons Sign Redeemed CB to 2-Year Contract Extension
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are rewarding one of their biggest defensive surprises this season, agreeing to a two-year contract extension with cornerback C.J. Henderson. The deal is worth up to $20 million with $11 million guaranteed, according to Ian Rapoport , tying the team financially to Henderson for next season with a club option in 2028.
Henderson was the second of two extensions announced by the Falcons on Friday. Edge rusher Cameron Thomas got a three-year deal worth up to $33 million as well.
Henderson stepped into a starting outside cornerback role after A.J. Terrell suffered an injury in Week 2 and has taken full advantage of the opportunity.
What initially appeared to be a temporary replacement assignment has turned into a breakout season for the veteran defensive back, who has established himself as an important piece of Atlanta’s secondary. He was officially moved ahead of Mike Hughes on the depth chart this week.
The two-year extension gives Henderson additional security while allowing the Falcons to retain a player who has become increasingly valuable to their defense. PFF has him as the No. 22-ranked cornerback in the NFL, the highest of any Falcons player.
Through eight games, Henderson has recorded 41 total tackles, 32 solo tackles, nine passes defended, and one forced fumble. His nine pass breakups are already a career high, surpassing his previous best of six, which he recorded during the 2020 and 2022 seasons.
His production has been particularly impressive considering the circumstances surrounding his expanded role. Henderson entered the season competing for opportunities in Atlanta’s secondary, but Terrell’s injury created an opening that he has not relinquished.
The 28-year-old has demonstrated the ability to handle consistent responsibilities on the outside while providing the Falcons with another dependable option in coverage. His performance has also helped Atlanta navigate an important injury in its defensive backfield without having to completely overhaul its secondary.
Henderson’s emergence is especially notable given his NFL journey. The Jacksonville Jaguars selected him ninth overall in the 2020 NFL Draft out of Florida. He spent the first part of his career in Jacksonville before moving to the Carolina Panthers, where he played three seasons.
After appearing in just four games with Atlanta last season, Henderson has found a much larger opportunity in 2026. He entered the year with 33 career starts and has continued to build on that experience with an expanded role.
For general manager Ian Cunningham and the Falcons, extending Henderson represents an investment in a player who has earned a larger place in the team’s defensive plans.
Henderson has earned a starting spot at one of the outside corners, which could push Avieon Terrell inside to nickel. Billy Bowman Jr. hasn't been able to stay healthy long enough to solidify a spot there, and Sydney Brown is a depth piece forced to play starting minutes.
The extension also provides some continuity for a secondary that has dealt with personnel changes throughout the season.
Henderson arrived in Atlanta looking for an opportunity to reestablish himself in the NFL. He delivered the best statistical season of his career and earned a two-year extension from the Falcons.

title: Free-Falling Ravens Franchise Hits New  Lows In Loss To Winless Chargers. 4 Key Takeaways
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers were the worst team in football, and it was not particularly close.
The basically never played with a lead in 2026, let alone keep games tight. They had no discernable strength (losers of 11 in a row), they shocked the football world by not selling off players at the deadline after an 0-8 start and their season was over before the flew to Baltimore for a Monday night game. Still, there was reason to like their chances, with Ravens overmatched and outclassed head coach Jesse Minter lacking confidence and gravitas and much of clue, and his mentally soft football team hanging by a thread.
And so it stands to reason, that right now, with the Ravens (4-6) falling immediately behind the Chargers and unable to comeback, losing, 23-20 at M&T Bank Stadium , that this failure of a franchise is among the very worst in the NFL. This defeat cements everything warped and entitled and overhyped about the Ravens “football culture” throughout Eric DeCosta’s inglorious tenure as general manager. It laid all of their self-mythologizing to bare, and further exposed how naïve and callous it was to fire head coach John Harbaugh and replace him with sycophantic replacements who simply were not ready for the job, while DeCosta amassed unchecked power in the process.
This was a football humiliation, even with starting quarterback Lamar Jackson on Injured Reserve (he’s not throwing another pass this season as we told you all along ). The Chargers, who recently went 37 straight possessions without scoring, accomplished things they have not done all season; Baltimore is now 3-10 in its last 13 home games (losers of five straight home prime time games) and 6-10 in its last 16 overall.
"Not good enough," Minter said, defaulting to his usual rhetoric about the rot starting with him. if he has a strength as an NFL head coach it has yet to become anything close to obvious.
Quarterback Jacoby Brissett was as good as anyone could have hoped for thrust into a new team midseason after going three-and-out three straight times to start the game. But Zay Flowers’ fumble with about two minutes left negated any chance at a comeback. The Ravens were thrashed yet again at the line of scrimmage on both sides of the ball, and this front office has been thoroughly exposed – not selling at the trade deadline another signal of their misguided hubris, and Derrick Henry ran 10 times for 10 yards.
Here’s what you need to know:
Whichever half Minter needs his defense to show up for, they wilt and collapse and walk all over him and make him look meek.
Monday, it was the first half, with the Ravens starting their fourth different quarterback in four weeks and with there going to be a learning curve with Brissett. So instead of bow up and show up against the worst defense in the NFL, of course Minter’s failure of a unit let LA march all over the field in the first quarter.
The Chargers took a fast 7-0 lead, with Justin Herbert carving them his legs and completing big passes when they needed it. They yielded repeated 10-yard runs and quarterback Justin Herbert capped the drive with a 22-yard TD run on third and long. Baltimore showed why it’s the worst third-and-long defense in the NFL., and could not get a sack when they needed it yet again (the Trey Hendrickson signing will go down as a massive failure for a GM who specializes in them).
"We let them off the hook," Minter said of the early mistakes.
The Ravens allowed 8.0 yards/play in the first quarter to quicky fall behind by two scores. The Chargers had not scored more than 10 points in the first half all season and rolled up 17 Monday. The Chargers had not led at the half all season, but of course they did here.
The Chargers have the worst OL in the NFL, Herbert was sacked eight times in his last game and 31 on the season and went down once at the line of scrimmage in the first half, caught from behind by Mike Green. And Green got to him late, but the Ravens could not win up front and allowed 160 rushing yards in the process.
The Ravens had zero rushing yards in the first half. When they tried to run the ball under center, $17M center Cam Jurgens was absolutely obliterated and tossed around. It was pretty ugly to watch, Jurgens was getting abused and rookie guard Vega Iaone, on the injured report quite a bit this season, was getting pushed around too before leaving with injury. Right tackle Roger Rosengarten’s blatant tripping attempt was a nice touch to open the second half.
“Jurgens is terrible,” one NFL personnel exec told me during the game. “You don’t have to wait for the film. He can’s handle strength or speed … He looks awful.”
The only chance this team has to run the ball came on sprint plays out of the pistol with Justice Hill. Keeping 32-year-old RB Derrick Henry at the trade deadline is going to go down as yet another ridiculous mistake from DeCosta. He has no chance behind this line, he is cut down behind the line of scrimmage with abandon and without Lamar Jackson creating with his legs Baltimore will not move this ball on anyone on the ground.
The line is an embarrassment to the organization. It should get DeCosta fired if nothing else . Frankly, that should have happened after three QBs got hurt in about 15 snaps in Buffalo a few weeks back.
HENRY AVERAGED -2 YARDS BEFORE CONTACT IN THE FIRST HALF. YOU READ THAT RIGHT. THAT HAPPENED!
"Too many missed chances in the run game on both sides of the ball," Minter said.
Close up shop. The yards before contact have somehow gotten horribly worse every week since DeCosta got fleeced by the Eagles to take Jurgens, who was getting benched, off their hands for a second-round pick before he was benched in Philly. (He was awful on some sacks, too).
Oh, and rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has gotten pretty predictable, especially with the under center runs. “You can key on the under-center running game, so obvious,” one defensive coach from another team texted me during the game.
This head coach – hired to be a functionary for a power-hungry front office – came out last Monday with his notebook filled with talking points and made hints about benching people. He kinda sorta talked tough – as much as someone who has proven to be an utter pushover for his front office and locker room this far can – and then backed it up with nothing.
No messages were sent. It was essentially the same people doing the same things. He made one change – and we told you on “The Daily Flock Show” for a week we thought it was coming. He dropped Kyle Hamilton more in coverage, and he got destroyed by it.
The Chargers kept getting receiver Tre Harris matched up on Hamilton and he killed him on crossers. And he came up with a huge 31-yard sliding catch on an out. Harris had 85 scrimmage yards in the first half and it was often at Hamilton’s expense.
The offensive line isn’t just terrible, it’s penalty filled.  Doyle, an alleged “genius” during seven-on-seven drills, has the most penalized offense in the NFL and they also lead in pre-snap infractions, and we got plenty of that from the start Monday.
Struggling left tackle Ronnie Stanley – who also needed to be moved at the deadline – bookended the first half with holding penalties in critical spots. He negated Justice Hill’s 14-yard burst from Baltimore’s endzone (John Simpson got the call but it was Stanley’s penalty) and he negated Brissett’s scramble in the two-minute drill at the end of the half. Oh, and there was a delay-of-game in that two-minute drill as well, and of course they had a false start.
In a game that was going to be this close, and with Brissett already having to overcome so much, the rash of early penalties was too much.
"it was mostly self-inflicted things," Brissett said.

title: Five Pivotal Ravens Matchups to Watch vs. Chargers
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens' Week 10 primetime bout against the Los Angeles Chargers could ultimately be decided by battles between specific position groups or individual players outperforming their counterparts on the other side of the ball.
In the team's first game with journeyman veteran Jacoby Brissett under center after he was acquired from the Arizona Cardinals via trade, they're entering this matchup as only slight favorites to come out on top over the last winless team in the league.
If the Ravens prevail, they will improve to 5-5 and will still be in last place in the AFC North standings since they're the only team without a division win. Here are the five  matchups that can either make or break this game:
Coming off back-to-back quiet games in which he was held without a catch for the first time in his career and a season low in scrimmage yards among games where he received a single touch with just 23 yards last week, the two-time Pro Bowler is primed and hungry to get back on track.
In games where he's gotten competent quarterback play, Flowers has been unstoppable, and offensive coordinator Declan Doyle should get back to trying to find ways to get him isolated in single coverage on off-ball linebackers over the middle of the field. However, the primary responsibility for limiting his impact will be the Chargers' Derwin James-less defensive backfield that got toasted for five passing touchdowns and allowed a pair of wideouts to eclipse 100 receiving yards last week.
Los Angeles has a pair of Pro Bowl edge rushers in Khalil Mack and Tuli Tuipulotu, both of whom have three sacks on the season and neither of whom was able to bring down Brissettt in the season-opener when he helped the Cardinals hand them the first of their eight straight losses. The motivated duo will be going up against the Ravens' tackle tandem of two-time Pro Bowl veteran Ronnie Stanley and third-year pro Roger Rosengarten, who held them both without a sack and a combined one quarterback hit between them the last time they played against each other in Week 12 of the 2024 season.
Going up against an offensive line and pass-blocking unit that just allowed Justin Herbert to get sacked a career-high eight times last week, the second-year pro has a chance to break his tie for the team lead in sacks with injured fourth-year pro Tavius Robinson. Since four-time Pro Bowler Trey Hendrickson lines up predominantly across from the left tackle, he'll be facing off with fellow Pro Bowler Joe Alt, which means Green will get to go up against fourth-round rookie Travis Burke, who has a pass-blocking grade of 56.1 from Pro Football Focus that ranks 61st out of 71 qualifying tackles.
During his last season and a half with the Cardinals, Brissett excelled at throwing over the middle of the field and heavily targeted the tight end position as he helped turn Trey McBride into a household name around the league. While the Ravens' resident multi-time Pro Bowler, Mark Andrews, is clearly on a steep decline, he can still be a solid possession option, while rookies Matt Hibner and Josh Cuevas can emerge and be utilized as more dynamic weapons on screens and stretching the seam of the defense. They'll be going up against a Chargers' off-ball linebacker tandem of Daiyan Henley, whom they attempted to trade last week, and former Ravens special teams ace Del'Shawn Phillips.
With the Chargers downgrading leading wide receiver Ladd McConkey to out for this matchup with a back injury, their top big-play threat in the passing game left standing is the big-bodied fourth-year pro. Johnston leads the team with 20 yards per catch but only has 13 receptions in eight games, as his inconsistent hands make him a boom-or-bust big-play target whenever the ball comes his way. Wiggins possesses the speed to run stride-for-stride with any receiver in the league and is physical at the catch point, making him the ideal one-on-one matchup to line up against Johnston in this game when Herbert looks to push the ball downfield.

title: Four Ravens X-Factors For Clash vs. Chargers
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens will continue the 2026 regular season with a second straight home primetime game in Week 10 against the Los Angeles Chargers . Going up against a winless opponent desperate to taste victory for the first time, the difference in the game could come down to how an individual player performs when it matters most or over the course of the game by capitalizing on opportunities when presented with them.
With a win, the Ravens would improve to 5-5 and would still be last in the AFC North division standings but would stay in the hunt for a wildcard playoff berth. A loss would be inexcusable and would drop their record further below .500.
Here are four players who could wind up tilting the scales in favor of the Ravens and first-year head coach Jesse Minter.
The Ravens have a new starter under center in veteran quarterback Jacoby Brissett , whom they acquired in a trade with the Arizona Cardinals ahead of the deadline. During his time in the desert over the last season and a half, he helped two-time Pro Bowl tight end Trey McBride become a household name and earn First Team All Pro honors in 2025.
Projecting the Ravens' fourth-round rookie to be the next McBride is overly optimistic, but he shares some similar traits when it comes to his ability to rack up yards after the catch and threaten the seams of defenses vertically. While Brissett might be more inclined to target veteran Mark Andrews early and often, offensive coordinator Declan Doyle should have some plays schemed up to get the ball in Hibner's hands as the first or primary read.
Coming off a much-needed mini bye in which the coaches claimed to have done a lot of self-scouting, one of the shakeups that Minter all but vowed they'd make on defense should be playing the third-year pro more moving forward, starting in this game. Tampa has seen 20-plus snaps on defense in each of the Ravens' last two games since returning from injured reserve. Between his play in coverage, run support and being in the right place at the right time to recover a fumble in Week 8, he's shown he's deserving of a regular role as part of a rotation at outside corner at the expense of four-time Pro Bowl veteran Marlon Humphrey, whose recent struggles have come in too many high-leverage moments.
The Ravens' running game hasn't been the same since they lost veteran blocking tight end Durham Smythe to injury, and their attempts to have others step up and replace him haven't yielded the desired results. However, they might have the next best thing by deploying the second-year swing tackle more often in jumbo formations as an extra blocker on the end of the line. The chunk plays his blocks helped spring were some of the few impressive highlights from their last game, especially the one that resulted in running back Justice Hill for a 65-yard touchdown. Instead of forcing the issue with traditional 12 and 13 personnel, taking off Andrews or one of the young tight ends in favor of Vinson when they want to get the ground game going will tremendously aid in the effort.
Carson Vinson 👀 pic.twitter.com/SyI6piSQEV
Under first-year offensive coordinator Mike McDaniels, the Chargers dial screens on 10.2% of their dropbacks through Week 9, which is the ninth-highest rate in the league . This could lead to a very active game for the Ravens' fourth-year off-ball linebacker, who is a heat-seeking missile when coming downhill. Simpson can snuff out screens and checkdowns for tackles for loss and minimal gains and even spy the quarterback. Los Angeles' Justin Herbert is averaging 5.6 yards per rushing attempt through eight games and could be more prone to scrambling coming off a game in which he was sacked a career-high eight times.
