title: NFL Execs Grade the Raiders: Hondo’s Exclusive Weekly Report Card
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-6) are going to Denver to take on the Broncos (7-2) this weekend, and before we can fully turn the page to that game, we have to offer one final evaluation, after watching the film and speaking to several people about the loss to the Seattle Seahawks.
Each week, we dig deep into the film of the previous weekend’s game, speak to coaches and players, and finally seek outside evaluation from people associated with other NFL teams. So, without further ado, I offer you my Raiders vs. Seahawks report card.
I wish grades could be dichotomized, but we all know they can’t. The offensive grade here is not good, and I feel bad because the offense was terrible in the second half, while the first half was much better.
The Raiders held the lead after scoring 10 points in the first half behind a brilliantly called game by Klint Kubiak.
Rolling Fernando Mendoza to his right and left, using his legs, and the play action opened up the running and passing lanes. They didn’t look like the elite Seahawks offense Kubiak led last year to the Super Bowl, but they were the better offense.
In the second half, Mendoza was a human piñata for the Seahawks, and the Raiders could do nothing. It's easy to credit the Seahawks' defense, but the Raiders shut themselves down.
Kubiak said as much: “I think we had a really positive first half but you have to play four quarters of football, run game as well in order to get the result you want. We only played two quarters."
As different as the first and second halves were, this poor overall grade for the offense doesn’t reflect Fernando Mendoza, who I believe earned an A. Kubiak talked about his first start.
“In his first start, I was very pleased with him getting out of the huddle, him making the correct checks, the correct cans. That’s what he has shown in practice, his ability to do that and to be able to run the show that way. There’s room for growth, but in his first start, I thought that he operated the game like he does in practice.”
An NFL executive said of Mendoza, “I think he looked exactly what I thought he would look like. As you know from our previous evaluation I was very high on him, and I still am. Would have liked to see Klint stay calling the game like he did in the first half.” More from this quote later.
Michael Mayer said, “We got to play better, we got to do better, we got to block better in the run game. End of story.”
The goal in the NFL against an average offense is to hold them to 20 points or fewer. They allowed the world champions to score 21. Despite the uproar of disgust toward DC Rob Leonard, who can only coach with the players he is given, and more than one veteran struggling, the discipline showed up, and the Raiders hung in.
Was the Raiders defense as good as the Seahawks? Of course not, but the Raiders' defense was improved, and Kubiak spelled out why he is encouraged.
“I just thought the way that we started the game. I thought Rob [Leonard] did a really good job this week of getting our guys ready to play, getting them ready to start fast, getting turnovers, executing the game plan. There’s plenty of things that we have to do better, but I just saw, overall, as a defense, us play better football.”
Maxx Crosby spoke candidly about an improved defensive performance. “Yeah, it wasn’t perfect, but I think we took the ball away. We played really hard. We did some good things. It wasn’t perfect. I know we can be better, but I think as a group and a collective, we’re playing with a relentless style of play. We’ve been getting, I feel like, at least two turnovers a week, and we just have to keep tightening up little things. And we’ll keep going where we need to go.”
One NFC team executive told me, “I like what the Raiders want to do on D, but trying to run that Baltimore Ravens-type D is great, but I would want to see those defensive ends opposite of Maxx (Crosby) going wider, trying to establish the edge."
I asked Kubiak about that. "I think each play is unique. Each front is unique. I thought we had some excellent edge sets by Kwity Paye, stands out. He's shown some good stuff, but there there's some ones that we let the defense get to the edge and it cost us a touchdown, especially on that right side."
Robbie Leonard has a boss, and I respect that, but if someone is being fair, that was a much more impressive performance than what we saw the week before.
Nakobe Dean spoke of the fast start by the defense: “Always important to come out fast. You got to finish faster, though. You got to come out fast and finish faster. So, yeah, we just got to finish as a team.”
Matt Gay, Alex Ward, AJ Cole, and STC Joe DeCamillis, and every one of those units were terrific. One mishap by Dylan Laube was quickly corrected, but overall, under Joe D's leadership, the Silver and Black shone.
I have a ton of respect for Klint Kubiak, and I have never been as sold on a first-time coach as I am on him. That said, he led his offense like a first-year coach on Sunday. He admitted, when I asked after the game, that he shouldn’t have abandoned the rollouts in the second half, and that the play-action moving away was nonsensical. One NFL executive mentioned above told me what he thought happened.
“Klint knows that Seahawks staff like the back of his hand. He isn’t a good coach, he’s a great coach, but I think he out thought himself on Sunday. I think he assumed what they would do so he went away from what was working. Love his first, and love even more that he admitted he should not have. He learned a tough lesson against the Super Bowl champs, no shame in that.”
Again, I thought Leonard did a good job; DeCamillis did what he does. Kubiak is better than he performed on Sunday; look at the nine games prior. A poor performance doesn't erase all of the tremendous progress.
He is better than he was on Sunday, and so are the Raiders. Lesson learned, but I, for one, am squarely on the Kubiak train, and I believe in him more today than I ever have.
Once again, Raider Nation, after nearly 30 years as a sports reporter, does something I have never seen and makes me respect them even more.
Wanting to honor Mendoza’s mother, Elsa, who is in a wheelchair, they asked each other, at a fan's request, to sit when he scored his first touchdown. Tens of thousands did so in a moment that went viral, and I asked him about it after the game.
A visibly moved Mendoza said, “I was not aware of that. However, I’m super grateful to the Silver and Black for doing that. Means a lot to my family and I just can’t thank you guys enough. On a dark day, that brings a smile to my face. So I really thank everybody for respecting my family and appreciate all their support.”
One long-time source from the league office, after seeing my question, sent me this message. "Not gonna lie, my eyes may have started sweating a little bit, that was pretty cool." Well done, Raider Nation.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: Raiders QB Mendoza Shares Mindset, Expectations, Biggest Lessons
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-6) are headed to Denver this week to face the Broncos (7-2) and, yet again, another top defense.
Fernando Mendoza had a terrific first start on Sunday, but heading to the home of a longtime AFC West foe in Denver won’t be easy for the rookie.
The Raiders rookie, whom NFL executives ranked the best QB prospect of the last four NFL Drafts, was not perfect. This is the NFL, and no one is. The defending Super Bowl champions taught him some tough lessons, but every hit, new look, and scheme shift is now on tape, and the contemplative Mendoza will study it fiercely and be ready next time.
The issue was not preparedness; it was simply experience. The Raiders lost on Sunday in the win-loss column, but they won in the long term.
I asked Mendoza moments after the game if he could look at the loss to the Seahawks through the lens of win or lose, or if he could go behind the proverbial curtain and appreciate the long-term lessons learned. The reigning Heisman Trophy winner didn’t hesitate to pounce on that.
“I believe that it is more of a win or lose mentality. Coach [Klint] Kubiak holds us to a very high standard, and that’s what it comes down to at the end of the day. And there’s a lot of things that I need to prove on that field. I’m excited to watch the film and get back to work.”
Getting your first start in the NFL is a dream come true, but the Seahawks' defense is elite, and Mendoza didn’t get here by ignoring the obvious.
“Yeah, Seahawks have a fantastic defense. We’ve seen it all season, so a lot of credit to them and Coach [Mike] Macdonald. Fantastic. And it’s good to get punched in the face because now it’s a great opportunity to grow and learn and to really unveil all the deficiencies that I have in my game, as a future hopeful leader of this offense.”
In my nearly thirty years, the elite players are never happy. Many seem immune to criticism or praise from the media and fans because their standards are so high. That is the case with a superstar on the rise in Mendoza.
“I think it’s always about doing your job. That’s what Coach [Klint] Kubiak always preaches, is doing your job. And in the first half, I thought we got off to a good start. However, in the second half, being 0-for-7 on third downs, and those being passing downs, not throwing the ball away enough."
"There were a lot of sacks there, but we should have had half as many, if not even less than that. So I need to mature as a quarterback, throw the ball away, throw more accurate balls on third down, and make sure we can move the chains to give our defense time to recuperate on the sideline and really get it going in the second half.”
The first half felt like a Hollywood movie, but the real struggles for Mendoza and the Raiders' offense came in the second half. Something he was very aware of.
“Yeah, in the second half, because of how the game was going, our defense did a fantastic job, but because of how we were playing offensively, at the forefront myself, we got behind there, and so it’s a little bit more of a passing situation. And then Coach [Mike] Macdonald dialed it up and did great. There was a couple times that we tried to check someone else's protection, and he was playing chess, and he fooled me, and he got me a couple times."
"And I think it’s important to learn and grow from this, to throw my hot routes more often, to throw accurate balls when getting hit, and to practice that rather than everything just being sunshine and rainbows, then move forward and give our team a better chance each and every week.”
Kirk Cousins miraculously led the Minnesota Vikings to a monster win in Green Bay on Sunday, and even with him 1,842 miles away from Allegiant Stadium, his shadow - his mentorship of Mendoza - was still felt by the rookie.
“Well, I think one of the biggest lessons that he showed and displayed to the entire team is that, especially in NFL games, you’re never out of it. Even in the fourth quarter, having a pretty awful third quarter performance, we were able to almost get back into it, and it was a one-score game."
"And so Kirk [Cousins] always fighting and having great leadership on the sidelines, keep on fighting through thick or thin, no matter what the momentum of the game is like or whatever the situation is, is something that popped up in our little quarterback sideline meeting huddle, whatever you call it, when we recoup and watch the film in the huddle.”
So how much did a front-row seat to Cousins for nine games help? “I think it helped me a lot. Evidently, I didn’t play up to the standard of the quarterback room or to the team, but I felt that if I started like week one, it would have looked a lot different without Kirk’s [Cousins] mentorship. So his mentorship has helped me a lot. And although it was a tough performance and not up to the standard, I really do appreciate him and all the learning and teaching that he’s helped me with.”
One of the things we have discussed often with a rookie QB with a terrific running skill set is trusting the pocket in the NFL and learning when to, and when not to, run. There is very little argument that Patrick Mahomes is the best QB in the NFL, and he right now is the master of the best runners, who demonstrate that patience. Mendoza has the proper mindset and will get there, and he talked about that skill set.
“Yeah, I need to stand in there more. I was a little sped up today. There were some times that if you can extend the play and it gives a good chance to get out clean, not take a sack, and extend the play because the defense did a really good job covering, then that’s acceptable."
"But there are some times that I should have stayed in there, stepped up with one hitch, and then delivered a strike, rather than already looking to scramble. And it’s credit to Seattle’s defense. However, I need to be better, be more composed in the pocket.”
Mendoza was sacked six times on Sunday; as few as three of them (perhaps more) wouldn’t have happened under Kirk Cousins, who was terrific at the pre-snap and post-snap reads—identifying hot routes and making adjustments. That is the proverbial learning curve in a rebuilding year that Mendoza is undergoing, and I asked him about that skill set and how it impacted him on Sunday.
“Yeah, it’s a lot different. The NFL is a whole different level, and you need to understand your hot routes, which I need to do better, and we need to understand and essentially be a master at the protection scheme, because it’s one thing when we’re in the meeting room saying, ‘Okay, I would do this, this’ rather than in the heat of the battle. So those are things I need to improve on and will improve on and aspire to improve on to best help my team.”
For a 15-year veteran like Kirk Cousins, Brock Bowers is a trusted resource. Still, for a rookie, he is much more - a security blanket without a doubt - and Mendoza addressed the enormity of losing him for the second half.
“Brock’s [Bowers] a fantastic player. He’s a special human being on and off the field. However, Coach [Klint] Kubiak always preaches everybody doing their job. So the next guy up, I have as much confidence in, and so I just need to get the ball to the right players on time, efficiently and accurately.”
This organization has protected Mendoza, supported him, and done a masterful job of getting him to this point. He isn’t the first.
“I can’t thank everybody enough for all the ‘apoyo’, which is support in Spanish, especially all the fans and my teammates, my coaches who had a lot of support in me, giving me this opportunity and chance, and I need to be better for them."
"However, it’s always great to get the experience of a first NFL start, and now have more tangible items to improve off of and see the deficiencies, then attack them this week. As opposed to the game reps are always more valuable than practice reps, although they’re all valuable.”
Mendoza didn’t mince words when going back to discuss the Seahawks' blitz…

title: What Mendoza Showed, Where Raiders Can Improve After First Start
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders lost to the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday, but Sunday was about much more than just winning or losing. Sunday marked the official start of the next chapter in the storied franchise's history.
Given the Raiders' significant needs elsewhere on the roster, there were many positives from Fernando Mendoza's performance on Sunday.
A quarterback and a coaching staff that can work well with their current roster, missing pieces and all, have eluded the Raiders in recent seasons. This has been an overlooked issue.
Las Vegas is in the early stages of rebuilding what has been arguably the league's worst collection of talent over the past three seasons. It must be noted that the roster that John Spytek took over was that bad. That is not hyperbole or an exaggeration.
The Raiders' 2025 roster earned the No. 1 overall pick that they used to select the rookie signal caller. It was not always pretty, but when Mendoza and the offense were effective, it was more than evident that he has the skill set to work with a sometimes-shaky offensive line.
He has the mobility to leave the pocket when that line breaks down, as he showed several times on Sunday. He has the ability to make something out of nothing and extend plays with the roster the Raiders currently have, as broken as it still is. This is what a true, quality rebuild looks like.
The Raiders had a rookie quarterback starting his first game. Brock Bowers did not play the entire second half. Las Vegas' loss to Seattle was arguably their best loss of the season. They were down by 11 points entering the fourth quarter against the Seahawks.
The Raiders were down by 18 points entering the fourth quarter in Week 9. They were down by 22 entering the fourth quarter in Week 7, down by 10 entering the fourth quarter in Week 6, and down by 25 entering the fourth quarter in Week 5.
It would be hard to argue that Mendoza's ability to escape pressure, make plays with his legs, and fit the ball into tight windows did not help the Raiders' offense extend drives. This also gave their defense a rest. It is no mistake that Las Vegas' defense played its best in weeks. It all connects.
Wins are, and always will be, a team stat largely determined by quarterback play. Yet it takes more than just a good quarterback to win consistently in football. This is one of the sport's many beauties. On Sunday, Mendoza did not do many things wrong. His mistakes were minimal and understandable.
As expected, a rookie quarterback will miss certain nuances of the game in his first career start, which came against the defending Super Bowl champions and possibly the league's best defense. However, most of those things were minimal and had little to do with the loss.
Most potential complaints about Mendoza's first start can be alleviated with more experience on game days. The Raiders' defense likely wasn't sending full-speed corner blitzes at Mendoza in practice like the Seahawks did on Sunday. Game repetitions are more valuable than practice.
A more experienced Mendoza likely leads the team to a Week 10 win. Following Sunday's loss, Mendoza had a measured analysis of his first start. Despite the odds stacked against the entire roster, Mendoza knows there is room for improvement, and the real work is just beginning.
“I think it’s always about doing your job. That’s what Coach [Klint] Kubiak always preaches, is doing your job. And in the first half, I thought we got off to a good start. However, in the second half, being 0-for-7 on third downs, and those being passing downs, not throwing the ball away enough,” Mendoza said.
“There were a lot of sacks there, but we should have had half as many, if not even less than that. So I need to mature as a quarterback, throw the ball away, throw more accurate balls on third down, and make sure we can move the chains to give our defense time to recuperate on the sideline and really get it going in the second half.”
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Breaking Down Every Raiders Position Group After Loss to Seahawks
full_text:
Las Vegas Raiders rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza started his first game as a professional. On Sunday, the Raiders officially began a new era. Mendoza's first career start marked a historic day for the franchise as its second-ever No. 1 overall pick took the field.
The Raiders lost to the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday. Personally, I don't think it was a bad game or a bad loss. I believe it was the best loss they have had all season.
Below are the grades for each of Las Vegas' position groups following their Week 10 loss.
A loss is a loss, and he could have done some things better, but in his first start, he showed he has the physical tools for success in the league. Sunday was Mendoza's first meaningful football game since last season's College Football Playoff. That was almost a full calendar year ago.
He had a solid first start . Sunday was another accurate look at where the Raiders stand. They now have a quarterback who has the skill set to improve their offense, even compared to what it was under Kirk Cousins. However, he needs more experience and a better supporting cast.
The Raiders weren't going to beat the Seahawks with Cousins or Mendoza, but out of their six losses this season, Sunday was arguably the most competitive game they've played. Week 10 was not about wins, losses, or stats. It was about finally letting Mendoza take the next step in his development.
Mendoza was two yards away from leading the team in rushing on Sunday. Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington were largely unproductive out of the backfield. However, Jeanty led the team in receptions and receiving yards, which undoubtedly helped Las Vegas' passing game.
Until the Raiders fix their offensive line, it may not matter who the running back is.
Connor Heyward is underrated.
Entering Week 10, the Raiders' line had only allowed 11 sacks through nine games, making the unit statistically one of the league's best in the category. Sunday, the unit allowed six sacks. Most of those were coverage sacks. Some were because of poor offensive line play.
Some of the sacks were on Mendoza as well, but that is where the offensive line is supposed to pick up the slack for a rookie quarterback in his first start. Some of the sacks on Mendoza were clean shots where the defender was not touched at all. That can happen once. Not repeatedly.
The six sacks were not all on the offensive line, but most of the blame will be. That is how life works in the NFL. Let's hope Week 10 was an anomaly for the unit.
Losing Brock Bowers for the entire second half predictably impacted Las Vegas' offense. The blocking seemed worse across the board after Bowers left the game.
As a unit, the Raiders' receivers were nonexistent on Sunday. Losing Bowers mid-game made the second half tough for Las Vegas' committee of receivers.
Las Vegas' interior defensive line is thin. Tonka Hemingway has struggled to stay healthy. Thomas Booker is hobbled. Kwity Paye left the game with a neck injury. Patrick Johnson is on injured reserve. Las Vegas recently released Jonah Laulu. Keyron Crawford has been out all season.
What once was their deepest unit has quickly been depleted. The Raiders must thoroughly address the unit in the offseason.
Aside from filling the incorrect hole on a few running plays, Las Vegas' linebackers played well on Sunday. The unit made an impact early, recovering two fumbles. The Raiders are a few more roster additions away from maximizing the talent they recently signed at linebacker.
Las Vegas' defensive backfield gave up chunk plays against the Seahawks, but battled long enough and hard enough to keep the team in the game. It was not pretty, but Sunday may have been the best the unit has played since Week 4 against the Kansas City Chiefs.
The Raiders' defensive backfield played better in their loss to the Seahawks than in their win against the New York Jets.
It may have been against a backup quarterback, but Sunday was unquestionably the best the unit has played in the last five weeks. The same is true about the Raiders' defense as a whole.
Kicker Matt Gay scored over half of the team's points on Sunday. AJ Cole averaged of 56 yards per punt.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Overreactions to Raiders' Struggle in Loss vs. Seahawks
full_text:
Another week, another loss to a winning team for the Las Vegas Raiders, who fell to 4-6 on the season against the Seattle Seahawks and the No. 1-ranked defense in the NFL.
It was a special week for the organization as rookie No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza made his first career start. It certainly wasn't a special performance, and the Raiders were smothered on both sides of the ball. It was another week where the organization looked outmatched and outgunned against a quality opponent, and it won't get any easier in the coming weeks.
Having all of that in mind, here are my overreactions to Sunday's 21-13 loss in Las Vegas as the Raiders move on to another road trip to Denver next week.
I did not think it was possible for the Raiders' run game to be arguably worse than last year, as this time a year ago, we were already seeing terrific flashes of Ashton Jeanty. Instead, it seems Klint Kubiak cannot figure out who to play at running back, how to deploy them, and how to give them avenues to succeed while managing a bad offensive line with their $25 million-per-year center underperforming.
The Raiders' head coach has tried everything, but this is a sad state of affairs for a Raiders run game that had so much potential coming into the season. I don't think this will improve anytime soon, and Raider Nation needs to start looking at the top offensive linemen for the 2027 NFL Draft.
We haven't seen a ton of games this season where Crosby took over the game, but the Raiders did a great job positioning Crosby against Abraham Lucas and Josh Jones. Crosby has a handful of pressures paired with a sack while dominating in the run game, with four tackles for loss in one of his best performances of the season.
It was great to see Crosby show up against a quality opponent like the Seahawks. It wasn't enough to slow down Jaxon Smith-Njigba, but his presence up front for the Raiders' defense remains invaluable as the season goes on.
It wasn't the prettiest debut for a rookie quarterback by any means, especially for the former top pick in the draft. Mendoza completed 17 of 29 pass attempts for 143 yards, was sacked six times, and was pressured numerous times.
He showcased several things to be excited about, whether that is the arm arrogance as a passer, the pocket mobility, the poise that made him so great at Indiana and Cal, or his impressive out-of-structure ability and legs that allowed him to get his first NFL touchdown early in the game.
Mendoza began to falter when the pressure came, and he did not have Brock Bowers for most of the game due to an ankle injury, while also playing against the league's best defense. Overall, it went as I would've expected, and Raider Nation should be patient for Mendoza's breakout game.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: Winners & Losers: Raiders Fall to Seahawks in Mendoza’s First Start
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-6) fell last night to the Seattle Seahawks (6-4) 21-13.
The Raiders remain overachieving given preseason expectations , and holding the defending world champions to only 21 points, despite a defense with clear deficiencies, was an accomplishment.
Each Monday morning, throughout the season, I have a winners-and-losers article for you detailing what worked and what didn’t. Once again, we dig into the last game.
When you are a team like the Raiders, without a WR1, you can often compensate for that with the best tight end in the National Football League: Brock Bowers.
After an impressive first half in which they led at halftime, the Silver and Black came out for the second half without their superstar tight end, Brock Bowers, who was ruled out with an ankle injury.
With the absence of the aforementioned WR1, the Raiders' offense, unable to run the ball against good defense, is sunk. One person, not a doctor but part of the organization, told me they didn’t think it was anything long-term, but said that was only a cursory opinion from a non-professional. Klint Kubiak had some preliminary news.
“Brock Bowers…we’ll reevaluate him tomorrow.”
In the first half, Kubiak had tremendous success moving Mendoza out of the pocket and rolling him to the outside. Stunningly, the Raiders went away from it in the second half, and so I asked Kubiak, who has had a great first year, about it. Was it because of the loss of Bowers?
“No, should have done more for sure.”
One of the biggest reasons that Klint Kubiak, the hottest candidate of the last coaching cycle, took this job was because he knew he would get a franchise QB in Fernando Mendoza. Mendoza was the young man that NFL executives ranked as the best QB prospect in the NFL Draft over the last four years. So what did he think of the rookie’s first start? “He was well prepared. He started the game really well, and overall, for his first start, I thought was a good start.”
He went further on what he thought Mendoza should take away from playing against a team like Seattle. “There’s a lot. We’ll watch the film together. We can learn a lot from this game. But overall, we have to play better. We've got to support him better. I've got to help him better in the second half. What happened in second half to go 0-for-7 on third down is unacceptable. No reason that we should do that. Credit to Seattle.”
Kubiak was very vociferous with his offensive line about a rough performance, and he talked about that moment and what it meant. “We expect more from ourselves coming out of the tunnel in the third quarter, and I expect more of myself as well. So obviously, the second half was not good enough. You don’t give yourself a chance to win. I thought defensively, we took a step forward today. They kept us in the ball game, and we had to play complementary football.”
Kubiak was asked whether he simplified his game plan for the rookie, but he thought someone else impacted the plan more in the second half, and I bet you can already figure it out.
“I thought overall when we lost Brock [Bowers], you definitely saw a big change in production. So I look at myself; I have to do a much better job of moving the ball, getting and spreading the ball around.”
In fact, the Raiders enlarged the game plan thanks to Mendoza’s legs. “Yes, that helps. His mobility helps. Gives us a different dimension.”
Mendoza’s poise and composure stood out considering the beating he took, and you can count his coach as a fan. "Yeah, that’s not a surprise. That’s who he is. He’s obviously an excellent player, but he’s got poise, he’s got maturity, he’s got leadership, and that showed all throughout the week.”
The reality is that you can’t take six sacks and expect to win in the NFL. “Yeah, well I think there’s a lot that goes into that. Number one, credit Seattle; they did a good job. Number two, we have to be better up front for our quarterback. And then number three, I think obviously with a rookie quarterback, there’s chances to throw the ball away at times, and there’s a lot more than just one thing. But you’re not going to win a game taking six sacks.”
The Raiders' running game was interesting in the first half, but once Bowers went down, it collapsed in the second half, and Kubiak addressed the woes.
“It was a positive first half. You have to sustain it for four quarters. Weren’t able to do that. Try to come out of the tunnel and run the ball. The first call of second half is run, and we take a loss. But I put it on myself. There’s no one else to blame but me.”
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: Raiders Stock Report: Risers & Fallers After Loss to Seahawks
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders entered their Week 10 home matchup against the Seattle Seahawks as a different team than they were last week. After nine games and another loss against a quality opponent that Las Vegas could have competed better against, the trade deadline forced the Raiders' hand.
The Raiders' front office received an offer they could not refuse from the Minnesota Vikings. After using the No. 1 overall pick on Fernando Mendoza, Las Vegas acquired a third-round pick from the Vikings in exchange for Cousins, paving the way for Mendoza's first start.
All eyes were on Las Vegas' rookie in Allegiant Stadium, as the Raiders have long sought a young, talented quarterback with Mendoza's skill set. Those skills have been tucked away on the bench and the practice field this season, up until Sunday, that is.
The Raiders' offense looked competent on Sunday, and they did so early in the game for one of the first times all season. Following a Seahawks turnover, Mendoza led the Raiders on an 11-play, 46-yard touchdown drive, making several plays that wouldn't have been possible previously.
This included an 11-yard touchdown run on third-and-goal that put the Raiders up 7-0 early in the game. Mendoza finished the first half as the team's leading rusher. That literally would never have happened previously.
Offensively, the Raiders played arguably their best first half of the season. Mendoza completed 11 of his 13 first-half passes for 90 yards, leading Las Vegas to a 10-7 lead. The Raiders' offense looked formidable in the first half.
This was the case even when the unit didn't score points. Furthermore, Las Vegas sustained drives significantly better in the first half than it did in recent weeks. It was far from glamorous, but the unit moved the ball better in general.
Las Vegas' defense came to play on Sunday. The unit held the Seahawks to one touchdown in the first half, responding well to the spark their teammates on offense started the game with. Even that touchdown they allowed was a fortunate play for the Seahawks.
The Raiders' defense was one tackle away from holding Seattle scoreless in the first half. After allowing multiple rushers to run for 100 yards in the first half in recent weeks, Las Vegas' defense held the Seahawks to 52 rushing yards in the first half.
Yes, the defense gave up big plays in the second half, but that's after the unit was again left on the field for way too long. In the first half, Las Vegas won the time of possession by nearly nine minutes. Early in the fourth quarter, the Seahawks held the ball for 13 of the second half's first 17 minutes.
Leonard's unit also forced two turnovers, helping keep the team competitive. The unit could have performed better, but today's loss wasn't on the defense .
Both of Las Vegas' safeties made costly mistakes on Sunday. Jeremy Chinn and Treydan Stukes are two of the best defensive backs on the roster. If defenses can successfully complete passes against those two, it is likely to be a long day for the Raiders.
The Raiders have struggled to run the ball long before any of their current running backs were on the roster. Las Vegas has invested heavily in the running back position in each of the last two offseasons. It is unlikely the Raiders whiffed on both players. The reason for the struggles is up front.
The Raiders have changed head coaches, offensive coordinators, running backs, and quarterbacks, yet they struggled to run the ball for the fourth straight season. That was the case on Sunday against the Seahawks , even with Mendoza's runs adding to the total.
The only position group the Raiders have not adequately addressed that impacts their ability to run the ball is the offensive line. Tyler Linderbaum was a solid addition. However, Las Vegas has question marks at every other position on the offensive line.
Kolton Miller has lost a step. Both starting offensive guards are mediocre, at best, regardless of who Las Vegas plays at those positions. DJ Glaze's durability is top-tier, but he still needs further improvement. The Raiders essentially have question marks at three or four offensive line positions.
This has significantly impacted the Raiders' ground game. Through three quarters, Las Vegas had 65 rushing yards. That was not enough to help the Raiders sustain drives in the second half. With four minutes remaining in the fourth quarter, Las Vegas had scored zero points in the second half.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Instant Reactions to Raiders' Fernando Mendoza's First Start
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders entered their Week 10 matchup against the Seattle Seahawks looking for their first win against a team with a winning record this season. Yet the historical importance of the day did not escape those in attendance.
Of all the issues the Raiders have had in recent seasons, and there have been many, the quarterback position has been the one where Las Vegas has lacked stability the most. The only position with a comparable turnover rate is the head coach position.
Las Vegas' front office addressed both this offseason, hiring Klint Kubiak and Andrew Janocko to lead their revamped offense and drafting Mendoza with the first overall pick. However, through the first half of the season, the trio had yet to work together on the field.
After trading veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins shortly before the trade deadline, that all changed on Sunday. After years of subpar play at the quarterback position, Las Vegas trotted last season's Heisman Trophy winner onto the field. If all goes as planned, he'll be the last for a while.
Las Vegas got off to the perfect start, forcing a turnover on Seattle's first drive. This gave Mendoza a short field on his first drive as a pro. The short field opened up the playbook for Kubiak and Janocko in ways rarely seen this season. It was a methodical, well-planned first drive.
Mendoza and the Raiders' offense marched downfield on an 11-play, 46-yard touchdown drive. Those seven points tied Las Vegas' season-high in first-quarter points, and Mendoza did it on his first drive.  The first drive gave a glimpse of how well the offense can run with Mendoza under center.
Mendoza's mobility and accuracy helped open up Las Vegas' offense directly and indirectly. Mendoza's mobility forced the Seahawks' defense into difficult situations. The possibility of Mendoza moving the pocket or scrambling only made Mendoza's pinpoint accuracy that much more lethal.
For the first time this season, Las Vegas' quarterback put opposing defenses in a similar situation as their own defense in recent weeks. The Raiders' defense has struggled against mobile quarterbacks who throw well on the run or can run well altogether. This time, Las Vegas' opponent had to deal with it.
The Raiders had a chance to score right before halftime but did not. They received the ball first in the second half, and didn't score then either. A score on either drive would have put the Raiders up by multiple possessions. Instead, things went the opposite direction.
Las Vegas did not score a single point in the third quarter and went nearly the entire fourth quarter without scoring. The Raiders followed arguably their best first half of the season against teams with a winning record, with a forgettable second half.
Yes, everyone knows Bowers is one of one. He is undoubtedly the best tight end in the league when healthy. However, things were much more difficult for the Raiders' offense once the Seahawks did not have to worry about him. Bowers missed the second half with an ankle injury.
Las Vegas' offense looked completely out of sorts without Bowers on the field. Not having Bowers on the field changed the flow of the game for the Raiders' offense and, therefore, its defense. Las Vegas' roster is still a work in progress, but they have to figure out how to be productive without Bowers.
That is much easier said than done, especially until the Raiders make additional roster moves in future offseasons. However, for the rest of the 2026 season, Kubiak and Janocko will have to draw up better plays when Bowers is not on the field.
Bowers is a critical part of Las Vegas' offense, but there have to be answers available to the Raiders' coaching staff this season, should he be unavailable.
A loss is a loss, and there are few positives that can come from it. However, the Mendoza got valuable experience on Sunday. The fact that the Raiders kept the game close against a team with a winning record proves they are headed in the right direction.
It was far from pretty, but it was a productive day in the grand scheme of things for Mendoza, Kubiak, and the Raiders.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Why Win Over Seahawks Could Legitimize Raiders Playoff Aspirations
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders have had a unique season to watch in 2026.
Starting out of the gates hot with a three-game winning streak, everything was looking up for this team. Then a four-game skid followed, and the Raiders currently sit at 4-5 after a win against the New York Jets and a loss to the San Francisco 49ers.
The Raiders are not currently in the playoff picture, but it would only take a few wins for them to enter the conversation. This would be impressive considering it is the first year under Klint Kubiak , with a lack of household names on the roster and a team in its initial rebuilding season.
Las Vegas takes on the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks this afternoon, a true test for No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza in his first career start. The Seahawks feature one of the NFL's best defenses, so Mendoza would impress the NFL world if he can help them get the win.
Not only would that win get the Raiders to 5-5, but it would also show they have every capability of being a postseason team, despite a rebuild underway.
The Seahawks may not be the force they were last year en route to a Super Bowl victory, but they are still a solid team capable of making the postseason. These are the kinds of teams the Raiders need to beat if they want to have a shot at the playoffs.
While they are still good, there are weaknesses in Seattle. The Seahawks cannot move the ball the same way they did last year (Raiders fans are well aware of why ), and the defense is gettable if the opposing offense finds a rhythm.
The NFL media will be asking whether the Raiders are a legit playoff team if they win this game, which would be an incredible place to be in the middle of November. Raiders fans were rewatching Indiana games from the previous Saturday at this time last year.
The Raiders would sit at 5-5 with a win, and they'd be watching the New England Patriots and Cleveland Browns, hoping for losses so they would have the same record as those teams. There is a chance both those teams lose, considering their opponents, which makes this game that much more important for Las Vegas.
A loss doesn't necessarily knock the Raiders out of contention; they'd still be in the hunt. However, it would more than likely show they aren't ready just yet.
There are no outcomes that would ruin the Raiders' future, so fans shouldn't worry too much about what happens. The upside, however, is too exciting to ignore.
Carter Landis studied journalism at Michigan State University where I graduated in May of 2022. He currently is a sports reporter for a local television station, and is a writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders

title: Zeek Biggers News Is Another Big Setback for Dolphins D-Line, But It Could Get Worse
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are going to be running out of bodies at the rate they're going — big bodies, that is.
In their first game with Zach Sieler on injured reserve, the Dolphins watched both Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips leave their 24-22 loss against the Indianapolis Colts with injuries, and the verdict has come on the severity of one of them — and it's not good news.
Biggers is done for the season after sustaining a meniscus injury in his right knee, according to NFL insider Ian Rapoport, citing sources.
#Dolphins DT Zeek Biggers, a former 7th round pick who has earned a starting role, will have knee surgery to repair his lateral meniscus, sources say, a procedure that ends his season. Biggers will make a full recovery in time for 2027. pic.twitter.com/nK6i2JzrPM
The question now is whether Phillips' injury wil be as severe after he left Lucas Oil Stadium with an arm in a sling and was scheduled for an MRI on Monday.
Head coach Jeff Hafley said Monday afternoon that both players needed more tests to determine the severity of the injury, but now the best the Dolphins will be able to do is salvage a second of the four defensive tackles from last year.
If Phillips is sidelined for a while, the Dolphins will be down to 2025 first-round pick Kenneth Grant and Keith Cooper Jr. on the 35-man roster, with Jordan Jefferson the lone defensive tckle on the practice squad.
The bad luck, of course, began when Sieler sustained a season-ending biceps injury in the Week 9 loss against the Detroit Lions.
Biggers' injury means the Dolphins will need to add at least one defensive tackle to the 53-man roster, and that number will go to two if Phillips also winds up having to go on injured reserve.
Two names to watch would be Fatorma Mulbah and Matthew Butler, who both were with the Dolphins in training camp before being among the final cuts to the 53-player limit.
Former Dolphins first-round pick Christian Wilkins certainly is an interesting name, but there's been no indication that any team has reached out to him this year and he hasn't played in a bit more than two years after sustaining a serious foot injury while with the Las Vegas Raiders in 2024.
Now that any time would be good for these kind of injuries, the timing really isn't good because the Dolphins are about to face one of the best rushing teams when they travel to Buffalo on Sunday.
Biggers was injured during Seth McGowan's touchdown run in the first quarter that gave the Colts a 7-0 lead.
He played in all nine games this season and made two starts, contributing at both defensive tackle and defensive end.
He was a seventh-round pick in 2025 after the Dolphins had selected Grant in the first round and Phillips in the fifth round.

title: How Jarrett Kingston Is Emerging as the Best Waiver Wire Pick-Up for the Dolphins As Another One Bites the Dust
full_text:
Hours after the much-publicized move to waive kicker Zane Gonzalez, the Miami Dolphins made another transaction Monday, that one involving edge defender Jamree Kromah.
And, like Gonzalez, Kromah was waived, ending his brief time in Miami that began after he was claimed off waivers from the Chicago Bears.
Kromah was let go after appearing in two games for Miami, including the 24-22 loss against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday when his playing time occurred strictly on special teams.
The move left the Dolphins with three openings on their 53-man roster because they were at 52 players when they faced the Colts and haven't yet replaced either Gonzalez or Kromah.
More significantly, the move with Kromah provided more evidence that picking up players on waivers is a sound practice for rebuilding teams looking for hidden gems wherever they can find them, but it also rarely provides great answers.
This isn't to suggest the Dolphins should stop looking at the waiver wire in the hope of finding a good player on whom another team gave up too quickly, but at the same time understanding that the pieces to what the organization ultimately hopes is a contender likely will come through other methods, such as the draft or free agency.
Kromah was the 16th and most recent waiver wire acquisition by the Dolphins so far in 2026, a total that's just four shy of what they did in 2019 when they were undergoing another rebuilding project.
Of those 16 players picked up through waivers this year, exactly half already have come and gone. Of the other eight, only safety Julius Wood and guard Jarrett Kingston have started a game, and it's been one start each.
At this time, none of the waiver wire pick-ups has a significant role, though Wood is a core special teams player and Kingston just became the team's sixth offensive lineman for the game against Indianapolis on Sunday.
But the chances of any of the waiver wire pick-ups becoming key contributors on the team's road back to contention are pretty slim, and that's just the reality of making those moves.
And the Dolphins likely aren't done with moves like that because, who knows, maybe one of them could turn into Zach Sieler.
That's what happened in 2019 when the Dolphins claimed the defensive lineman from the Baltimore Ravens. Nearly seven years later, Sieler is well established as a core player for the Dolphins, a team captain and a major loss now that he's on IR.
To a much lesser degree, the Dolphins also hit in 2019 with Mack Hollins, but the success stories are extremely rare when it comes to waiver wire pick-ups.
It's why we always caution against expecting too much whenever a newcomer arrives, whether it's Kromah or even former Seattle Seahawks third-round pick Christian Haynes, who was claimed just a few days before Kromah.
The rationale is pretty simple: There's a reason the player's former team let them go.
Yes, there will be an exception to the rule at some point, which is why there's no harm in "turning over stones," as the saying goes. That's what the Dolphins did with Kromah.
And even though it didn't pan out, it still was worth the gamble.

title: What the Week 10 Film Told Us About the Miami Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins nearly completed a 14-point comeback, but ultimately fell 24-22 to the Indianapolis Colts in Week 10. Struggles in the trenches litter the all-22 tape of a game that Miami failed to win in key moments, so let’s take a look at some of the biggest lessons from the film review.
Without Aaron Brewer and Malik Willis, communication and protection issues were to be expected, and this game certainly had its fair share of them. Late rushes and rotations led to unblocked defenders in the run and pass game. What’s more worrisome, though, is the seemingly downward trend of individual performances that continued against Indianapolis.
pic.twitter.com/8GAzhCBXjk
The right side tandem of Jonah Savaiinaea and Austin Jackson remains ineffective when stressed, both in one-on-one protection and as the point-of-attack blockers on rushing plays. Miami attempted to prop them up with pullers and misdirection, but it led to a few whiffs by Kadyn Proctor, Patrick Paul, and Will Kacmarek, and players left unaccounted for by the aforementioned late rotations.
In the absence of Chris Bell, Miami also used Kevin Coleman and Malik Washington as key blockers from the slot on runs to their side, and considering both of them are listed under 200 pounds, it went about as well as you’d expect.
pic.twitter.com/cpSmtaHevF
In this game, Miami was without its best offensive lineman, and the duo of Patrick Paul and Kadyn Proctor, who have a combined 38 starts between them, were asked to be the steady-handed adults in the room. Both are capable of high-level reps (and even had some in this game) but lack the refinement to consistently prop up the others around them with such little margin for error. They were put under a microscope and often asked to overcompensate, and thus bear the least of the blame among the starting five.
Miami’s defensive line was a mirror image of their offensive counterpart: without their best player, and unable to make up for it, with young players failing to provide consistent performance.
Kenneth Grant and Jordan Phillips were knocked off the ball consistently. While both have done a solid job standing their ground against double-teams in recent weeks, this was an abysmal showing. The Colts’ 1.75 yards before contact per attempt ranks eighth in the league in Week 10, pending Monday Night Football.
pic.twitter.com/EmtBJdTanv
Much like the offense, Miami tried to make up for their one-on-one deficiency, this time by slanting their edge defenders inside. Indianapolis was able to exploit it, however, and used Miami’s aggressiveness against them to find creases along the outside.
With the primary goal of this season being player development, it’s important to look at Miami’s rookie class, whose performances were a mixed bag in Week 10.
Caleb Douglas once again flashed, making a couple highly contested catches, including one on a dagger concept where the safety triggered down late. Douglas showcased his strong hands and body control by maintaining possession of the ball through the contact. For the second straight week, though, he dropped a pass on his body that he had to lower his hands for, so he definitely has something to work on.
pic.twitter.com/kXBmeGOonl
Kevin Coleman Jr. struggled in his increased role due to the absence of Chris Bell. His size profiles him more as a slot receiver, but with the Dolphins' lack of depth, they've attempted to use him on the outside. His lack of physicality showed on an early curl route that was broken up by Charvarius Ward, and he was unable to get going.
Outside of their interceptions, Chris Johnson and Michael Taaffe struggled. Miami threw out plenty of unorthodox looks, as they continued their trend of putting more and more on the secondary’s plate, and there were several instances of receivers running open in between the second and third levels. Furthermore, Taaffe took some poor pursuit angles, and was dominated by blockers on a screen pass to Jonathan Taylor. Jacob Rodriguez also wasn’t very impactful, as the struggles of Miami’s interior defensive line allowed blockers to move up to the second level with relative ease.
Undrafted rookie DJ Herman was inconsistent, but made a few high-level blocks that really created displacement and afforded Ollie Gordon room to run. The linebacker-convert has continued to get better in recent weeks. Kadyn Proctor and Will Kacmarek were similar, moving bodies, but also having a few standout misses that killed opportunities for the run game to create explosives.
Tyler DeSena is currently a journalism student at the University of Central Florida. Prior to joining Dolphins On SI in 2026, DeSena worked with dolphinstalk.com, and created independent social media content on X, YouTube and TikTok.

title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 10 Snap Counts Stories: Tolbert Time, First-Round Picks Pick It Up
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 24-22 loss against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, which was highlighted by injured players Aaron Brewer, Chris Bell and Jared Wayne.
The only Dolphins players who were active but did not play were backup quarterback Brady Cook (after he was elevated from the practice squad) and guard Christian Haynes.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to seven rookies with fourth-round pick Kyle Louis again starting as a nickel back. The other six starters were Kadyn Proctor at left guard, DJ Herman at fullback wide receiver Caleb Douglas, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- The Dolphins offense was on the field for 69 snaps, and what stands out here is the heavy work load for wide receivers Malik Washington (59 snaps) and Caleb Douglas (58).
-- Active again because of the absences of Bell and Wayne, Jalen Tolbert played only 11 snaps on offense and had the first touchdown of the game for the Dolphins and one can't help but wonder why he didn't get more work.
-- At tight end, one has to think that Will Kacmarek continuing to show up on the injury report every week is playing a role in his limited snap count. He got 20 offensive snaps against Indy, with Greg Dulcich leading the way at tight end with 42. Regardless, the Dolphins aren't getting enough production out of their tight ends.
-- Jarrett Kingston took over for Caedan Wallace as the extra offensive lineman for this game and played eight snaps when the Dolphins had six linemen on the field and another two when center Andrew Meyer left the game with an apparent hand injury.
-- Jaylen Wright played only 12 snaps at running back to give Ollie Gordon II a spell and again wasn't productive. Kaytron Allen played only two snaps on offense.
-- Five players were on the field for all the team's 59 defensive snaps, the exact same number as the Detroit game in Week 9 — LB Jordyn Brooks, LB Jacob Rodriguez, S Michael Taaffe, CB Chris Johnson and S Dante Trader.
-- Chop Robinson, who is playing the best football of his career, tied his season high with 50 snaps, but in this game it represented an eye-opening 84.7 percent of the team's defensive snaps. This easily was the highest percentage of his career, topping the 71.2 percent against Kansas City in the home opener this season.
-- Kyle Louis not only got a start for a second consecutive game, but he also doubled his snap count on defense to 25 against the Colts after playing 11 against Detroit.
-- With Zach Sieler on IR, and Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips both getting injured in the game, Kenneth Grant saw his work load increase dramatically. He played 41 snaps against the Colts, a big jump from the 21 he played against Detroit. The 41 snaps tied for the second-highest total of his career behind only the 44 snaps against the Colts in the 2025 season opener, Grant's NFL debut.
-- On the edge, it was pretty much all about Robinson and Josh Uche (44 snaps), with Malik Herring next in the snap count with a modest 18.
-- Jason Marshall Jr. again didn't start at cornerback, but he did get a good amount of work along with Johnson and JuJu Brents, with a little more than 50 percent participation (31 of 59 snaps).
-- There were six non-specialists who saw action only on special teams: LB Shaka Heyward, S Julius Wood, LB Jackson Woodard, CB Jaylin Simpson, EDGE Jamree Kromah and T Chukwuebuka Godrick.
-- Rookie tight end Seydou Traore and Woodard again tied for the team lead in special teams snaps, this time with 23. They were followed with 19 for Louis, Zayne Anderson, Wood and Heyward.

title: What Now at Kicker for the Dolphins After the (Overdue) Gonzalez Move
full_text:
The only question really was when, not if, and the answer became Monday morning as to when the Miami Dolphins would move on from Zane Gonzalez as their kicker.
The Dolphins' decision to waive the veteran kicker — all NFL players now are subject to waivers because the trade deadline has passed — after he missed three kicks in the 24-22 loss against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday seemed like a foregone conclusion and the Dolphins are going to be asked and should be asking themselves when they stuck with him for another game after his earlier struggles.
Regardless, the focus now will shift to who might take over the kicking duties with Gonzalez waived and 2025 record-setter Riley Patterson about to kick for the Baltimore Ravens on Monday night.
The first place to look for a Gonzalez replacement would be the list of kickers the Dolphins brought in for tryouts in recent weeks, a list headed by veterans like Justin Tucker and Daniel Carlson.
Tucker, who would be an interesting and certainly controversial choice, is a member of the Kansas City Chiefs practice squad and therefore could be poached, with the Dolphins then committed to keeping him at least three games.
While his addition would be controversial because of the accusations against him that led to a 10-game NFL suspension, the Dolphins were comfortable enough to bring him in for a tryout, so we wouldn't rule out that possibility.
The better choice from here would be Carlson, the former Raiders All-Pro.
He was in for a tryout last week and we quite frankly couldn't understand why the Dolphins didn't sign him right then and there.
Other kickers the Dolphins have brought in include Ben Sauls, Will Ferrum, Joshua Kanty and former Chargers and Lions kicker Michael Badgley.
There's also nothing preventing the Dolphins from having another kicker tryout session, like the one that led to Patterson being signed last year after Jason Sanders sustained a hip injury in the preseason.
Because of the nature of the position, it's not like the Dolphins need to sign somebody immediately. They actually could go until Saturday and have somebody ready to kick.
The bottom line is the Dolphins just need better kicking.
The team's field goal percentage this season is at 68.4 percent, which ranks next-to-last in the NFL ahead only of the aforementioned Chiefs at 63.2 percent.
Gonzalez was waived after going 6-for-10 on field goal attempts after Patterson went 7-for-9. The Dolphins also have missed two extra-point attempts,
Whether some fans believe that or not, the Dolphins are trying to win games at this early stage of their rebuilding project and the game at Indy is one they should have had with any kind of decent kicking.
This has been a very disappointing turn of events after Patterson set a franchise record for single-season field goal accuracy last year when he went 27-for-29.
Even Gonzalez was very good last year, going 19-for-22 for the Atlanta Falcons are losing out in the Dolphins kicker tryouts to Patterson.
The problems began from the start, with Patterson missing a field goal attempt against the Las Vegas Raiders in the opener.
The most damning stat actually is this: The Dolphins have had five games this season with multiple field goal attempts and have missed at least one in each of those five games.
Time to see if somebody else can take care of that problem.

title: Four Losers And Four Winners From Miami's Week 10 Loss
full_text:
The second losing streak of the season reached three games for the Miami Dolphins after they fell against the Indianapolis Colts in a 24-22 thriller (?).
Miami, a team full of rookie talent and an equally young coaching staff, faced off against a Colts team with a gutted roster thanks to multiple trades before the deadline when the organization dumped veteran experience for draft capital. The result is what you'd likely expect: a pretty even contest with plenty of mistakes made by each team.
For the Dolphins, it doesn't get much closer in a loss — literally, they lost by two points. Rookie quarterback Kyle McCord made his NFL debut, but it's clear he wasn't the biggest problem for Miami.
Social media and multiple media outlets, including us, already have credited his performance as being one of the biggest reasons Miami lost this game, and unfortunately for Gonzalez, it's justified.
He might have drilled a 53-yarder in the third quarter, but no one remembers that. Gonzalez missed a pair of field goals — from 47 51 yards out — as well as an extra point after their final touchdown in the fourth quarter. In a game where the Dolphins lost by two points, he was unable to score SEVEN by himself.
This has been a brutal kicker carousel for the Dolphins. Field goals between 40 and 50 yards are becoming automatic for the new wave of kickers in the NFL and college football. For goodness sake, the college football game between Indiana and Minnesota on October 31 featured back-to-back 60-yard field goals. There's no excuse for this to be a recurring issue for Miami.
A player named Malik threw a passing touchdown in this game, except it wasn't the injured quarterback from Liberty. Instead, it was the wide receiver from Virginia who aired the ball out to Jalen Tolbert for a 34-yard score in the second quarter.
Combine that with an efficient day receiving — three targets, three receptions for 50 yards — and Washington showcased his unique versatility to Miami's offense. He and Caleb Douglas combined for 111 receiving yards off six receptions. While the two might not be considered one of the best in football, the wide receiver duo was exactly what McCord needed to count on in his debut.
Entering this game, Indianapolis had one of the worst run defenses in football — 137 yards per game given up, the third-most in the NFL. Despite that, the Dolphins struggled to establish the run from the start, certainly not what McCord wanted to see.
Gordon did all he could with 20 carries and collected 76 yards for his troubles. But Wright? A whopping negative 2 yards on three carries. It feels brutal to say, but he's a magnet for defenders in the backfield. Miami's rookie quarterback managed a better job evading tacklers for 4 yards and a touchdown on the ground.
It's hard to pin this on Wright, but he's technically responsible for injuring backup center Andrew Meyer when he ran into him on a screen pass. Regardless, there needs to be new life in the backfield when Gordon is not in the game, whether it's more snaps for Kaytron Allen or someone else getting an opportunity.
As mentioned earlier, McCord didn't have a running game to fall back on, so it was up to him to move the ball down the field. It wasn't always pretty, but McCord played better than a lot of people thought he would, finishing with 209 yards on 17 completions, along with the aforementioned rushing touchdown.
While he didn't throw an interception, poor ball security led to a fumble when he was sacked by Justin Walley, which turned into a touchdown to start the second half. It was one of those split-second decisions a quarterback has to make — either throw the ball away or hold on and take the sack. In this case, McCord did neither, a fairly common rookie mistake.
But take a step back for a second. McCord still found a way to give the Dolphins an opportunity to win this game by giving Gonzalez two opportunities to do his job. Overall, there's potential for McCord, but it's going to take more than one game to decide whether to let him ride out the season or bring back Willis once he's healthy.
McCord threw to Dulcich a few times in this game. The first was a deep shot in the first quarter that was out of reach. The second was thrown behind him on fourth down after it was tipped at the line of scrimmage, turning the ball over to the Colts. Lastly, an incomplete pass on the two-point attempt to begin the final quarter.
Miami played a clean game of football with three penalties, but one of them was a false start on Dulcich on their opening drive. Considering the struggles of the Colts' defense going into this game (with no exception to tight end coverage), it was disappointing to see Dulcich be this ineffective.
Johnson was an automatic "no thank you" for Daniel Jones when deciding where to throw the football. He was targeted twice in this game, denying a single reception on either opportunity. When he wasn't doing that, he was playing cleanup duty with four tackles, a TFL, and a pass deflection.
However, his highlight for the day was his interception in the third quarter, then returning it 59 yards for a touchdown. Miami was down by 11 before that play, and the Dolphins remained within reach of the lead for the rest of the game. Johnson has been red-hot since the Chiefs loss, allowing less than 25 yards in coverage in all but two games — Detroit (39) and the New York Jets. (127)
Miami's defense was reeling from the loss of Zach Sieler, and it didn't get any better with Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips getting hurt as well. Rodriguez had more pressure on his plate to deliver as a result, but aside from one tackle on Jonathan Taylor at the line of scrimmage, he didn't make a noticeable impact.
The Colts, to their credit, found ways to take him out of the play, either targeting opposite sides of the field or sending additional blockers to make him a non-factor. Hopefully, Rodriguez can bounce back against Buffalo on November 22 and return to DROTY status, because with how hurt the defense currently is, it looks grim with Josh Allen and James Cook around the corner.
The season may have started ugly for Chop, but he has slowly turned into one of the best pass rushers Miami has to offer. He did a bit of everything against Indianapolis, with six pressures, five tackles, a sack, and two QB hits. His effectiveness at stopping Jonathan Taylor, considered one of the best backs in football, should not go unnoticed.
Just like that, Robinson has already passed his sack total from last season with eight games to go. If he can bring it home, it'll be one of the best comeback stories for the Dolphins after the way he regressed in 2025. Just like with Rodriguez, Miami will need him to keep it up with matchups against Buffalo, Denver and Chicago on the horizon.

title: Five Instant Overreactions to the Dolphins-Colts Matchup
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins fought back late, but ultimately couldn't pull out a win against the Colts, falling 24 to 22. Let's overreact to this Week 10 matchup, where Miami once again lost in key moments.
The Dolphins’ kicking game was at DEFCON 1 over a month ago, and every week since then has just made things more embarrassing. Zane Gonzalez, who has missed field goals in each of the last two weeks, missed another two today, along with a PAT.
Entering this game, Miami was bottom eight in field goal and extra point percentage, and that only got worse against the Colts. It’s clear that wholesale changes are necessary, but on a week-to-week basis, it might be time to take extreme measures.
At this point, outside of obvious field-goal situations, it might be in Miami’s best interest to try a new strategy, either being more aggressive with fourth down decision-making or playing the field-position game and punting deeper into enemy territory. Their special teams unit has done nothing to inspire confidence, and it may be time to take the ball out of the hands of their kicker.
Two of the coolest highlight plays of the week came courtesy of third-year receiver Malik Washington. Early on, he caught a backwards pass, and lofted the ball down the field right into the hands of Jalen Tolbert for a 34-yard touchdown. Then, he made a stellar one-handed catch on a pass that Kyle McCord floated into the area of several Colts defenders.
Washington’s growth has been one of the few bright spots for Miami’s offense in 2026. His route-running has improved, and with increased opportunity, he’s produced his fair share of standout reps. He should be one of the focal points of Miami’s offense in the weeks (and potentially years) to come, and it’s in Bobby Slowik’s best interest to find ways to get the ball in his hands.
The highlights of individual performances have overshadowed the truth: this group hasn’t been good enough. Yes, Paul, Proctor and Brewer (who missed this game) have all flashed, but neither Jonah Savaiinaea nor Austin Jackson have solidified themselves as unquestioned, and consistency from all five spots has been questionable.
This game, without Brewer, was much of the same. Ollie Gordon had 76 yards on 20 carries , and Kyle McCord faced immediate pressure in crucial situations. Some of that, naturally, falls on the protection-adjustment skills of a backup quarterback and center, but performance hasn’t been nearly good enough.
Miami's interior defensive line bears a significant amount of blame in this one. In their first game without Zach Sieler, the Dolphins allowed 172 rushing yards, with both Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan averaging over 5 yards per carry.
The pass rush was slightly better, pressuring Daniel Jones on his two interceptions. However, they only finished the game with one sack. The trio of Kenneth Grant, Jordan Phillips and Zeek Biggers (who left this game early) still have plenty of room to develop, and without their leader, they become easier to exploit.
As has been said after just about every game Miami has played, the rookies stood out in this one. Caleb Douglas made multiple stellar catches, DJ Herman created displacement on a few blocks, and Michael Taaffe and Chris Johnson both recorded interceptions.
For the first time in years, the Dolphins have drafted a class of players that truly look like core contributors for the foreseeable future. This roster was (and largely still is) bereft of talent, but this infusion will pay dividends if they can continue to develop.

title: Miami Dolphins Week 10 Instant Takeaways: Dolphins Should Kick Themselves for Missed Opportunity
full_text:
In this season where wins have to hard to come by for the Miami Dolphins, they really let one slip away against the Indianapolis Colts in Week 10.
We might even suggest they should be kicking themselves for not being able to beat a reeling Colts team that's not only bad but was down their top three cornerbacks in the second half.
Kicking themselves ... get it?
If you're among those who believe the Dolphins are tanking, organically or ethically or otherwise, then what happened at Lucas Oil Stadium was perfect because Zane Gonzalez really doesn't fit into the team's long-term plans, so him missing three kicks isn't damaging for the future of the organization.
If the Dolphins are trying to win games as part of establishing a foundation and some belief, then we'll repeat what we said last week, that the Dolphins absolutely need to move on from him.
That's the biggest and most obvious takeaway from this game, which was all about quarterback Kyle McCord and his NFL debut.
As expected, it was an uneven performance by McCord, with some good and some bad.
The good included his touchdown run on a QB keeper and a couple of nice throws, but he also didn't do anything to suggest that Malik Willis is the one who's been the problem on offense.
The biggest negative, of course, was the sack he took that turned into a Colts touchdown when he fumbled. McCord very clearly saw the free blitzer early in the play and wasn't anywhere near quick enough to get away from the pocket and put himself in position to throw the ball away. And at worst, he should have been able to protect the ball even if he needed to take the sack, and that was a clear rookie mistake that showed a lack of awareness.
The bottom line is his performance should have been good enough to help the Dolphins win against a very bad Indy team.
Instead, the Dolphins dropped to 1-8 on the season as they continue to look like a team headed for a top 3 picks at worst and maybe with a shot at the first overall pick.
-- As an indication of how depleted the Colts are, former Dolphins WR Nick Westbrook-Ikhine was signed from the practice squad to the 53-man roster and promptly let the first third-down pass go right through his hands. Later in the game, he was flagged for offensive pass interference and he finished with zero catches.
-- Pretty amazing (and not in a good way) that barely after the CBS analyst says the Dolphins need to avoid pre-snap penalties that Greg Dulcich gets flagged for a false start. Oy. Outside of that, though, the Dolphins played a relatively clean game with three penalties for 30 yards. Indy, on the other hand, was flagged 13 times for 83 yards, including a defensive holding that nullified a pick-six that might have sealed the outcome early in the fourth quarter instead of the Dolphins have a shot at the end.
-- Of course, it would have been nice had the Dolphins bothered to block linebacker C.J. Allen instead of letting him run free on a blitz between Kadyn Proctor and Patrick Paul, though we don't know for sure who's to blame there.
-- One thing that stood out with McCord is he sure got quite a few passes batted down at the line of scrimmage, including the final failed fourth-down attempt. Though it looked like intended receiver Kevin Coleman Jr. was surrounded at the 35-yard line when he needed to get to the Colts 32.
-- McCord banging his thumb on a helmet following through early in the game was  the last thing you wanted to see happen. But that is going to happen with all the penetration the Dolphins offensive line usually allows.
-- This may come as a surprise to some fans, but Dolphins receivers in the first half weren't getting any more open with McCord at QB than they did with Malik Willis.
-- In addition to continuing his strong run as a pass rusher, including a sack with a nice bull rush, Chop Robinson had maybe the best run stop we've ever seen from him against Jonathan Taylor.
-- Already missing Zach Sieler, the Dolphins really didn't need to have Zeek Biggers leave the game with a knee injury. That the run defense struggled probably was not a coincidence. And then to make matters worse, Jordan Phillips suffered an arm injury. Ugh.
-- Big performance by Malik Washington doing a little bit of everything, including his TD pass to Jalen Tolbert off a double pass. First Dolphins TD pass by a non-quarterback since, yes again, Mountaineer Shot, the Matt Haack throw to Jason Sanders against the Eagles in 2019. Great call, nice throw by  Washington.
-- Great catch by Michael Taaffe on his third pick of the season, though someone could point out he cost the Dolphins 6 yards because this was going to be a fourth-down incompletion. It's not very significant in terms of lost yardage, but we hope the Dolphins don't do the same thing if we're talking about 20 or 30 yards.
-- DJ Herman has made a couple of really nice lead blocks already in this game. Also was the recipient of Kyle McCord's first NFL completion.
-- Truly amazing that every time Jaylen Wright gets a carry, there is major penetration from the defensive line and he almost invariably gets hit in the backfield. At this point, it's almost laughable.
-- Zero issue with the Dolphins going for it on fourth-and-2 in the first half ... regardless of the result. It's an evaluation season. Shame a good drive ended without points, but the point remains.
--  Don't know what was better, Chris Johnson's pick-six or the touchdown celebration. And, of course, Gonzalez misses the PAT. Doesn't matter actually because Johnson is going to be a good player for a while and Gonzalez might be gone this week (maybe).
-- Not to take anything away from a great Dolphins defensive series in the fourth quarter, but it’s pretty easy to see why the Colts are 2-7 (2-14 over their last 16).
-- I'm going to go ahead and say it, Dolphins receivers made more good catches for Kyle McCord in this game than they have for Malik Willis all season.
-- Jordyn Brooks was really, really good and it's time to acknowledge that for all the accolades Jacob Rodriguez has been getting for his strong rookie season, he's the best linebacker on the team and probably the best player overall.
