title: Patriots Offense Doesn't Exist Without Drake Maye at QB
full_text:
The New England Patriots dropped their Week 10 game against the Detroit Lions and lost their franchise quarterback on the way to a 35-10 defeat.
After Drake Maye brought the Patriots into the red zone on their first and most productive offensive drive all day, the third-year quarterback was sacked by Aidan Hutchinson and left the game with an ankle injury .
The 60-yard drive that Maye orchestrated was the second-longest drive the Patriots had all game. After Maye left the game, the Patriots offense was seemingly broken, putting up 91 total yards in the remainder of the game.
"I don't think Drake being in or not would have really — I mean it may have," head coach Mike Vrabel said postgame.
Backup quarterback Tommy DeVito entered the game in the first quarter for Maye, who was ruled out mid-game for the first time since sustaining a concussion his rookie year.
With DeVito at the helm, New England struggled to move the ball downfield, having nine out of 10 drives end in either a punt or a turnover. The Patriots also failed to keep the offense on the field, holding the ball for just 27 minutes and three seconds during Sunday's contest.
DeVito finished with just 81 passing yards, while Maye threw for 48 on the opening drive. The fourth-year quarterback completed half of his passes, and threw both a touchdown and an interception.
Maye's withdrawal from the game put a lackluster Patriots team on full display Sunday morning. Following his exit, it was clear that the Patriots can't succeed without their franchise player.
Maye has thrown for 2,282 yards this season , with 18 touchdowns in the air. Maye has faced criticism for his tendency to put the ball in defenders' hands as his 11 interceptions are tied for a league high.
The Patriots are nothing without Drake Maye. pic.twitter.com/m1ECGHp3T7
However, after watching DeVito attempt to operate the offense, it's obvious that the Patriots can't compete without their star quarterback, despite his turnovers.
Maye was the runner-up for MVP a year ago , and led the Patriots to their first Super Bowl appearance since 2018.
New England will return from Germany and enter the bye week, with its next game happening in Week 12 on Sunday Night Football against the winless Los Angeles Chargers.
After the game, Vrabel refused to provide specific information about his quarterback's injury, and said that the team would assess the severity of Maye's diagnosis when they return to the United States.
If Maye's ankle injury causes him to miss an extended amount of time, the 5-5 Patriots may need to look outside of the organization for a solution at quarterback — especially if they want to compete for a playoff bid.

title: Drake Maye Hurt and 6 More Instant Takeaways from Patriots' Loss to Lions in Germany
full_text:
It's hard to imagine that the New England Patriots would have had a worse game than their 45-27 loss last week. But it somehow happened.
In their second-ever game in Germany , the Patriots got thrashed — and injured even more — as the Detroit Lions boat-raced their way to a 35-10 win in Munich. Drake Maye would end up leaving the game with an ankle injury suffered in the first quarter and the Patriots offense, reeling from that, couldn't muster up anything that looked productive.
They're now losers of two in a row and will go into next week's bye sitting at .500 — and limping into what could be a really interesting stretch run these next two months.
Here's what happened, and what it means going forward.
The Patriots came out firing. Maye went 3-for-4 for 48 yards and picked up several first downs to Hunter Henry and Mack Hollins (on a flea flicker). They were driving down the field and looked poised for an opening drive touchdown.
But then pre-snap penalties — a false start on Will Campbell and a delay of game — backed them up from the three-yard line to the 13-yard line. Then Aidan Hutchinson broke through on third down to sack Maye and force the Patriots to settle for a field goal.
On the sack, Hutchinson would go down with an injury as he was celebrating. He'd be ruled out with an knee injury. But it would get much, much worse...
A.J. Brown and Rhamondre Stevenson were back in the lineup after injuries, so the Patriots' injury luck had to be turning, right? Nope. It got worse.
After Maye was sacked on the first drive, he would get looked at on the sideline . He'd slowly make his way to the locker room with what the team announced was an ankle injury. Maye would be ruled questionable to return and wouldn't end up coming back.
In his place, second-string Tommy DeVito would come in and not have much success. He'd go 12-for-23 with 81 passing yards, a touchdown, a really bad interception to Roger McCreary over the middle and a couple of hospital passes. He'd also add 19 yards with his legs.
After a game where he allowed 11 receptions to Matthew Golden and Christian Watson , the Patriots cornerback had the perfect opportunity to rebound from the worst outing of his career.
On the opening drive, covering Amon-Ra St. Brown on third down, Gonzalez got juked as the Lions wideout made one cut and took it 56 yards to the house.
He'd eventually get his get-back in the second quarter, undercutting St. Brown across the middle for his first interception of the season — one of two they got in the game.
Would that help the Patriots get some more momentum? Nope, they'd punt it away almost instantly. The Lions would tack on a touchdown on a Jahmyr Gibbs five-yard touchdown up the middle to take a 21-3 lead into halftime.
After missing the last two weeks, getting Brown back was supposed to help elevate the Patriots' passing attack. In his first three games, he combined for nine total receptions and 101 yards. Without Maye throwing him passes and the offense as a whole out of sorts, Brown wasn't able to break out of the funk.
He finished the day targeted five times and caught two passes for 27 yards. On his second target, he dropped a pass on third down that forced the Patriots to punt it away. He would also get called for a false start in the third quarter to back the Patriots up into a 3rd-and-12.
Brown also recovered a fumble after Reggie Gilliam lost control along New England's sideline. He'd also suffer a hamstring injury and leave the game in the fourth quarter.
There's a reason Gibbs is one of the league's best players. He ran the ball 22 times for 153 yards, caught seven passes for 99 yards, scored two times and was untouchable all game. His 252 total yards of offense easily outpaced the Patriots, who were only able to muster 151 net yards all game.
On the drive that ended in Gibbs' first touchdown, the Lions running back amounted for a 50-yard catch-and-run that set them up inside the Patriots' 10. Then Gibbs would punch it home from five yards out for his 12th touchdown of the season.
Maye got hurt and that will be the headliner. But the Patriots — who have started a league-high 42 different players this year — also had a lot more players get banged up in the loss. Offensive tackle Morgan Moses would leave the game for a bit with a knee injury, but would come back.
Several other Patriots had to get medical help.
It took until deep into the game, but the Patriots finally scored a touchdown. After a defensive penalty helped set the Patriots up deep into Detroit territory, DeVito connected with running back Lan Larison for a 10-yard touchdown.
That score was the first of Larison's young NFL career , and felt similar to other obscure Patriots touchdowns to happen in international games in recent years (JaMycal Hasty and K.J. Osborn both scored against Jacksonville in 2024).
The Lions weren't deterred. Gibbs struck once again, bouncing off the right side of the line and scored from 28 yards out. The lead then ballooned to 35-10, meaning the Patriots had allowed 80 points in the last two games.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly: Can the Saints Do Anything Right?
full_text:
Sign up for the daily Saints Newsletter by clicking here .
The New Orleans Saints had an opportunity to take control of the NFC South on Sunday, but instead delivered another frustrating performance that raised more questions about the direction of the franchise.
New Orleans (3-6) suffered a heartbreaking 20-17 loss to the Carolina Panthers at the Caesars Superdome, surrendering a game-winning 54-yard field goal by Ryan Fitzgerald as time expired.
Despite Carolina committing 17 penalties for 152 yards, the Saints couldn't capitalize, finishing with just 49 rushing yards, two turnovers and another disappointing offensive performance under head coach Kellen Moore .
The loss dropped New Orleans to 1-4 at home and 0-2 against NFC South opponents, leaving the Saints searching for answers as their season continues to unravel.
Here is the good, bad and ugly from Sunday's loss.
Rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson led the Saints with 11 receptions, the most since Pierre Thomas caught 12 passes against the Chicago Bears in December 2007.
After missing the first seven games of the season, the rookie wideout has wasted little time demonstrating why New Orleans selected him eighth overall in April's NFL Draft.
His separation, contested catches, and reliability complement Chris Olave and should make this passing attack even deadlier.
However, the offense has become too predictable.
After a strong performance last week, the Saints' rushing attack went back to its old ways, gaining just 49 yards on 23 carries (2.1 yards per carry) against Carolina.
Quarterback Shough led New Orleans with 25 rushing yards, while Travis Etienne Jr. (14 yards), Audric Estime (6 yards), and Alvin Kamara (4 yards, 3-yard touchdown) combined for minimal output.
Although the absence of right tackle Taliese Fuaga and center Erik McCoy provides important context, the struggles within the ground attack were already present prior to their injuries.
Moore was hired because of his success as the offensive coordinator of the Philadelphia Eagles , one that had the NFL’s top rushing offense in 2024 and propelled them to a Super Bowl victory. He must fix the run game for New Orleans to sustain drives and score consistently.
Through nine games this season, the answer has been a firm no.
Carolina repeatedly handed the Saints chances by committing 17 penalties and struggling offensively, but New Orleans failed to capitalize.
The Saints were shut out in the first half, committed two turnovers, and generated insufficient offense against a sub-.500 Panthers squad. Even after Charlie Smyth tied the game with a 55-yard field goal with 41 seconds remaining, a pass interference penalty on Kool-Aid McKinstry set up Fitzgerald's game-winning kick.
More concerning is the lack of progress under head coach Kellen Moore.
Over nine games, the Saints have struggled with offensive inconsistency, poor execution and an inability to close games. Their 3-6 record inspires little confidence, and individual flashes from Tyson, Shough, and the defense cannot mask overall failure. To make matters worse, the Saints have trailed in all but one of the 26 games that Moore has coached in as the head coach of the Saints.
With upcoming road trips to Chicago and Cincinnati followed by a home game against the Green Bay Packers , the schedule provides no relief. Instead of making a statement in the NFC South, New Orleans showed just how far it remains from contention.

title: Saints Find Another Way to Lose as Panthers Steal NFC South Victory
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints had chance after chance to build momentum and secure their first consecutive wins of the season. Instead, it was another game that left a sour taste in everyone’s mouths like tomatoes in gumbo.
Kicker Ryan Fitzgerald connected on a game-winning 54-yard field goal as time expired, lifting the Carolina Panthers to a 20-17 victory over the Saints on Sunday afternoon at the Caesars Superdome.
The loss dropped New Orleans to 3-6 under second-year head coach Kellen Moore , while Carolina improved to 4-5 and strengthened its position in the NFC South standings.
Despite overcoming a sluggish first half and taking a fourth-quarter lead, the Saints couldn't finish the job, and Carolina escaped with a crucial divisional win.
Tyler Shough went 25-for-36 for 187 yards, with a touchdown and an interception, while rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson had a breakout game, leading New Orleans with 11 receptions for 80 yards.
Running back Alvin Kamara provided the Saints' biggest offensive spark, scoring twice in the second half on a 3-yard touchdown run in the third quarter and a 4-yard touchdown catch in the fourth.
However, New Orleans struggled offensively throughout the opening two quarters, committing two turnovers and failing to score before halftime.
Shough's first interception came on the Saints' opening possession when cornerback Marco Wilson deflected his fourth-down pass intended for Chris Olave , and linebacker Devin Lloyd intercepted it.
The Saints' defense kept Carolina from capitalizing, with Carl Granderson sacking Bryce Young on fourth down near the goal line.
Another costly mistake came in the second quarter when Shough and Audric Estime mishandled a handoff, allowing Panthers linebacker Jaelan Phillips to recover the fumble.
Carolina capitalized on the turnover with a 2-yard touchdown run by Chuba Hubbard , taking a 7-0 lead into halftime.
New Orleans finally found some traction in the third quarter.
Kamara capped a nine-play, 64-yard drive with a 3-yard touchdown run, tying the game at 7-7 with 6:33 remaining in the period.
However, Fitzgerald answered with a 55-yard field goal to restore Carolina's three-point advantage entering the fourth quarter.
The Saints responded with their best offensive sequence of the afternoon.
Shough connected with Kamara on a 4-yard touchdown pass, giving New Orleans its first lead at 14-10.
That advantage proved short-lived.
Hubbard scored his second touchdown on a 1-yard run, putting Carolina back ahead 17-14 late in the fourth quarter.
New Orleans refused to go away, with kicker Charlie Smyth drilling a clutch 55-yard field goal to tie the game at 17-17.
But Young and the Panthers orchestrated one final scoring opportunity, setting up Fitzgerald's game-winning kick as time expired.
Young finished with 200 passing yards, while Hubbard rushed for 92 yards and two touchdowns on 27 carries.
For the Saints, the defeat represents another frustrating setback in a season defined by inconsistency, offensive mistakes and an inability to capitalize on opportunities.
The Saints will now prepare for a road trip to the Buckeye State to take on the Cincinnati Bengals .

The New Orleans Saints (3-5) return to the Caesars Superdome on Sunday looking to build momentum following last week's victory over Cleveland as they host the Carolina Panthers (3-5) in a crucial NFC South showdown.
With both teams looking to turn their seasons around, the Saints will need another strong performance from quarterback Tyler Shough and their defense to secure consecutive victories for the first time this season.
Here are our Saints ON SI staff predictions for Sunday's matchup between New Orleans and Carolina.
I think this will be a relatively close game for the Saints.
While the defense is flawed in some areas, New Orleans arguably has the best pass rush duo in Chase Young and Carl Granderson , who are both in the top five in sacks. However, I’m still worried about its inability to stop the run, especially when the opposing team has a solid running back. Unfortunately for the Saints, Carolina has a pretty dadgum good running back in Chuba Hubbard , who has rushed for 619 yards and reached paydirt five times this season.
On top of that, the Saints’ defense will go up against a better quarterback in Bryce Young , who has thrown for 2,197 yards with 18 touchdowns and six interceptions and is the face of the fourth-best passing attack in the NFL and one that features wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan (46 receptions, 625 yards, 3 touchdowns).
The good thing for the Saints is that the Panthers aren’t the greatest defense when it comes to stopping the run as they are 28th in the league in rushing yards allowed. The Saints were able to run the ball effectively last week against the Cleveland Browns , who also had a similar issue, but execution will be key.
Can the Saints pull off the win and remain in first place? It’s definitely a possibility.
However, I cannot trust Kellen Moore’s ability to manage and put together a game plan for four quarters because Tyler Shough and the Saints have won three games despite the offensive staff’s ineptitude.
Also, add on the fact that the Saints are missing two of their starting offensive linemen on an already porous offensive line in center Erik McCoy and right tackle Taliese Fuaga , the Saints’ chances of winning decrease.

I'm not quite sure what to think of this "new" Saints team. It's almost like there's a new set of faces each week in different places.
On Sunday, the Saints and Panthers play for first place in the NFC South in the Superdome. Admittedly, both teams have three wins in their eight games, but first place is on the line, nonetheless. It's hard to believe, but it was just 2021 that Tampa Bay , a team tied for the bottom of this division, won it all.
Point being, things change rapidly in this professional sport Americans love so much.
Neither of these teams is impressive in its own right, but here we stand with the mid-season top-of-the-totem position on the line.
Are the Saints finally starting to find an offensive rhythm? I mean, they did score in the first quarter against Cleveland, the first time this season they've put any points in the first period column.
Is the defense poised to stop the run better? They held Cleveland to under 100 yards rushing as a team, only the second time this year, the other being against the New York Giants .

Is the field goal crap shoot fixed with Charlie Smyth ? The Irishman made three of four field goals last week, missing from almost 50 yards from that pesky left hash mark.
There is hope, and I am going with it.

The 27-year-old running back joined New Orleans during free agency on a three-year contract after four seasons with the Jacksonville Jaguars , who selected him in the first round of the 2021 NFL Draft. A Louisiana native out of Jennings High School, he played at Clemson, earning All-America honors three times and twice winning ACC Offensive Player of the Year.

Moore indicated Fuaga's injury is not expected to require a stint on injured reserve, although McCoy's recovery timeline remains uncertain.
McCoy's absence could prove particularly challenging as he plays a critical role in identifying defensive fronts, communicating protection adjustments and helping maintain continuity across the offensive line as the center.
Without him, New Orleans must rely on Cesar Ruiz to handle those responsibilities while adjusting to a reshuffled interior with Jeremiah Wright taking Ruiz’s spot at right guard.
Fuaga's injury creates another significant concern at right tackle, where Asim Richards could be called upon to step into the starting lineup.
The Saints also dealt with injuries involving left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. (ankle) and guard David Edwards (knee) throughout the week. While both returned to full participation Friday, it’s another sign that this unit is not even close to 100%.
Even with Banks and Edwards, losing two starters makes it hard for an offensive line that has struggled with pass protection and consistency in the running game.

title: Saints Stock Up: Audric Estimé Makes a Statement, Pass Rush Keeps Rolling
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints gave their home crowd reason to celebrate on Sunday at Caesars Superdome, clinching a thrilling 23-22 victory in overtime over the Cleveland Browns .
While improving the Saints to 3-5 and snapping a home slump, the win was far from flawless.
The result grants head coach Kellen Moore a brief reprieve, but ongoing flaws demonstrate that his standing stays uncertain.
With a tough slate ahead, New Orleans needs to fix key errors to sustain progress.
Below are the Saints players and units whose stock rose after Sunday's thrilling finish.
Despite rejoining the Saints via waivers after getting cut after training camp, running back Audric Estimé made a compelling argument for an expanded role in New Orleans' backfield despite being back in New Orleans for a week.
The second-year running back rushed for 72 yards and a touchdown on 15 carries, averaging 4.8 yards per attempt.
His biggest contribution came late in regulation when he powered into the end zone from 2 yards out to give New Orleans a 16-13 advantage.
Beyond the touchdown, Estimé provided the physicality and downhill running that the Saints have struggled to establish consistently.
Charlie Smyth made the most of his opportunity after he became the starter after the Saints released Daniel Carlson .
The Irish-born kicker connected on three of his four field-goal attempts against Cleveland, converting from 30, 27 and 48 yards.
With both offenses struggling to finish drives, Smyth accounted for all nine of New Orleans' points through the first three quarters.
His 48-yard field goal in the fourth quarter briefly gave the Saints a 9-6 advantage.
The Saints' pass rush continues to emerge as one of the team's biggest strengths, with Carl Granderson and Chase Young leading a pass rush that made life miserable for Cleveland quarterback Shedeur Sanders .
Granderson recorded two sacks against the Browns, extending his streak of games with multiple sacks to four. According to the Saints, he became the first NFL player since 2013 to accomplish that feat.
Young added his eighth sack of the season, while Kaden Elliss and Khristian Boyd also got into the action as New Orleans finished with five sacks.
The Saints' defensive front also made its presence felt against the run, limiting Cleveland to 95 rushing yards while consistently disrupting the Browns' offensive rhythm.
Perhaps the unit's most impressive moment came near the goal line, when New Orleans delivered a critical fourth-down stand to keep Cleveland out of the end zone.
Although the Saints' secondary remains vulnerable to explosive plays, the defensive front has become a reliable source of pressure and physicality.

title: Giants Poach Special Teams Help from Two NFC Rosters
full_text:
The New York Giants have signed defensive back Tavierre Thomas off the Minnesota Vikings practice squad and receiver Xavier Gipson off the Philadelphia Eagles practice squad.
Thomas, 30, was originally signed as an undrafted free agent in 2018 out of Ferris State by the Arizona Cardinals, with whom he spent that summer in training camp.
The 5-foot-10, 212-pound Thomas, who is primarily a special teams player, has had stints with the Browns, Texans, Bucs, and Vikings.
He has appeared in 116 games with 22 starts and has 262 career tackles (163 solo), six tackles for loss, two interceptions (including one returned for a touchdown), six pass breakups, and one sack.
Last season, Thomas led the Vikings in special teams tackles with 19. It is anticipated that he will fill a punt gunner role with the Giants.
Gipson, who spent time with the Giants last season at two different times, was with the team this summer in training camp. Howeer, he was waived as part of the final roster cuts on August 30 and was signed by the Eagles on Sept. 11.
With Thomas and Gipson signed to the 53-man roster, the Giants released receiver Charlie Jones and defensive back Nikko Reed. Jones had been the Giants' return specialist, but he had his ups and downs in that role, prompting New York to seek an upgrade.
Gipson will presumably take over the return specialist duties for the Giants.
The Giants don’t practice until Tuesday, and the first injury report for Week 12 isn't due until Wednesday.

title: J.J. McCarthy: Giants Must Be ‘Crisp’ After Painful Loss to Commanders
full_text:
New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy was on the threshold of earning his seventh win as an NFL starting quarterback until he wasn’t.
In the fourth quarter of Big Blue’s Week 10 showdown with the Washington Commanders at MetLife Stadium, McCarthy engineered a 69-yard scoring drive in just three plays. The series ended with a 66-yard touchdown pass to tight end Isaiah Likely, giving the Giants a 21-17 lead with only 8:17 left.
Unfortunately, New York couldn't capitalize on its two interceptions of quarterback Jayden Daniels, leaving the door open for an eventual 24-21 comeback win for Washington in what was a major kick to the gut for the Giants.
While the loss has left a bitter taste in the mouths of the players, who have had an extra four days to stew on it, the team’s focus is on what the Giants do moving forward.
“For me, a takeaway is just do whatever you can to get a fast start, not hurt ourselves in whatever moment it is,” McCarthy said.
Despite their loss to the Commanders, the Giants are still firmly in control of first place in the NFC East — and they intend to keep it that way.
“We just gotta be so crisp, detailed, and execute on every single play like it’s the last play from snap one to the last snap," he said.
"We just got to do a better job of tightening things up, be consistently on the same page, all 11, and do whatever we can, find a way to get a win in those critical situations.”
The Giants will get that chance on Sunday against a red-hot Jacksonville Jaguars team that has been dominating the AFC South. So great is the interest in that game between two division leaders that it was flexed to the nationally televised slot, with kickoff set for 4:25 p.m. ET.
McCarthy, who certainly wasn’t the lone reason for the Giants’ loss to the Commanders, recognizes that he must be part of the solution moving forward, and that it starts with him correcting any mistakes he’s made that have hurt the team.
“Now it’s ‘What’s next?’ and ‘How can we prepare for Jacksonville?’” he said. “We just need to find a way to get that next win. That is really the main focus.”

title: 4 Unsung Giants Free Agents Who've Made Their Case to Stay in 2027
full_text:
The last thing the New York Giants front office brass are probably thinking about right now is which of their pending unrestricted free agents they will aggressively look to re-sign after this season.
Granted, the Giants have already extended one pending free agent on an expiring contract: cornerback Greg Newsome II, who signed a three-year extension coming out of the team’s bye week. But a case could be made for prioritizing re-signing several other Giants on expiring contracts, such as the players below.
Remember when head coach John Harbaugh, when asked about his inside linebackers, said that the team had three starters at the position? Two of them, Arvell Reese and Tremaine Edmunds, were actually starters, at least until a season-ending injury cut short Edmunds’ season.
The third starter, who has delivered in Edmunds’ absence, is Micah McFadden. The Giants’ 2022 fifth-round draft pick out of Indiana was a starter before Edmunds' injury, and when pressed into a bigger role, McFadden has responded.
Per PFF, McFadden has the highest season grades of his career in run defense (70.1) and pass rush (85.2).
In 202 total defensive snaps, McFadden already has six pressures. By comparison, he had 11 in 2024, his last year as a starter, when he played 668 defensive snaps.
McFadden has also cut down on missed tackles, posting just three so far after 41 in 2023 and 2024 as a starter.
In short, it’s been a nice comeback for McFadden, who missed most of last season with a foot injury that came when he was getting ready to enter a contract year.
Yes, Banks has had some issues lately with defensive pass interference flags, though at least one of those calls was “iffy.” But the fact remains that Banks has found new life under this coaching staff and in this defensive scheme.
Per PFF, he’s currently carrying his best grades overall (62.7) and in coverage (64.3).
But if you need more proof of how good Banks has actually been after beating out big-ticket Paulson Adebo for a starting job, consider that Banks has his second-best NFL coverage rating (85.2), behind only his rookie season (84.7).
He’s one pass breakup away from tying his career high of eight, set in 2024, and one interception away from matching his career best of two, set in his rookie season.
His attention to detail, scheme fit, and consistency have all contributed to Banks’ resurgence.
The Giants reportedly tried to extend Banks’ contract during the bye week but couldn't. But fear not, as the Giants can always cut Adebo’s high-priced contract in the offseason and apply the $14 million in cap savings toward the projected $23.119 million franchise tag for cornerbacks.
In case you missed it, Tyler Nubin, the Giants’ second-round draft pick in 2024, has quietly lost his starting job to Ar’Darius Washington, who has been as solid as they come in coverage.
Washington, who had a clutch interception in Thursday night’s loss to the Commanders, currently boasts a career-best 53.5 coverage rating and has allowed just 12 of 18 targets for 82 yards (6.8 yards per reception), with only 19 yards after the catch.
Part of Washington’s rise is undoubtedly tied to his prior connection in Baltimore to head coach John Harbaugh and defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson, his position coach during the 2023 season with the Ravens.
But give credit where it’s due: Washington has progressed to the point where the Giants’ one-year contract gamble on him has not only paid off but also set up a promising situation at safety if the Giants can reach an extension with him.
Zaire Barnes doesn’t get his name called very often, but opponents sure know a lot about him. An inside linebacker by trade, Barnes has made his living on special teams and has been simply invaluable in that regard.
Currently, he is tied for second in the league in solo special teams tackles (8). Add his assisted tackles, and he has 14 altogether, which ties him for first (with Donovan McMillon of the Cleveland Browns) among special teams tacklers. Barnes also has a forced fumble.
In two years with Big Blue, Barnes has 27 special teams tackles. Add in the fact that it probably wouldn’t break the bank to extend him, and this becomes as much of a no-brainer as any.

title: Former Scout Weighs In on Vikings’ Trade of J.J. McCarthy to Giants
full_text:
By all accounts, the New York Giants are very happy to have acquired quarterback J.J. McCarthy in a trade with the Minnesota Vikings, and McCarthy seems eager to use a fresh start to show the NFL world he’s not the draft bust that seemed to be taking shape in Minnesota.
But not only was McCarthy’s road to respectability difficult due to various factors, such as his season-ending knee injury in his rookie campaign and struggles running the offense that saw him sink to the bottom of the position’s depth chart, but former scout John Middlekauff also offered a rather shocking opinion on the relationship between McCarthy and Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell.
“If you’re a Vikings fan watching (the Giants-Commanders) game tonight, you have to be asking yourself—and I’m not trying to play Monday morning quarterback, it’s just a reality—the move was made because he didn’t play well and the coach hated him,” Middlekauff opined during a segment on the 3 and Out podcast last Friday.
Middlekauff didn’t stop there, continuing his criticism of O’Connell, whom he also acknowledged “by all accounts is a nice guy,” and pointing to McCarthy’s success in New York as an indication that maybe the Vikings thought the quarterback was better than he was.
“I wanted to speak for you regarding J.J. McCarthy; you hated his guts as a player,” Middlekauff alleged. “You couldn’t (expletive) stand him because you were clearly the driving force for making him the third quarterback and helping the GM: ‘We gotta get this guy out of here. Fifth-round pick, I’ll drive him to the airport.’
“Then a couple of weeks later, when you’re starting Carson Wentz, who couldn’t hit water from the middle of the ocean, and then J.J.’s making plays like that for (Matt) Nagy and Greg Roman, you’re like, ‘No one is acting like this guy is Joe Montana, but this is way better than what we had.’”
McCarthy led the Vikings to a 6-4 record as a starter and currently has a 2-1 record as a starter for the Giants. In just two NFL seasons, the former University of Michigan signal-caller has a 59.4% career completion rate and has thrown for 2,547 yards, 13 touchdowns, and 16 interceptions, with a 41.7% overall success rate.
Thus far with the Giants, McCarthy, in five games played (three starts), has a 63.5% completion rate and has thrown for 915 yards, two touchdowns, and two interceptions, with a 43% success rate, and head coach John Harbaugh’s confidence in McCarthy is growing by the day.
“I think he’s proven that he’s capable of winning games and making the plays, and I probably feel more strongly about that now than ever,” Harbaugh said last week after the Giants’ loss to the Washington Commanders.
“It was his third game; I think maybe now starting. So we’re definitely in the process of building that confidence. … I’m excited about where he’s going, going forward, and our chance to close out some games.”

title: Giants Incentives Check-In: Which Players Are on Pace to Earn Bonuses?
full_text:
One of the New York Giants ’ new approaches this past offseason was adding a slew of “not likely to be earned” (NLTBE) incentives to player contracts.
NLTBEs can benefit a team’s cap because, if the player reaches them, the charge doesn’t hit until the following year’s cap. An NLTBE incentive differs from a “likely to be earned” (LTBE) incentive because it’s based on what the player achieved in that statistical category the year prior.
For example, if a contract promises $1 million based on a player achieving 50 receptions in a season and that player achieved 55 receptions the prior season, the incentive is classified as an LTBE because the player has already reached that mark recently.
As an LTBE, the bonus counts against the current year’s salary cap; if the player doesn’t earn the incentive, the team gets a credit toward the following year’s cap space.
But if that same $1 million promise is based on 50 receptions and the player, in the prior season, had only 40 receptions, it becomes an NLTBE because the player didn’t reach the milestone the year prior. And if an NLTBE incentive isn’t earned, it doesn’t count against the following year’s cap.
The Giants offered players $28.3 million in NLTBE incentives. With 10 weeks of the NFL season in the books, thus far the team owes the players involved $2.25 million or roughly 8% of that total.
Who is set to cash in and who isn't? Here is the rundown with data provided via Spotrac .
Newsome, who recently signed a three-year, $46 million contract extension with $36 million guaranteed, originally had a chance to earn up to $2 million in incentives if he hit playing-time metrics.
Thus far, Newsome has played in 80.2% of the team’s defensive snaps, so he’s currently on pace to earn $1 million of the $2 million originally promised to him.
If he finishes having played in 90% or more of the team’s snaps, he’ll earn an additional $1 million in incentives for a maxed-out total of $2 million.
Winston is currently on pace to earn $500,000 of the $2 million max attached to a playing-time incentive. The quarterback has participated in 59.8% of the team’s offensive snaps.
He’s 0.2% away from hitting the next payout in that metric (60% playing time), which, if he hits it, will pay out another $250,000, boosting Winston’s incentives to $750,000.
Reader has two incentives in his deal, one for playing time and one for sacks. He has already picked up $250,000 of the max $750,000 for playing time, having taken part in 56.8% of the team’s defensive snaps (the minimum criterion was 53% of the snaps).
He also needs two more sacks to reach three, which would trigger a $500,000 incentive payout.
Likely, who is having a breakout year this season, is on pace to hit a number of his contract incentives.
He has already picked up $250,000 for hitting seven receiving touchdowns, which crossed the first criterion of a minimum of six. If he records one more touchdown, that total will double to $500,000. And if he hits 10 receiving touchdowns, he’ll max out at $750,000 in that metric.
He has likely also met half of a playing-time/playoff incentive. He needs to participate in at least 60% of the offensive snaps, and the team needs to make the postseason for him to get an additional $150,000.
Likely has already met the first part of that criterion, having played in 75.4% of the snaps. He needs the Giants to win the division, which will secure a postseason spot and trigger that incentive payout.
There are two more incentives that Likely is on pace to reach. The first is receptions. Likely needs five more receptions to hit 60, which would then trigger a $250,000 payout. He can max out at $750,000 if he hits 80 receptions.
The other incentive is receiving yards. He can max out at $750,000 if he reaches 850 receiving yards. Currently, he has 575 and is just 75 yards away from hitting the first benchmark, which would pay him $250,000 if he hits 650 receiving yards.
Pancake Pat has a playing-time incentive in his deal, and he has already hit the first benchmark: playing in 30% of the team’s offensive snaps.
Ricard, having played in 36.4% of the snaps so far, has hit $250,000 in incentives. If he finishes with 40% of the team’s offensive snaps, he can max out at $450,000 in that incentive.
McFadden has up to $2 million in playing-time incentives, and he’s well on his way to hitting the first benchmark: $250,000 if he plays in 35% of the defensive snaps.
McFadden has stepped in for the injured Tremaine Edmunds, and he rarely comes off the field. He’ll earn an additional $250,000 if he plays in 40% of the defensive snaps and then $375,000 per tier for hitting the following playing-time benchmarks: 50%, 60%, 70% and 75%.
The following Giants are unlikely to earn their contract incentives.
Thomas can earn up to $500,000 for a Pro Bowl and first-team All-Pro nod. Unfortunately, thanks to a groin injury, he’s not having a promising season and is unlikely to earn either of those honors.
Burns had an opportunity to earn up to $1.8 million if he reached 12.5 sacks, earned first-team All-Pro honors, or made the Pro Bowl. Unfortunately, a season-ending knee injury suffered in Week 3 ended those hopes for this season.
Austin had three incentives (receiving yards, receptions and playing time), each paying out $1 million apiece. Unfortunately, he never made it to the regular season after tearing his ACL in training camp.
Golston stood to earn up to $500,000 if he reached 10 sacks. His first level, though, was six sacks, which would have brought him $125,000 had he reached it. Unfortunately, Golston is on season-ending injured reserve with a neck ailment.
Mooney has $7 million in incentives at stake between playing time, receptions, receiving yards and touchdowns.
Currently, he’s not close to hitting any of those incentives, which include $250,000 for playing time, a minimum of $375,000 for 35 receptions (max is $2.5 million for 75 catches), a minimum of $375,000 for at least 450 receiving yards (he has 175 at the moment) and a max of $2.5 million if he tops 900 receiving yards, and a max of $1.75 million for nine receiving touchdowns (he can earn $375,000 for three touchdowns).
Singletary needs to hit at least 56% of the offensive snaps to earn a $250,000 payout (he’s currently at 27.3%). With Cam Skattebo as RB1, Singletary is facing an uphill battle there. He’s also facing an uphill battle to hit the minimum 1,100 scrimmage yards needed for a $125,000 payout.
Holland has been playing lights out for the Giants this year, and if he finishes strong enough to earn both Pro Bowl and first-team All-Pro honors, he’s looking at up to $500,000.
Adebo can earn $500,000 each if he makes the Pro Bowl and earns first-team All-Pro honors. Given that he’s not only lost his starting job but also been a healthy scratch a few times this year, he’s clearly not reaching that incentive.
Robertson-Harris suffered a ruptured Achilles in the spring, so he obviously has zero chance to earn up to $250,000 in playing-time incentives this year.
Barnes is a mainstay on special teams, where he has performed well this season. Unfortunately, that won’t help him earn the $400,000 incentive in his contract, which he would earn for playing 45% of the defensive snaps.

title: Harbaugh Preaches Resiliency as Giants Chase First Playoff Berth Since 2022
full_text:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh knows who is on the schedule in the coming weeks. And while the focus is on winning one game at a time, Harbaugh emphasizes a recurring theme with his players.
“You’ve watched us play. People have watched us play. You know where we are. We’re going to do everything we can do to try to win the game. Our guys are going to fight like crazy. They’re going to compete, and we’re capable of making plays,” he said.
The NFC East-leading Giants don’t always make things easy on themselves, which is probably why they still have their fair share of doubters. Currently slotted as the third seed in the NFC postseason race, the Giants have a 50% chance of making the postseason for the first time since 2022.
But Harbaugh, unfazed, believes his first Giants team has as good a chance as any team to make some noise, and he’s not quaking in his boots about the tough opponent Big Blue faces next weekend when it hosts the Jacksonville Jaguars.
“It’s pretty obvious that we can make plays on both sides of the ball. We’re chasing consistency, just like every single team in this league is chasing consistency,” he said.
“The so-called heavyweights, I’ve seen them play bad games too. I’ve seen them have plenty of bad plays. There’s no perfect team in this league. Is that pretty obvious to everybody? This is a tough league. It’s pretty even. We’re in it just like everybody else. We’ll be fighting there just like everybody else.”

title: Why Giants Fans Should Be Rooting for the 49ers on Sunday
full_text:
Whether you’re enjoying a rare autumn Sunday without New York Giants football or you’re tuned into the slate of games, if there is one game Big Blue’s faithful might want to keep tabs on, it’s the San Francisco 49ers at Dallas Cowboys clash.
If the Cowboys (4-5) pull off the upset over the 49ers (7-1), that moves Dallas to 5-5, with a game the following week against the Tennessee Titans, who were 1-7 at the start of Sunday’s 10 games.
The 5-3-1 Giants, who lost to the Washington Commanders 24-21 on Thursday night, host the Jacksonville Jaguars, 6-2, at the start of Sunday’s slate.
New York, however, does hold the head-to-head tiebreaker over Dallas thanks to the teams’ Week 1 game. Still, the circumstances can quickly change who is at the top of the NFC East if the Cowboys upset the 49ers.
However, if the Cowboys lose this week, they fall to 4-6, and the Giants, who have the head-to-head tiebreaker, will gain more cushion in their division lead, which should carry them into early December.
The Giants, per Tankathon, have the seventh-most difficult remaining schedule, with their upcoming opponents holding a combined .543 winning percentage.
Dallas, meanwhile, has the 14th-most difficult remaining schedule, with its upcoming opponents holding a combined .507 winning percentage at the start of Week 10’s games.
The Cowboys and 49ers kick off their game at 4:25 p.m. ET.

title: Giants Face Stretch of Tough Opponents, but Harbaugh Says Expectation Stays the Same
full_text:
The good news for the New York Giants is that they still lead the NFC East with a 5-3-1 record. Their wins have come against teams that, except for the Los Angeles Rams, all had losing records heading into their Week 10 games.
The bad news is that things are about to get real for the Giants, schedule-wise. New York is set to face teams with winning records in five of its next six games: Jacksonville, San Francisco, Seattle, Cleveland and Detroit (with a Week 12 game against the struggling Colts sandwiched in there).
Four of those five opponents, except Cleveland, rank in the top 10 league-wide in point differential. Jacksonville is the runaway leader at +108 heading into Sunday’s Week 10 games.
The Giants aspire to win the NFC East despite their 24-21 loss to Washington on Thursday night. If they also hope to hang around in the postseason once they get there, the quality of opponents they’re about to face over the next few weeks will make for a good litmus test of what this group is really made of for head coach John Harbaugh and company.
Harbaugh said his confidence is high in every opponent they face and in their chances of winning, noting that the expectation is to win every single game.
“Every game that we go into play, we’re taking the field planning to win,” he said. “We’ll be preparing that way, and that’s what we’ll be doing. We’re going to win as many of them as we can. If we win them all, we win them all, but we’ll win as many as we can.”
And lest anyone think the pressure to win against the tougher opponents is any higher for the Giants at 5-3-1 than it would be if they were 6-2-1, it is not.
“We don’t live in that scared world. I said it was an important game before the game for that very reason. But now you don’t sit back and go, ‘Oh no, we’ve got to beat a heavyweight or whatever you want to call it,’” he said.
“It’s the National Football League. We’re planning on going out there, playing, and winning the game. So we don’t look at it from that perspective.”
In other words, it doesn’t matter what record the opponent brings to the table when it comes up on the Giants’ schedule. The stats don’t matter either.
“These guys are going to go play the game. They’re not going to go into the game saying, ‘Oh man, this is going to be a tough one for us to win,’” Harbaugh said.
“They’re all tough to win. Every single one of these games is going to be a big challenge. Every single one of these games is going to be really hard to win. It’s tough to win football games in this league. I think we all understand that, don’t we?
“So we’re going to be fighting in every single one of those games to win every single one of those games when they come up, starting with the Jacksonville game. That will be our focus. We’re going to expect to win the game.”

title: Giants’ Sneak Over Tush Push Call Remains a Head-Scratcher
full_text:
Most New York Giants fans agree that the team’s decision to run a quarterback sneak on a 3rd-and-1 rather than a classic tush push in its 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders was a head-scratcher.
And apparently, if the stats are to be believed, the questions are justified. According to TushPush.fyi , the Giants have run three tush push plays this season, all of which were successful.
What about quarterback sneaks? Per PFF’s advanced data , quarterback Jameis Winston ranks fourth among quarterbacks with 11 sneaks, and his eight first downs on sneaks also rank fourth in the league.
Given the success of the tush push, then, why not go for that play on 3rd-and-short rather than a sneak?
There are a couple of potential reasons. The first, as head coach John Harbaugh noted to the media on Friday, is that the offensive line did a much better job run-blocking against a banged-up Washington defensive front.
While Harbaugh didn’t say much, perhaps offensive coordinator Matt Nagy felt more confident calling for a sneak than a tush push, given how the offensive line was blocking.
Statistically, the Giants averaged 4.3 yards per rush attempt against Washington, with two rushing touchdowns in the loss. Against the Eagles, they struggled to run the ball, averaging 2.6 yards per carry without Cam Skattebo, who was inactive.
In addition, against the Eagles, the Giants had eight rushing attempts that went for zero or negative yards. Against Washington, they had only two such unsuccessful attempts.
Along those lines, the Giants averaged 4.16 yards per attempt on rushes between the tackles in the loss to Washington. In contrast, against Philadelphia, they averaged 2.2 yards per attempt between the tackles.
All that being said, the question of how they decide between a sneak and a tush push is the one Harbaugh sidestepped when it was put to him on Friday.
“We have four or five of those different types of calls and motions and pushes—not pushes, check-with-me plays. There are different things that we have. One of those was called,” he said.
“We have different calls that go with quarterback sneaks, so we didn’t call the same one that we’ve been calling. That’s really the only answer I have for you.”
The other unanswered question is whether Winston checked out of a play. Asked about the 3rd-and-1 on which Skattebo stayed in the backfield for almost two seconds, Harbaugh clarified that the play “was a normal quarterback sneak and a certain check involved in it that is part of the play.”
The bottom line is that the play, regardless of what was called versus what was executed, failed to convert. It could be one that Nagy wishes he had back, and he will almost certainly be asked about it the next time the coordinators speak with the media on Thursday.
That play itself isn’t why the Giants lost, but it added to a night of frustration for fans who were expecting a Big Blue win in a critical divisional game.

title: The Inches That Are Affecting Giants’ Rookie Kicker Dominic Zvada's FGAs
full_text:
The New York Giants head coach is not ready to give up on rookie placekicker Dominic Zvada despite the former Michigan kicker’s inconsistencies over the last few weeks, which have seen him go 8-for-14 after making his first nine field-goal attempts.
Zvada’s recent woes have come from the right hash, including his lone 33-yard field goal attempt that sailed wide left in the Giants’ 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday night. That 33-yard miss was his first under 40 yards this season.
“There’s a technique issue there with his plant foot that we’re kind of looking at,” head coach John Harbaugh said on Friday. “And he needs to clean that up from a consistency standpoint. He knows that. Popped up again in that one kick there. I had a chance to watch it this morning. There is an issue on the right hash, no question.”
Harbaugh didn’t go into detail on what the issue is with Zvada’s plant foot, but according to retired Giants kicker Lawrence Tynes, the issue may be that Zvada’s plant foot is too deep and close to the ball.
Tynes, in a social media post on Oct. 14 referencing one of the rookie’s misses from the right hash, said Zvada’s plant foot is “too deep and close to the ball.”
He added, “Out in front and close to the ball can cause you to hook or push it.”
One on left is a make. Ankle in plant leg is lined up with the ball. This is good. One on the right is a miss. Plant foot is too deep and close to the ball. Out in front and close to the ball can cause you to hook or push it. Not good. Can be caused by trying to go too hard… pic.twitter.com/q6diGyURZL
Tynes further explained that Zvada’s issue in front of the ball can be caused by trying to go too hard at the ball to create power on longer kicks. “You get too deep and close with the plant. We are talking about inches here.”
Assistant head coach and special teams coordinator Chris Horton told reporters last month, after Zvada’s struggles on Washington’s wet grass field, that the playing surface can also affect a young kicker’s effectiveness.
“Footing is definitely a lot different,” he said. “Obviously, the turf, your plant foot sticks a little bit; it sticks a little bit better. When you’re on grass and things like that, your foot might slide a little bit more.”
Tynes, who called himself “a huge fan” of Zvada’s, endorses the patient approach Harbaugh and the Giants are taking, despite any frustration over the lost points.
“He is an elite talent learning how to become a consistent NFL kicker,” Tynes told New York Giants On SI .
“His leg talent does not grow on trees. He has more talent in his pinky toe than I ever had. Patience is required.”

title: Aaron Glenn's Biggest Mistake vs. Bills (And What Jets Need to Change in Week 11)
full_text:
Despite making it competitive in the first half, the Jets once again failed to keep pace throughout Week 10 as they suffered a 31-12 loss to the Bills , dropping their fifth consecutive game as the season continues to unravel from them.
The Jets were even the healthiest they have been in a long time coming into the game and seemed ready to at least put up a compelling fight. That quickly proved to not be the case as rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. exited early after getting his right ankle rolled on and quarterback Geno Smith left the game twice after getting evaluated for a concussion and suffering an ankle injury after he returned.
While the special teams unit did its part and kicker Jason Sanders was a perfect 4-of-4 on his field goals, the same issues remained in the injury-riddled loss to the Bills . The Jets kept it close in the first half and only trailed 10-6 going into the break, but they were just 3-of-13 on third down, 0-of-2 in the red zone, committed seven penalties for 53 yards and allowed four sacks.
Aside from the two drives that ended in made field goals from Sanders in the second half, the Jets punted twice, threw an interception, committed a fumble and turned it over on downs. To make matters worse, the fumble took place as they were nearing the red zone, trailing 24-12.
The Bills immediately made them pay as running back James Cook broke free for a 74-yard touchdown run on the next play (h/t NFL).
74-YARD TD FOR JAMES COOK BUFvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/DFRLVP17FL
From head coach Aaron Glenn's lack of adjustments coming out of the locker room to his conservative nature as he continues to settle for field goals, the same problems continue to plague the Jets each week.
He has made it clear that play-calling is his "superpower," but Glenn has done nothing to back that notion up so far and even gave his play-calling to defensive coordinator Brian Duker, who had zero prior experience calling plays. That is just the latest bad look for a HC who is now 5-22 in Gotham and 0-9 against AFC East opponents.
That said, here's the biggest mistake that Glenn made on Sunday.
Coming into the game, it was going to be key for the defense to create pressure on Bills QB Josh Allen and keep him from using his mobility to make them pay. While they limited his production on the ground (five carries for five yards), he still had three total TDs (two rushing) and was only sacked once.
The Jets knew beforehand that Buffalo had the highest-scoring offense in the league (31.9 ppg) and a susceptible pass defense (241.9 ypg), so it was going to be important for them to be as aggressive as possible offensively to keep pace and limit the big plays defensively.
Not only were the Jets 0-of-2 in the red zone, but they got inside the 10-yard-line twice and even advanced the ball to the four-yard-line before settling for field goals both times. Instead of trying to tie the game at 10 before the half and going for the lead coming out of the break, the Jets played not to lose again and paid the price as the Bills converted their drives into TDs.
As a result, the Jets were playing from behind the entire game and it only seemed like a matter of time until the Bills pulled away. That is exactly what happened as Cook and the run game combined for 201 yards and 6.3 yards per carry to wear the defense down.
Glenn noted that "it's hard to win games when you operate that way," per Sports Illustrated's Nick Faria, when referring to the decision to opt for field goals.
It remains to be seen if Glenn takes back over the play-calling duties or not, but as poor as the second-half adjustments continue to be on that side, the lack of aggressiveness in short-yardage situations and heavy reliance on field goals is not going to cut it with a 2-8 record.
As the Jets prepare for a two-game road trip against the Chargers on Sunday and the Dolphins on Nov. 29, you would think that would be a favorable stretch for them against two of the bottom-dwelling teams in the league. Sure, the Dolphins beat them back in Week 7, but these should be two winnable games for Gang Green regardless if they play to their potential.
As a team that struggles with turnovers, protecting QB Justin Herbert and ranks last in scoring offense, the opportunity is in front of the Jets to capitalize on those vulnerabilities on Sunday. In addition to eliminating the self-inflicting penalties and getting more aggressive when points are available, Glenn needs to commit to a defensive play-caller and get his group to generate more pressure.
DC Brian Duker: "our group has really embraced our approach" pic.twitter.com/5ZA3HgfQia
Glenn and offensive coordinator Frank Reich need to make sure the best players are continuously being fed the ball, as well as getting off to quicker starts to set the tone from the opening kick. Additionally, the aggressiveness on both sides needs to be a priority, whether it be more disguises or pressure looks defensively or more explosiveness offensively.
Glenn continues to sink lower as his time remaining in Gotham runs thin, and if he cannot be more adaptable throughout the game and ramp up his aggressiveness, it is hard to see much changing.

title: Geno Smith Injury Makes Drafting a QB an Even Bigger Jets Priority in 2027
full_text:
On top of everything else that went wrong on Sunday, Geno Smith suffered an ankle injury after taking a hit to his lower body in the Jets' 31-12 loss to the Bills. The 36-year-old quarterback played only one drive in the second half, ceding the rest to rookie Cade Klubnik.
While Smith's injury may not end his season, questions remain.
Smith was a long shot to be anything more than a bridge quarterback. The Jets' record and Smith injury make that fact painfully obvious. With Smith's expiring contract and Klubnik behind him, New York will have to start worrying about what to do at the position.
With three first-round picks in the 2027 draft, the Jets must decide whether to use any of them on a QB.
Smith is not getting any younger. The QB is also only on a one-year, veteran minimum contract. Smith's injury is unfortunate if he misses time, but it might be a sign that the answer to the Jets' woes is still out there. When Klubnik was on the field, it was very clear what Smith has been lacking.
Smith is clearly one of the elder statesmen at the quarterback position. He is a Honda in a league full of Ferraris, serviceable but leagues away from other top QBs. Smith lacks escapability, as shown by his taking the third-most sacks in the league in 2026. That was even more evident once Klubnik took his place in Week 10.
Cade Klubnik's first NFL pass is a completion to Garrett Wilson! BUFvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Cyxg8tuqzq
Klubnik brought movement into the pocket immediately. The rookie had 26 rushing yards against Buffalo. Smith has 54 rushing yards for the whole season. Mobility at quarterback is crucial in today's NFL, and Smith clearly lacks it. His injury proves that point further.
Whether or not Smith misses extended time, his inability to escape the pocket has been a bane to the Jets' offensive success.
At 36, Smith was never supposed to be the franchise quarterback. Despite his success throwing the football this season, his age has shown in his play. With his lack of mobility leading to an injury, it's evident the Jets must start thinking about which young buck is going to take his place in 2027.
The bad news is the Jets are in the NFL's cellar with a 2-8 record. The good news is that they currently hold two picks in the first six picks of the draft . This would give New York an opportunity to do something it hasn't since 2021: draft a QB in the first round.
With Smith's injury, depending how severe it might be, this may become an even higher priority.
Klubnik had flashes on the field, but he looked like what he was: a fourth-round pick. Between an interception, some accuracy issues, and holding the ball too long, Klubnik didn't look like the savior Gang Green has been waiting for. While he figures to get more time to stake his claim, Klubnik has a mountain to climb if he wants to change minds about drafting high at the position.
Smith's injury has shown that Klubnik isn't ready to take the helm of an NFL franchise just yet. The rookie showed talent, but the project seems longer than that of a top-five pick. Smith's injury could mean the Jets may have to invest come April if they are looking for a franchise savior.

title: Jets' Aaron Glenn Problems Run Much Deeper Than the Surface
full_text:
It was a mistake the moment Jets head coach Aaron Glenn uttered those words.
At the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine in Indianapolis, Glenn defended his decision to call plays for the defense this year. Glenn claimed play-calling was his "superpower" and was excited to pass along the success he found in Detroit to New York.
Perhaps that was the first indicator that things would not go well for the Jets this season.
Glenn's Jets are 2-8 following their dismal 31-12 loss to the Buffalo Bills on Sunday. It was also the first game Glenn seemed to give up play-calling to defensive coordinator Brian Duker—the same man the team was confident in believing they wouldn't need to turn to for those duties.
Aaron Glenn’s “superpower” for the #Jets lasted 10 weeks. Brian Duker calling plays for the team on Sunday is further a bad look for this current defensive staff.
There are many reasons why the Glenn era has failed. But his play-calling decisions and struggles to get the most out of his talented rookie class show that his 5-22 head coaching record is only the surface of his problems.
Glenn announced on Monday that Duker was the one who actually called plays. He also didn't commit to calling plays in the future for the remainder of the season.
"I gave Duker the lead when it comes to that, but again, I'm still a huge part of what we call," Glenn said. "There's been a collaboration throughout the whole season, to be honest with you. I had the lead the first game going up until this point, and this game, I wanted to give him the lead."
There are different ways to look at this decision from Glenn.
All these three options are more alarming than the next. And it also highlights the full failings of Glenn as a coach. The open bravado he first displayed to the media and fans is long gone. Instead, they have been replaced by a coach unable to answer questions his team has.
And it's only compounding the issues the team is dealing with.
The Jets simply don't know how to use the talent currently on their roster. That much was clear by the end of the first month of the regular season, and it's gotten worse since.
New York made four draft selections inside the first 50 overall picks. Each player has had an impressive play or game to show the team has quality things to build on with this young core.
There's just one problem—these small plays aren't being built up like they should.
In Sunday's loss, second-round cornerback D'Angelo Ponds received just seven defensive snaps compared to 28 for third safety Malachi Moore. Ponds was the third-highest-graded Jets defender by Pro Football Focus, compared to Moore, whose 28.6 grade was the lowest on the team.
" He's still not there yet , and I think he would tell you the same thing, but he's improving every week," Glenn said on Monday.
Turn your attention to the offensive side, and the confusion is even more so. 16th overall pick and rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq caught one pass all game—a screen pass on the first play on offense. The play went for three yards and led to the injury of fellow first-round pick Omar Cooper Jr.
Why was Cooper—a player dealing with an ankle injury going into the game—blocking on a screen pass that can see players get rolled up on consistently? Why did the Jets only target Sadiq once on a screen?
These are questions the Jets haven't had answers to. Their most consistent defense, though, is that there "is only one ball to go around."
But do the San 49ers have trouble getting the ball to Christian McCaffrey, George Kittle, Mike Evans, Keenan Allen or their full collection of receivers? Of course not. Because their play-caller understands matchups and is able to scheme people open. New York's staff cannot.
And that is a direct reflection of how poor they have been under Glenn this season.

title: Handing Out 5 Jets Awards After Another Humiliating Divisional Loss in Week 10
full_text:
If you've seen one Jets game this season, you've seen them all .
On Sunday, the Jets crumbled in the second half against the rival Bills, leading to a 31-12 blowout loss. The loss drops New York to 2-8 on the season and winless across the division for the second straight year.
With seven games remaining in the 2026 regular season and a coaching staff that appears to be in the final months of the job, the Jets have little to look forward to for the remainder of the season.
In Sunday's loss, though, there were still plenty of awards to give out.
New York became the second team this century to lose back-to-back games by over 17 points despite having four or more scoring drives in each game. New York has competed hard in almost every game it has played this season.
Despite the clear competitiveness, the Jets keep finding ways to lose. The loss to the Bills is Gang Green's eighth in their last nine games and fifth in a row. It feels like fans have watched the same game in each contest as well.
In the first half of these losses, just as was the case on Sunday, New York competed and seemed on even footing. Their offense was moving the ball consistently, and their defense kept getting stops.
Then, in the second half, there would be coverage breakdowns, missed tackles, broken blocks, and mental mistakes.
This is all a sign of a failure of coaching , but no one is really surprised at this point. If anything, the Jets' struggles on Sunday are just further reason to eventually move on from their current staff.
Every game appears to be the same for the Jets, but one positive constant has been the improved play of their young core. On Sunday, many of New York's true stars came out to perform well.
There was Breece Hall recording 100 yards from scrimmage, Braelon Allen averaging over five yards per carry, Garrett Wilson recording a seven-catch, 100-yard game, and even received four clutch receptions from Mason Taylor. New York didn't get enough from their rookies, but that had more to do with coaching than a lack of execution.
Kenyon Sadiq was targeted on a screen in the first play of the game, but wasn't targeted again. Meanwhile, Omar Cooper Jr. suffered an ankle injury on that same screen play and did not play for the remainder of the game.
Omar Cooper’s right ankle gets yet another high ankle mechanism. Third time it’s been injured since Week 1 now. Likely misses multiple weeks with this one pic.twitter.com/sPRPYOtEe7
New York's stars are still good. The Jets' rookies are talented, but obviously need to be a focal point as well.
There was no better example of what the Aaron Glenn era has been like for the Jets than a two-play sequence late in the contest.
With five minutes to play and the offense driving, New York called a hook-and-ladder play from Wilson to another receiver. Except Wilson's lateral was woefully short and inaccurate, causing a fumble and turnover for the Bills' defense. On the very next play, James Cook ran for a 74-yard touchdown.
From the positive outlook of a drive to a fumble on a ridiculous play-call to an immediate long touchdown run.
Glenn's 5-22 record as a head coach and 0-9 record against the AFC East are reasons why he won't get a third year. But this two-play run is as bad as it gets in NFL history.
The new drought stands at nine. That is, nine straight quarters that the Jets have failed to score a touchdown. The drought extends all the way to their loss against the Raiders, when they were held to a field goal in the fourth quarter. In that game, New York's last touchdown came with eight minutes left in the f
New York kept that field goal mindset going into their last two games. Each time the Jets have been in a difficult situation in which they needed to be aggressive, Glenn and the offense opted to take points instead.
That's always a nice sentiment to make... if your defense is among the best in the league. Instead, New York's defense has been inconsistent all year, and they are simply not good enough to "go for points" in games against Patrick Mahomes or Josh Allen.
Glenn wants his team to play a certain way, but they don't coach or play like the identity makes much sense. And that's why you get most of these games of maddening conservatism.
Unlike in weeks past, the Jets did not get help from other teams around the league when it comes to their draft position. The biggest game of the day, outside of their own loss, came in Indianapolis, where the Colts found a way to hold on to a 24-22 win over the Miami Dolphins.
Miami missed several PATs including a would-be game-winning 54-yarder field goal late in the fourth quarter.
If the season ended today, New York would own the 4th and 6th picks inside the top 10. That's the exact same spot they had last week, but the important update here is that their own pick is at four overall, and Indy's is at six.
If the Dolphins can win a few more games and the Titans beat the Colts again, the Jets could be within striking distance of a top-two pick. Until then, though, there's no reason to hide that Sunday was a disappointment outside of their own game for the Jets.

title: Faria's Focus Week 10: 5 Jets Thoughts After Sunday's Blowout Loss to Bills at Home
full_text:
For a team that is 2-8 and on the cusp of another head coaching search, the Jets keep finding new ways to play the same football game over and over.
Gang Green's 31-12 defeat at the hands of the Bills on Sunday was similar to the other eight losses on their schedule this year: the Jets kept it close early, but ultimately crumbled in key areas down the stretch.
While it may seem like we're talking about the same things over and over, it's only due to the Jets' striking resemblance to other losses earlier in the year.
Let's break down some of the biggest thoughts and takeaways from New York's Week 10 defeat.
There's no saving the Glenn era in New York. That fact may have been well established before Sunday's loss, but it was only exacerbated by what happened.
Let's start at the top. Following the victory, Bills head coach Joe Brady explained the team's outlook from the first half to the second. His answer was a resounding indictment of the Jets' defense, their coaching staff, and plans moving forward.
“You knew it was going to be a tight game, a tough game in the first half, and we were going to be able to make adjustments and kind of wear on a team for the final 30 minutes,” Brady said.
In short, the Bills knew that the Jets would keep it close but wouldn't be able to adjust to their first-half plan, and understood they would dominate them on the ground in the second half. That's exactly what happened as well. Glenn's defensive plans were proven inconsequential in Sunday's loss. The rest of the NFL knows it.
Then there's the update on Monday morning.
Glenn announced that he actually gave play-calling to defensive coordinator Brian Duker during the game. The man who called play-calling his "superpower" had taken that power away after just 10 games.
Aaron Glenn’s “superpower” for the #Jets lasted 10 weeks. Brian Duker calling plays for the team on Sunday is further a bad look for this current defensive staff.
There's really no other way to put it. Glenn has been one of the worst coaches in recent memory for the Jets. His 5-22 record overall and 0-9 mark in the division tell the story. But as NFL teams speak out about the Jets' struggles, it's obvious that Glenn's' reputation across the league isn't as high as many would have thought.
New York's defense is an unmitigated disaster. The Jets are ranked third-worst in the league in rushing yards allowed, 22nd in points allowed, and their EPA is now 29th. Against Buffalo, the defense tried to get bigger by adding a third safety into the mix.
It didn't work. Buffalo still ran for over 200 yards against them. A big reason for that is the struggling play of their linebacker room. Demario Davis and Jamien Sherwood collectively have not played well enough together. Davis, in particular, has been a shell of the elite player he once was.
And as a captain of the team, he's had to wear the brunt of those struggles.
On Sunday, Davis was one of the worst players on the field for New York. Pro Football Focus graded his play at a struggling 34.6 . Sherwood, meanwhile, was better, but not nearly good enough to warrant his current contract.
Davis is still a very strong leader for the Jets, but his on-field play has clearly taken a major step back. It's so alarming at this point that one has to wonder if New York is better off giving more playing time to other younger players at the position.
New York isn't going to be making any changes at quarterback. If anything, rookie Cade Klubnik's performance shows the reason why the team is going to continue to rely on Geno Smith for the remainder of the season.
Klubnik completed 11-of-20 passes for 137 yards and an interception. Within the context of this being his first real taste of NFL action, as well as the Jets seeing Smith go down with an ankle injury during the game, Klubnik was perfectly fine in his debut.
That said, it's also obvious he still has a lot of learning and growing to do at the NFL level. His mobility will be a crutch for him early on, but his anticipation and timing were lacking in a game that he didn't get much prep time for with the starters.
Glenn confirmed on Monday that the team will continue to start Smith so long as he's healthy. That is the right move—especially for an offense that is talented and doesn't want to throw the white flag out just yet, even if they are 2-8.
I'm at a loss as to what the Jets' plans are for their rookie class . Even if Glenn were to miraculously get a third year on the job, I would question what their plans would be for the entire rookie class moving forward.
New York knows they have a budding star in David Bailey and a collection of fun talents to work with in  Omar Cooper Jr., Kenyon Sadiq, Darrell Jackson Jr, and even D'Angelo Ponds. Yet despite all the talent, they are consistently either put in situations that set them up to fail or not used at all.
Once again, I'm left perplexed by the #Jets plans for some of their rookies. - D'Angelo Ponds plays a grand total of 7 snaps - Kenyon Sadiq had one screen target on the first play of the game; Omar Cooper Jr. got hurt, and they never looked his way again. I don't think this…
On Sunday, for example, Ponds saw just seven snaps of action and recorded a quality pass breakup. Sadiq, meanwhile, caught a pass on the first play of the game, accidentally injured Cooper on the play, and never received a target again.
Glenn made it clear before the season started that his coaching staff had plans for all the rookies on the team. It is obvious, though, after 10 weeks , that they remain unwilling or unable to get the most out of their players.
The unequivocal good news for the Jets is that their chances for a top-five pick remain unchanged after Sunday. Despite the Colts beating the Dolphins thanks to three missed kicks by the Dolphins, New York owns the fourth and sixth overall draft picks if the season ended today.
It obviously doesn't, but the Jets should feel good about where they are.
First, their next two games against the Chargers and Dolphins are teams the Jets should beat but have had problems beating for years now. Most fans can foresee a situation where the winless Chargers get a victory over their Jets. New York is 0-9 in the division under Glenn, so a win in South Florida isn't exactly a foregone conclusion either.
The Jets have everything in front of them if they are looking to draft a quarterback in the 2027 class.
