title: Vernon Davis Q&A: Jayden Daniels, Redskins Homecoming and Life After Football
full_text:
Vernon Davis spent much of his NFL career away from Washington, but that's where his football story began. He grew up in the city, played at Dunbar High School and Maryland, and eventually returned home to finish his career in a Redskins uniform. Between those stops came the sixth overall pick in the 2006 NFL Draft, two Super Bowl appearances, and a championship with Denver. There is plenty of football to talk about, including how much the tight end position has changed, what Davis sees in Jayden Daniels, and what he learned during his years in Washington. But retirement hasn't exactly slowed him down. These days, Davis is acting, producing films, and pursuing an entirely different kind of career. In a Q&A interview with Commanders On SI, Davis answered questions about his NFL career, the modern game, his retirement, and his work in Hollywood. Here is the full exchange, organized by topic.
Philip Hughes : You came into the NFL as the sixth overall pick at a time when taking a tight end that high was unusual. When you watch the position in today's NFL, what has changed the most from the position you entered in 2006? Vernon Davis : When I came into the league in 2006, the tight end position was still viewed primarily as a guy who could block and make plays in the passing game when his number was called. I was fortunate to come in with the mindset that I could do both, but I also knew I was part of a changing position. The biggest difference today is how much the tight end has become a featured weapon in an offense. Teams are moving tight ends around the formation, lining them up in the slot, out wide, in the backfield—basically treating them like oversized receivers who can also block. The athleticism at the position has really taken off. When I watch today’s game, I see tight ends being asked to do things that weren’t as common when I entered the league. They’re creating mismatches against linebackers and safeties, stretching the field vertically and becoming major parts of the passing game. The position has evolved tremendously. That’s something I’m proud to have been a part of. When I was drafted sixth overall, there was a lot of discussion about whether a tight end should go that high. Today, I think people have a much better understanding of the impact an elite, versatile tight end can have on an offense. Philip Hughes : Your combination of size and speed was considered unusual when you entered the league. If a 22-year-old Vernon Davis entered the NFL today, how do you think an offensive coordinator would use him differently? Vernon Davis : I’d be a matchup problem every single week . They’d move me all over the formation and force defenses to decide how they wanted to cover me. If you put a linebacker on me, I’d take advantage of the speed. Put a safety on me, I’d use my size. The goal would be simple: create mismatches and get the ball in my hands. Philip Hughes : We hear so much now about tight ends being "matchup weapons," but the position still requires players to block defensive ends and linebackers. In your mind, what separates a great receiving tight end from a truly complete tight end? Vernon Davis : To me, a great tight end is somebody who can catch the ball and make big plays. But a complete tight end is somebody who can do it all. You’ve got to be willing to put your face in there and block a defensive end, block a linebacker, do the dirty work—even when you know you’re not getting the ball. That’s what separates you. You have to be a football player first. If you can block, catch, run and create mismatches, you’re a complete tight end. Philip Hughes : Which tight ends playing today do you enjoy watching most, and what specifically do you see in their games that you appreciate as someone who played the position? Vernon Davis : I love watching George Kittle. That guy plays with an attitude. He’s physical, he’ll block, he’ll catch the ball, and when he gets it in his hands, he’s looking to make something happen. I see a lot of the things I loved about playing the position in him. I also like Trey McBride. He’s got that toughness and versatility you want in a tight end. He’s not just out there trying to catch passes—he’s willing to do the dirty work, too. As a former tight end, that’s what I appreciate. I like watching guys who play the position like football players, not just big receivers. Philip Hughes : Defenses have become faster and more versatile since you played. Has that made life harder for tight ends, or has the way offenses create mismatches actually made the position more valuable? Vernon Davis : I think it’s made the tight end more valuable. Defenses are faster and more versatile, but that just creates more opportunities for a tight end who can do it all. If you can run, catch, and block, you’re a problem. Every time you line up, the defense has to make a decision—and that’s where you create the mismatch. Philip Hughes : From a tight end's perspective, what can the position provide a quarterback that a wide receiver or running back simply can't? Vernon Davis : I think it’s the versatility. As a tight end, you can help your quarterback in a lot of different ways. You can stay in and block, you can protect him, or you can release and go make a play down the field. And because you’re bigger than a receiver but can still run, you can create some real problems for a defense. When your quarterback knows you can do whatever the play needs, that’s a big advantage.
Philip Hughes : Washington currently has different types of tight ends in Chig Okonkwo, John Bates, Ben Sinnott and Colson Yankoff. How valuable is it for an offense to have tight ends with complementary skill sets instead of asking one player to do everything? Vernon Davis : I think it’s huge. You don’t have to have one guy trying to do everything. You can have a guy who’s really good at blocking, another guy who can go make plays in the passing game, and guys who can do a little bit of both. That gives your offense a lot of flexibility and makes it harder for the defense to know what’s coming. When you have a tight end room like that, everybody has a role, and you can play to each guy’s strengths. Philip Hughes : Okonkwo is an explosive athlete whose ability after the catch is one of the strengths Washington wants to utilize. When you have a tight end with that kind of speed, what are the best ways to create favorable matchups for him? Vernon Davis : You’ve just got to find ways to get him in space . Move him around, put him in the slot, motion him, line him up outside—make the defense figure out who’s going to cover him. Once he catches the ball, just let him do what he does. Get it in his hands and let him make a play. Philip Hughes : Ben Sinnott is now in his third NFL season. Tight end has traditionally been considered one of the more difficult positions to learn. Why can development take longer there, and what tells you that a young tight end is beginning to put everything together? Vernon Davis : It takes time because you’re really learning two positions at once. You’ve got to learn how to block, how to read defenses, how to run routes, and understand the timing with your quarterback. It’s a lot. For me, you know a young tight end is putting it together when the game starts slowing down for him. He’s not thinking about every little thing anymore—he’s just playing. He knows his assignment, he’s confident, and he starts making plays without having to think so much. That’s when you know he’s starting to get it. Philip Hughes : What does playing with two tight ends do to a defense before the snap? From a player's perspective, why can 12 personnel create problems even when neither tight end actually gets the football? Vernon Davis : When you put two tight ends out there, the defense has to think a little more. They’ve got to figure out what you’re doing—are you blocking, are you releasing, are you going in motion? You’re making them make a decision before the ball is…

title: Commanders and Cowboys Are Both Two Games Back. Why Is Dallas Still Second?
full_text:
Dallas scored 40 points Sunday and lost. San Francisco beat the Cowboys 46–40 , dropping them to 4–6. Washington had already done its part with a 24–21 win over the Giants on Thursday. The Commanders got help while they were off, but they’re still third in the NFC East. The difference is winning percentage. The NFL counts a tie as half a win and half a loss , giving Washington the equivalent of 3.5 wins in nine games. That’s a .389 winning percentage. Dallas has four wins in 10 games, or .400. There’s no head-to-head tiebreaker to apply; the Cowboys are still ahead.
Dallas began Sunday a half-game closer to first-place New York than Washington. Now both teams are two games back. That’s the ground the Commanders gained without playing. Dallas hosts Tennessee next Sunday, November 22, at 1 p.m. ET. Washington won’t face Cincinnati until Monday night. If the Cowboys lose, they’ll fall to 4–7 (.364), and the Commanders will move into second place before taking the field. They would still have to keep it. A loss to the Bengals in that scenario would drop Washington to 3–6–1 (.350) and put Dallas back ahead. And if both teams win next week, the Cowboys would remain second by an even thinner margin: .455 to .450. title: Commanders Midseason Report Card: Washington Is Wasting a Plus-Seven Turnover Margin
full_text:
This past Thursday's 24-21 win over the New York Giants gave the Washington Commanders their third victory in an up-and-down year in which they’re plus-seven in turnover margin but haven't been able to string together consecutive wins. In most seasons, we'd already be talking about the draft, but since the NFC East is still up for grabs, the eight games remaining on Washington's schedule still matter. The following grades are from the first nine games. Quarterbacks: B Jayden Daniels has thrown for 1,499 yards with 10 touchdowns, two interceptions, and a 97.1 passer rating in seven games, and has 280 rushing yards and two TDs in 42 rushing attempts. Both picks came against New York, which is precisely why his winning drive mattered: the offense had needed him to make up for possessions he had just given away. The elbow injury cost him two full games. Marcus Mariota threw four touchdown passes without an interception and looked good in relief before he reinjured his knee. Rookie Athan Kaliakmanis played in that game and went 15-of-33 for 186 yards, a touchdown, and an interception in London.
Jayden Daniels had an up and down night but came through late against the Giants. 23/33, 249 passing yards, 3 TD, 2 INT, 28 rushing yards. His late touchdown to Stefon Diggs completed the comeback for Washington. pic.twitter.com/NQZgUbb2Vr
Running backs: C− Washington has 1,051 rushing yards. Daniels has 280 of them. Rachaad White leads the actual running backs with 275 yards on 65 carries. Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt had 239 on 67 before his current trip to injured reserve, and Austin Ekeler has 109 on 33 since returning. White and Ekeler have helped as receivers, but the rushing attack hasn't provided a dependable answer when the offense needs a few extra yards. Blocking and play calls share in that result; the group grade reflects the overall production, not a claim that every short run is the back's fault. Wide receivers: B− Stefon Diggs has six of Washington's 15 passing touchdowns. His 36 catches for 386 yards lead the receivers, and the 32-yard winner against the Giants was his biggest play yet in the Burgundy and Gold. Rookie Antonio Williams has 28 catches for 326 yards and two touchdowns. He played 59 of 69 offensive snaps Thursday, more than any other Washington receiver, and has made a case for a starting role beyond this season . Treylon Burks has made 14 catches for 260 yards. Those contributions became more important when Terry McLaurin tore his patellar tendon and was lost for the season. The group has found answers, though it has not made the passing game consistently dangerous. Tight ends: C Chig Okonkwo has 27 catches for 263 yards but no touchdowns. John Bates contributes in the blocking game, where his five receptions don't tell much of the story. Ben Sinnott had one catch this season before Thursday . He caught four passes for 42 yards and a touchdown against the Giants, giving Daniels another option when the offense needed one. It was the tight ends' most encouraging recent development. One game does not rewrite what the group did over the previous eight. Offensive line: C− The center situation has supplied the clearest snapshot of the season. Lucas Patrick left the Rams game with a concussion. Rookie Matt Gulbin finished it, and Nick Allegretti started against the Giants after playing just two offensive snaps since Week 3. Washington allowed four sacks against Los Angeles. Allegretti played all 69 offensive snaps Thursday. The line gave Daniels much better protection in the rematch, allowing one sack and four pressures, although Brandon Coleman added another false start. Washington has allowed 21 sacks over nine games, with three players taking snaps at center. Sam Cosmi has played above the group’s C− grade. He has allowed just five pressures on 297 pass-blocking snaps. At Washington’s nine-game mark, PFF ranked him fifth among guards in pass-blocking grade—All-Pro-caliber work in that part of the game. The Giants' performance is the standard to build on, but it's not enough by itself to erase the earlier questions about the center plan. Defensive front: B− Odafe Oweh has five sacks, and K'Lavon Chaisson has 3½. Chaisson has also forced three fumbles. The team has 18 sacks and has allowed 934 rushing yards, roughly 104 per game. The run defense gives this grade some weight. Washington held Dallas to 66 rushing yards in Week 2 and Seattle to 44 the following week. Oweh had a sack, forced fumble, and recovery against Indianapolis. Daron Payne added a sack and forced fumble in the first meeting with the Giants. Chaisson has made that kind of play in three different games. The front has given the Commanders more than its sack total alone shows. The interior has changed since those early games. Payne and Javon Kinlaw went on injured reserve after Week 8, putting more on Shy Tuttle and Tim Settle as Jer’Zhan Newton returned from a torn pectoral muscle. Tuttle has two sacks, including one in the five-sack win over Philadelphia. Dorance Armstrong forced a fumble in that game that Charles Omenihu recovered. Five of Washington’s 18 sacks came against the Eagles; the other eight games produced 13 combined. The work against the run and the turnover plays earn the B−. The uneven sack production keeps it from going higher. Linebackers: B Sonny Styles leads Washington with 80 tackles. Frankie Luvu has 55 and two sacks. Styles’ 13 tackles against the Giants included a crucial third-down stop after Daniels’ second interception. He recognized the play before the snap , dropped McCarthy for a two-yard loss and forced a punt. Without it, there might not have been a final winning drive. Leo Chenal's season-ending neck injury removed an expected piece of the rotation. When Chenal went down against Seattle, Kain Medrano returned an interception 50 yards for a touchdown in a 33-31 win, on a play Styles called out at the line. Styles and Luvu have carried substantial work since. They have been among Washington's best answers on defense.
Sonny Styles’ INSANE play recognition led to his game-saving tackle against the Giants. The Commanders rookie LB is one of the SMARTEST apex predators in the NFL 😳🧠 pic.twitter.com/JCqOTPBNTc
Secondary: D Opponents have thrown for 2,341 yards in nine games. Isaiah Likely caught 11 passes for 94 yards and two touchdowns in the first Giants meeting. Puka Nacua caught 14 passes for 150 yards against Washington . Four days later, Likely went for nine catches and 127 yards, with 66 coming on a third-and-seven touchdown. Nick Cross has played better than the group grade suggests. Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones has moved him between deep safety, the box, and nickel , and Dan Quinn praised his nickel work after the Eagles win. Cross played all 75 defensive snaps against the Rams, finishing with eight tackles, three passes defensed, an interception, and a fumble recovery. He added six tackles and a quarterback hit while playing all 65 defensive snaps against the Giants. Rasul Douglas has three interceptions, and Trey Amos has returned to a significant role. Coverage, rush, and calls all affect a passing total. The repeated large games by opposing targets still make this the lowest grade among Washington’s position groups. Special teams: C+ Drew Stevens has been successful on 17 of 20 field goals and connected from 57 yards. He is 15-for-18 on extra points, with one of the failed attempts recorded as blocked. Those PATs have to be part of the grade, with the operation on each miss considered before assigning individual blame. Tress Way is averaging 48.7 yards on 40 punts. Luke McCaffrey has given the return game some life, including a 44-yard kickoff return against Philadelphia. The unit has produced field position. Its placekicking has been less even than the field-goal number alone suggests. Coaching: D+ The numbers Dan Quinn and David Blough can't talk around are the 40 conversions in 120 third-down attempts. title: Commanders Safety Quan Martin Fined $17,911 for Unflagged Hit vs. Rams
full_text:
The NFL fined Washington Commanders safety Quan Martin $17,911 for a hit on Tutu Atwell that officials did not flag in the 20–13 loss to the Rams . Washington got the third-down stop. Six days later, Martin appeared on the league’s Week 9 fine list for unnecessary roughness, listed as a hit on a defenseless player. The official gamebook places the play at 9:22 of the second quarter. Los Angeles faced third-and-2 at its own 28, and Matthew Stafford went to Atwell over the middle (the play is the second video below in the X embed). The pass fell incomplete, with Martin credited on the play. The Rams punted for the second straight possession. That stop was part of a day when Washington held Los Angeles to 3 of 14 on third down . Luke McCaffrey returned the kick 10 yards to Washington’s 29, and the Commanders moved the chains once before punting it back. Washington led 10–3 at the time.
Then on the next third down, Stafford gets an easy one to his WR. But *doink* its a PBU/drop from Tutu Atwell. pic.twitter.com/yYoNzaYJWi
Had Martin been flagged then, the Rams would have had a first down. Instead, the stop held up in the gamebook, and the fine came later. The NFL reviews every play for potential violations, whether the officials called a penalty or not. Its public list doesn’t spell out what part of Martin’s contact prompted the fine. He can appeal, though the listing doesn’t say whether he will. Former Washington cornerback Emmanuel Forbes also received a fine for a play in that game. The Rams had asked Forbes to do more with Jaylen Watson out before the game. The NFL assessed him $10,839 for a separate second-quarter incident it described as striking, kicking, or kneeing. Officials flagged Forbes at 12:25, giving Washington 15 yards and a first down. title: Commanders Beat Giants, Still Trail Cowboys by Half a Game | NFC East Roundup
full_text:
The Giants had two chances to make Jayden Daniels pay for his fourth-quarter interceptions Thursday night. They went three-and-out both times. Daniels got the ball back, hit Stefon Diggs for the winning touchdown, and Washington left New York with a 24–21 win. The Commanders cut the Giants’ division lead to two games and finished their season series against New York at 1–0–1. Dallas is still between them. If the 49ers beat the Cowboys on Sunday, Dallas falls to 4–6, and Washington gets a little closer to second place without taking the field. title: Commanders Daily: New York Giants Gained 399 Yards but Scored 21. Joe Burrow Is Next
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have held four straight opponents to 23 points or fewer, and Thursday’s 24-21 win over the Giants kept that run going. New York also gained 399 yards , 59 more than Washington, which makes the score a little harder to judge on its own. San Francisco scored 23 against the Commanders, Philadelphia 10 , the Rams 20, and now the Giants 21. That’s an average of 18.5 points over the last four games for Daronte Jones’ defense, but New York had chances to make Thursday’s number much worse. The Giants reached Washington’s red zone four times and scored touchdowns on two of those trips. Through Week 6, opponents had scored touchdowns on 18 of 22 red-zone trips against Washington . In the first quarter, they got to the 15 before the Commanders stopped Cam Skattebo for no gain and J.J. McCarthy threw an incomplete pass on third down. Dominic Zvada missed the ensuing 33-yard field goal wide left. Washington stopped the touchdown, but the missed kick was New York leaving three points on the field. Later, the Giants got back inside the 20, only for Frankie Luvu to punch the ball loose from Malik Nabers at the 16. Jeremy Reaves recovered it, ending another promising New York drive without points.
OUR BALL 📺 #WASvsNYG @nflonprime pic.twitter.com/htMKiTEWHg
Washington also held the Giants to 4-of-12 on third down, including two stops when it couldn't afford to give New York another first down. Jayden Daniels threw interceptions on consecutive fourth-quarter possessions, and the Giants went three-and-out after both . On the second, New York took over at Washington’s 46 with a four-point lead and 2:15 remaining. Skattebo gained seven yards on two runs, but Sonny Styles dropped McCarthy for a two-yard loss on third-and-three. New York punted, giving Daniels the chance he needed to win it. But Isaiah Likely’s nine catches for 127 yards are still on the film, including a 66-yard touchdown on third-and-seven that put New York ahead 21-17. Cincinnati is next, although the Bengals still play Pittsburgh on Sunday night before visiting Washington on November 23. Cincinnati enters this Sunday’s game averaging 30 points, the second most in the NFL , and Joe Burrow has thrown 16 touchdown passes in his last four games. The Commanders have 11 days between games to sort through what worked against New York and what didn’t. They forced a turnover in the red zone and made the late third-down stops they needed Thursday. If Burrow finds the kind of room Likely found, though, Washington may not get away with allowing 399 yards again.

title: Commanders’ Ben Sinnott Had a Career Night on Fewer Snaps. Will the Targets Keep Coming?
full_text:
Coming into this season, the Washington Commanders were hopeful that this was the year tight end Ben Sinnott would break out . Used mainly as a blocker over his first two seasons, he hasn't had the chance to showcase the skill set he displayed while at Kansas State. He entered Thursday night's game against New York with one catch for six yards this season. He finished the game with four catches (on four targets) for 42 yards and a touchdown , setting single-game career highs in catches and yards. The interesting thing is Sinnott did that on 24 offensive snaps, two fewer than he played against the Rams four days earlier. Sinnott played 26 of Washington's 62 snaps (42%) against Los Angeles and was not targeted. The question I've been asking myself since: Why did Jayden Daniels look his way four times Thursday after Washington had barely thrown to him all season? According to RotoWire , Sinnott ran eight routes against the Rams and nine against the Giants. Before Thursday, he’d drawn two targets on 66 routes all season.
Jayden Daniels against a blitzing Abdul Carter? TD to Ben Sinnott #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/UGWVyNTCXK
Sinnott caught a five-yard pass with 11:53 left in the second quarter. Chig Okonkwo was listed as questionable to return with a back injury at 10:23, then returned early in the third quarter. Sinnott got 37 of his 42 yards on two drives that put Washington ahead. Late in the first half, he caught a short pass on second-and-eight and hurdled a defender on his way to a 12-yard gain that brought Washington to the Giants’ 15. Sinnott caught Daniels’ one-yard touchdown pass in traffic on third-and-goal. Washington went into halftime up 10-7. The Giants took a 14-10 lead in the third quarter. On the first play of Washington’s next drive, Daniels hit Sinnott for 24 yards. Antonio Williams finished the drive with a 31-yard touchdown. Despite the back injury, Okonkwo still played 41 snaps and made four catches (on eight targets) for 24 yards. John Bates played 28 snaps, while Colson Yankoff was inactive with a knee injury. Sinnott caught two passes while Okonkwo was out, including the touchdown. His longest catch came after Okonkwo returned. "I got the opportunities tonight," Sinnott said after the game . "I took advantage, and it feels good."
It's good to see the offense finally shine a light on Sinnott; it's that much harder to defend when you can't just assume he's on the field as a blocker. In two-tight-end packages, Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough should give Sinnott a few defined passing-game opportunities on early downs and near the goal line. Blough should continue his approach of giving each tight end their own distinct role , but should also look to take advantage of Sinnott's receiving and after-the-catch ability that, until Thursday night, was going to waste. If Okonkwo is back to his usual workload against Cincinnati, I’ll be watching the snaps he shares with Sinnott. When Washington needs a first down and both tight ends are out there, does Daniels go back to Sinnott?
